title: 奶牛高效种植模式与经济效益分析
text:
High-Efficiency Forage Planting Patterns for Dairy Cows and Their Economic Benefit Analysis: Evidence From Intensive Dairy Farms in Northern China
*Journal of Sustainable Agriculture and Economics, Volume 12, Issue 3, 2024*  
DOI: 10.15302/J-SAE-2024-03-007

---

 Abstract
Rising global demand for dairy products, coupled with volatile feed costs and increasing pressure on agricultural land, has made efficient forage planting systems a critical determinant of dairy farm profitability and sustainability. This study evaluates three dominant high-efficiency forage planting patterns for dairy cows across 217 intensive dairy farms in Hebei, Inner Mongolia, and Shandong provinces (China’s core dairy production belt) between 2021 and 2023: (1) Pattern A: Double-cropping silage corn + winter ryegrass; (2) Pattern B: Alfalfa-silage corn rotation; (3) Pattern C: Monocropping high-yield silage corn (traditional baseline). Using propensity score matching (PSM) to control for selection bias and cost-benefit analysis (CBA) to quantify economic outcomes, we find that Pattern B delivers the highest net return per hectare ($3,287.42/ha/year), 37.2% higher than the baseline Pattern C, followed by Pattern A ($2,891.63/ha/year, 20.7% higher than baseline). Sensitivity analysis shows that Pattern B is more resilient to feed price fluctuations, while Pattern A delivers faster short-term returns for small-scale farms. Key constraints to adoption include high initial alfalfa seeding costs, limited access to high-quality forage seeds, and gaps in technical training for intercropping/rotation management. The study concludes that optimized forage planting patterns can reduce dairy farms’ reliance on purchased commercial feed, cut feed costs by 18–24%, and improve overall economic stability, with targeted policy support needed to scale adoption across small and medium-sized dairy operations.
Keywords: Dairy cow production; Forage planting patterns; Cost-benefit analysis; Propensity score matching; Agricultural intensification; China

---

 1. Introduction
 1.1 Research Background
Global dairy production is projected to grow by 1.6% annually through 2030, driven by rising per capita dairy consumption in low- and middle-income countries (FAO, 2023). For dairy farms, feed costs account for 60–70% of total production expenses, with self-produced forage quality and yield directly determining milk yield, milk composition, and long-term herd health (USDA, 2022). In China, the world’s third-largest dairy producer, structural transformation of the dairy sector over the past decade has seen a shift from smallholder backyard farming to intensive, large-scale operations, but a persistent mismatch between forage planting systems and dairy cow nutritional needs has kept domestic forage self-sufficiency at just 62% as of 2023 (Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of China [MARA], 2023). Over-reliance on imported alfalfa and commercial concentrate feed has exposed Chinese dairy farms to global supply chain disruptions and price volatility, as seen during the 2022 global forage shortage when alfalfa prices rose by 42% year-on-year, reducing average farm profit margins by 11.3% (China Dairy Industry Association [CDIA], 2023).
 1.2 Literature Review
Existing research on dairy forage systems has primarily focused on two strands: agronomic performance of forage varieties and partial cost comparisons of planting models. On the agronomic side, Li et al. (2021) found that double-cropping winter ryegrass and silage corn in northern China can increase annual forage dry matter (DM) yield by 28% compared to monocropped silage corn, while also improving soil organic matter content by 0.12% over three years. For alfalfa-corn rotations, Pikul et al. (2018) demonstrated in the U.S. Corn Belt that rotating alfalfa for 3 years with silage corn reduces nitrogen fertilizer application by 40% and increases corn silage crude protein content by 1.2 percentage points, due to alfalfa’s biological nitrogen fixation capacity.
On the economic side, most existing studies rely on small-scale plot experiments rather than farm-level empirical data. For example, Wang et al. (2022) compared planting costs of three forage patterns at an experimental station in Inner Mongolia, finding that alfalfa-corn rotation had 22% lower unit DM cost than monocropped corn, but did not account for farm-level heterogeneity in management skill, herd scale, or market access. A key gap in the literature is the lack of causal estimates of how different forage planting patterns affect dairy farm profitability, after controlling for endogenous selection of planting models (e.g., larger, better-managed farms may be more likely to adopt efficient planting patterns, creating upward bias in estimated returns).
 1.3 Research Objectives and Hypotheses
This study addresses the above gaps using large-scale farm-level survey data to evaluate the economic performance of high-efficiency dairy forage planting patterns, with three core objectives:
1.  Characterize the agronomic and nutritional performance of three dominant forage planting patterns in China’s northern dairy belt;
2.  Estimate the causal impact of each planting pattern on farm-level cost structure, forage self-sufficiency, and net economic returns, after correcting for selection bias;
3.  Identify barriers to adoption of high-efficiency patterns and provide evidence-based policy recommendations for scaling.
We test two core hypotheses:
*   H1: Rotation and double-cropping forage patterns deliver significantly higher net returns per unit land and per cow than traditional monocropped silage corn, due to higher forage yield, better nutritional quality, and lower input costs;
*   H2: The economic advantage of high-efficiency planting patterns is larger for medium and large-scale dairy farms, which can spread fixed costs of planting equipment and technical management over larger herd sizes.
 1.4 Paper Structure
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the study sites, data sources, and analytical methods, including the PSM framework for causal inference; Section 3 presents the results, including descriptive comparisons of agronomic performance, cost-benefit analysis, and heterogeneity analysis across farm scales; Section 4 discusses the results in the context of existing literature, sensitivity to price changes, and adoption constraints; Section 5 concludes with policy implications.

---

 2. Materials and Methods
 2.1 Study Sites
The study was conducted across three core dairy production provinces in northern China: Hebei, Inner Mongolia, and Shandong. These provinces collectively account for 58% of China’s total cow inventory and 61% of national raw milk output (CDIA, 2023). The study region has a temperate monsoon climate, with annual precipitation of 400–800 mm, average annual temperature of 8–12°C, and a frost-free period of 180–220 days, suitable for a range of annual and perennial forage crops.
 2.2 Data Collection
We collected primary data via structured face-to-face surveys with dairy farm owners and forage planting managers between March and May 2023, using a stratified random sampling approach. First, we selected 3 major dairy-producing prefectures in each province, then randomly selected 25–30 dairy farms in each prefecture, stratified by herd size: small-scale (<100 cows), medium-scale (100–500 cows), and large-scale (>500 cows). A total of 230 farms were initially surveyed; after excluding surveys with missing key production or cost data, the final sample included 217 farms, comprising 62 small-scale, 98 medium-scale, and 57 large-scale operations.
Survey data collected included: (1) Farm and household characteristics: herd size, operator age, education level, years of dairy farming experience, access to technical training; (2) Forage planting characteristics: planting pattern, cultivated area, seed cost, fertilizer/pesticide input, machinery cost, labor input, forage yield, nutritional quality (crude protein, neutral detergent fiber tested by local forage extension stations); (3) Economic indicators: cost of purchased forage and concentrate, raw milk yield per cow, milk sale price, other operating costs, total revenue. We supplemented primary survey data with 2021–2023 farm production records provided by farm operators to reduce recall bias.
 2.3 Definition of Planting Patterns
We classified farms into three mutually exclusive groups based on their dominant forage planting practice (covering ≥80% of their forage cultivated area):
1.  Pattern A (Double-cropping silage corn + winter ryegrass): Winter ryegrass is sown in mid-October after silage corn harvest, harvested in late May of the following year, followed by no-till sowing of silage corn in early June, creating a year-round double-cropping system. This pattern is designed to reduce winter fallow land and increase total annual forage output.
2.  Pattern B (Alfalfa-silage corn rotation): Alfalfa (a perennial legume forage) is planted for 3 consecutive years, harvested 4–5 times per year, then rotated with silage corn for 2 years before re-sowing alfalfa. This pattern leverages alfalfa’s nitrogen fixation to reduce fertilizer inputs and provides high-protein forage to reduce reliance on purchased protein feed.
3.  Pattern C (Monocropping high-yield silage corn, control group): The traditional dominant practice in the study region, where high-yield silage corn varieties are planted once per year in spring, harvested in early October, with land left fallow over winter.
 2.4 Analytical Methods
 2.4.1 Propensity Score Matching (PSM)
A key empirical challenge in estimating the impact of planting patterns on economic returns is selection bias: farm adoption of a given planting pattern is not random, but correlated with observable characteristics (e.g., farm size, operator education, access to credit) and unobservable characteristics (e.g., management ability) that may also affect profitability. To address this, we use PSM to construct a matched sample of treatment (Pattern A/B) and control (Pattern C) farms that are statistically identical in observable characteristics, allowing us to estimate the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) of adopting each high-efficiency pattern.
The PSM procedure follows three steps: First, we estimate a logit model to predict the probability (propensity score) of a farm adopting Pattern A or B, as a function of observable covariates: farm scale, operator age, education level, farming experience, access to technical training, cultivated land area, soil quality, and distance to milk processing plant. Second, we match each treatment farm to 1–3 control farms with the closest propensity score, using kernel matching with a bandwidth of 0.06, and impose common support to exclude observations with no suitable match. Third, we calculate the ATT as the difference in mean net returns between matched treatment and control farms, with bootstrapped standard errors (500 replications) to account for sampling variation. We test covariate balance after matching to ensure that mean differences in all covariates between treatment and control groups are not statistically significant at the 5% level.
 2.4.2 Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA)
We conduct CBA from the dairy farm perspective, using a 1-year time horizon for Pattern A and C, and a 5-year rotation cycle for Pattern B (3 years alfalfa + 2 years corn) to account for the multi-year nature of alfalfa establishment. We calculate the following indicators:
*   Total cost per hectare (TC): Sum of planting input costs (seed, fertilizer, pesticide, machinery, labor, land rent) and forage-associated dairy production costs (purchased forage, concentrate feed, veterinary costs linked to forage quality);
*   Total revenue per hectare (TR): Revenue from raw milk sales attributable to forage produced per hectare, calculated as (forage DM yield per hectare / annual forage DM requirement per cow) × milk yield per cow × milk sale price; we also include revenue from occasional surplus forage sales;
*   Net return per hectare (NR): TR - TC;
*   Benefit-cost ratio (BCR): TR / TC;
*   Forage self-sufficiency rate: Share of total forage used by the farm that is produced on-farm.
All costs and revenues are converted to 2023 U.S. dollars using the average annual exchange rate (1 USD = 7.12 RMB).
 2.4.3 Sensitivity Analysis
We conduct one-way sensitivity analysis to test how net returns of each pattern change under three scenarios: (1) 20% increase in purchased alfalfa price (simulating global supply chain disruption); (2) 10% decline in raw milk price (simulating market downturn); (3) 15% increase in nitrogen fertilizer price (simulating input price volatility).

---

 3. Results
 3.1 Descriptive Statistics of Sample Farms
Table 1 presents descriptive statistics of the sample, stratified by planting pattern. Of the 217 farms, 68 adopted Pattern A, 62 adopted Pattern B, and 87 used the traditional Pattern C. Farms adopting Pattern B were on average larger (mean herd size 482 cows) than Pattern A (279 cows) and Pattern C (214 cows), and had higher rates of technical training participation (74.2% of Pattern B operators had received forage planting training, compared to 51.5% for Pattern A and 32.2% for Pattern C). Average milk yield per cow was highest for Pattern B farms (9.2 tons/cow/year), followed by Pattern A (8.7 tons/cow/year) and Pattern C (8.1 tons/cow/year). All covariate differences between groups were statistically significant at the 10% level or lower, confirming the need for PSM to control for selection bias.

 3.2 Agronomic and Nutritional Performance of Planting Patterns
Table 2 compares agronomic and nutritional indicators across the three patterns. Pattern A had the highest annual DM yield (22.8 tons/ha/year), 26.7% higher than Pattern C (18.0 tons/ha/year), due to the addition of winter ryegrass harvest. Pattern B had lower annual DM yield (19.6 tons/ha/year, averaged over the 5-year rotation) but significantly higher forage quality: average crude protein (CP) content across all forage harvested was 16.2% for Pattern B, compared to 11.8% for Pattern A and 8.7% for Pattern C, due to the high protein content of alfalfa. Pattern B also had the lowest nitrogen fertilizer application rate (128 kg N/ha/year, averaged over the rotation), 45.3% lower than Pattern C, due to alfalfa’s biological nitrogen fixation.

After PSM matching, covariate balance was achieved: standardized mean differences for all covariates were below 5%, and no significant differences remained between treatment and control groups at the 5% level. In terms of revenue, Pattern B had the highest TR per hectare ($5,829.28/ha/year), due to higher milk yield per cow from better forage quality, followed by Pattern A ($5,409.66/ha) and Pattern C ($4,376.82/ha). These results confirm H1: both high-efficiency patterns deliver significantly higher net returns than traditional monocropping.
 3.4 Heterogeneity Analysis Across Farm Scales
Table 4 presents net returns per hectare across farm scales, to test H2. For Pattern B, net returns increase sharply with farm scale: large-scale farms using Pattern B have NR of $3,742.8/ha, 28.5% higher than small-scale farms using Pattern B ($2,912.3/ha), because large farms can spread fixed alfalfa planting and harvesting machinery costs over larger areas, and have access to better alfalfa storage (silage/hay making) equipment to reduce post-harvest loss. For Pattern A, the scale difference is smaller: large-scale farms using Pattern A have NR of $3,097.5/ha, only 13.1% higher than small-scale farms ($2,738.2/ha), because double-cropping ryegrass and corn uses similar machinery to traditional corn planting, requiring less additional fixed investment. For the traditional Pattern C, scale effects are minimal: large-scale farms have NR of $1,528.7/ha, just 14.7% higher than small-scale farms ($1,332.6/ha). These results partially confirm H2: the economic advantage of Pattern B is strongly correlated with farm scale, while Pattern A is more accessible and delivers consistent returns across scales.

 3.5 Sensitivity Analysis
Table 5 presents net returns under the three price volatility scenarios. Under the 20% alfalfa price increase scenario, Pattern B NR increases by 12.4% relative to baseline, because high on-farm alfalfa production insulates farms from purchased alfalfa price hikes

title: 油菜种植增收增产技术分析
text:
Analysis of Technologies for Increasing Yield and Income in Rapeseed Cultivation
Author: [Author’s Name]  
Affiliation: [Department/Institution, City, Postal Code]  
Corresponding Email: [email@example.com]

 Abstract
Rapeseed (*Brassica napus* L.) is a globally critical oilseed crop, serving as a major source of edible vegetable oil, protein-rich livestock feed, and industrial raw materials (e.g., biodiesel). With growing global demand for edible oil and renewable energy, improving rapeseed yield and growers’ net income has become a key priority for agricultural research and rural development. This paper systematically analyzes core technical systems for rapeseed yield enhancement and income growth, covering high-yield cultivar selection, precision sowing and field management, integrated pest and disease control, mechanized production, and value-chain extension. The study finds that the adoption of matched, context-specific technical packages can increase rapeseed yield by 15%–30% while reducing production costs by 10%–20%, thereby lifting net returns for smallholder and large-scale farms alike. This work concludes with targeted recommendations to address adoption barriers, including improved technical training and supportive agricultural policies.

Keywords: rapeseed cultivation; yield-increasing technology; cost-saving and income growth; mechanized production; integrated field management

---

 1. Introduction
Rapeseed ranks among the world’s top three oilseed crops, with China, the European Union, Canada, and Australia as major producing regions. In China, for example, rapeseed accounts for more than 45% of domestic edible vegetable oil supply, making it strategically important for national food security (Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO], 2023). In recent years, however, rapeseed production has faced persistent challenges: low and unstable yields from traditional extensive cultivation, rising labor and input costs, and weak comparative returns relative to grain crops, which have reduced growers’ willingness to plant.

Against this backdrop, developing and popularizing integrated technologies that raise both yield and economic returns is essential to stabilize rapeseed planting areas and strengthen industrial competitiveness. Unlike single-factor yield improvement measures, income-oriented cultivation technology requires simultaneous gains in output, reductions in production input, and optimization of product value. This paper aims to (1) sort key applicable technologies across the rapeseed production chain, (2) assess their yield-increasing and income-raising mechanisms and effects, and (3) propose evidence-based pathways to promote wider adoption.

---

 2. Core Technologies for Yield Improvement and Income Growth
 2.1 High-Quality, Stress-Tolerant Cultivar Selection and Regional Matching
Seed technology is the foundational determinant of rapeseed yield and quality. High-yield, double-low (low erucic acid, low glucosinolate) hybrid rapeseed varieties generally exhibit strong heterosis, with yield potential 10%–20% higher than conventional open-pollinated varieties (Wang et al., 2022). In production practice, cultivar selection must match local cropping systems and environmental conditions:
- In winter rapeseed regions along the Yangtze River Basin in China, early-maturing, cold-tolerant varieties are preferred to fit rice–rapeseed rotation schedules and avoid late-sowing frost damage.
- In spring rapeseed areas of northern China and Canada, drought-tolerant, early-maturing varieties with high pod-setting rates are selected to adapt to short growing seasons.
- For mechanized production, dwarf-stem, lodging-resistant, disease-resistant varieties with uniform maturity are prioritized to reduce harvest loss.

From an income perspective, high-quality double-low rapeseed also commands a market premium of 5%–12% over ordinary rapeseed due to better oil quality and feed value, directly increasing growers’ marketing revenue.

 2.2 Precision Sowing and Rational Population Construction
Traditional manual transplanting of rapeseed is labor-intensive (requiring 90–120 labor days per hectare) and prone to irregular planting density, which limits large-scale profitability. Precision direct seeding technologies, including mechanical strip seeding and no-till direct seeding in rice stubble fields, have become core technical measures for yield stabilization and cost reduction.

Key technical parameters include: sowing depth controlled at 1–2 cm, row spacing of 25–30 cm, and a target population of 300,000–450,000 plants per hectare for winter rapeseed (adjusted to soil fertility) (Zhang & Li, 2021). Compared with manual transplanting, mechanized precision sowing reduces seed usage by 20%–30%, cuts labor input by more than 70%, and establishes a uniform, high-quality population that improves light energy utilization. Long-term定位 (locational) trials in Hubei Province, China, show that no-till precision direct seeding increases rapeseed yield by 8.2% on average while reducing production costs by approximately 1,250 RMB per hectare, lifting net income by 22.6%.

 2.3 Scientific Nutrient and Water Management
Balanced fertilization based on soil testing effectively avoids excessive nitrogen fertilizer use (which causes lodging and disease) and nutrient deficiency that constrains yield. The recommended nutrient uptake ratio for high-yield rapeseed is N:P₂O₅:K₂O = 1:0.4:0.7, with 50%–60% of nitrogen applied as basal fertilizer, and the remaining as topdressing at the seedling and bolting stages (Liu et al., 2023). Boron fertilizer application (7.5–15 kg/hm² of borax as basal fertilizer) is particularly critical for rapeseed, as boron deficiency causes “flowering without podding,” which can reduce yield by 30% or even lead to crop failure in severe cases.

In terms of water management, rapeseed is vulnerable to both drought at the sowing and seedling stages and waterlogging in paddy-upland rotation fields. Supporting furrow ditching for drainage and supplementary micro-sprinkler irrigation during drought can increase seed-setting rate and 1000-grain weight. Integrated water-fertilizer technology demonstrated in demonstration bases raises fertilizer utilization efficiency by 15%–20%, reduces nitrogen fertilizer input by 10%, and increases average yield by 12.4%, realizing both yield gain and input cost savings.

 2.4 Integrated Pest, Disease, and Lodging Control
Major rapeseed diseases and pests include *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum* (sclerotinia stem rot), clubroot, aphids, and cabbage caterpillars. Among them, sclerotinia stem rot generally causes 10%–20% yield loss in epidemic years, and severe infections can reduce yield by more than 50%. The integrated pest management (IPM) strategy combines agricultural, physical, and chemical control measures:
1. Agricultural control: crop rotation with rice or gramineous crops, removal of infected plant residues, and rational nitrogen application to reduce field humidity and pathogen load.
2. Physical and biological control: yellow sticky traps for aphid monitoring and control, and release of parasitic wasps to reduce pesticide use.
3. Chemical control: uniform fungicide spraying at the early flowering to full flowering stage, with a second spray 7–10 days later under high disease pressure.

For lodging prevention, in addition to selecting resistant varieties and controlling density, plant growth regulators such as uniconazole applied at the bolting stage can reduce plant height by 10–15 cm and increase stem diameter, lowering lodging risk from 25% to below 5% in high-yield fields (Chen et al., 2020). Reduced disease and lodging losses directly stabilize yield, while reduced pesticide application frequency lowers both material costs and pesticide residues, supporting the production of premium green rapeseed.

 2.5 Full-Process Mechanization to Reduce Labor Costs
Labor cost accounts for 50%–60% of total rapeseed production costs in traditional smallholder planting systems, which is the primary factor eroding net income. Full-process mechanization covering mechanical land preparation, precision sowing, field management (mechanized spraying and fertilization), and combined harvesting dramatically compresses labor input.

Mechanical harvesting is divided into direct combine harvesting and swathing (windrowing) followed by pick-up threshing. Direct harvesting is suitable for fields with uniform maturity and dwarf, lodging-resistant varieties, with harvest loss controlled below 8%; swathing is conducted when 70%–80% of pods turn yellow, which can reduce shattering loss and improve harvest quality. Survey data from major producing provinces show that full-process mechanization cuts labor input to fewer than 45 labor days per hectare, reduces total production cost by 2,200–3,000 RMB/hm², and improves net profit by more than 30% even at the same yield level (National Agricultural Technology Extension and Service Center [NATESC], 2022). For large-scale family farms and cooperatives, mechanization also enables timely planting and harvest in multi-cropping rotation systems, avoiding yield losses from delayed sowing.

 2.6 Multi-Purpose Utilization and Industrial Value Chain Extension
Beyond seed yield, diversified rapeseed utilization opens additional income channels for growers. The “one crop, multiple harvests” model includes:
- Rapeseed as a vegetable: harvesting young bolting stems as a seasonal vegetable 1–2 times in winter, which can bring 3,000–6,000 RMB/hm² of extra income without significantly reducing seed yield when managed properly.
- Bee pollination and apiculture integration: rapeseed is a high-quality nectar source; arranging beehives during flowering increases rapeseed pod-setting rate by 5%–10% through pollination, while generating honey income for cooperating beekeepers and growers.
- High-value processing and branding: producing cold-pressed double-low rapeseed oil, branded edible oil, and rapeseed meal feed products extends the industrial chain, allowing growers’ cooperatives to capture processing and circulation profits rather than only selling raw seeds.

---

 3. Constraints on Technology Adoption and Optimization Recommendations
 3.1 Main Constraints
Field surveys indicate three major barriers to the widespread use of income-increasing technologies. First, smallholder farmers often have fragmented plots, which limits the operation of large and medium-sized machinery and weakens economies of scale. Second, technology matching is poor: many farmers apply high-yield varieties without supporting dense-planting, fertilization, and disease-prevention measures, leading to a large yield gap between demonstration fields and ordinary farmer fields (often 30%–40%). Third, the cost of improved seed, machinery services, and formula fertilizer is relatively high in the initial adoption stage, and risk-averse smallholders lack access to targeted technical guidance and agricultural insurance.

 3.2 Policy and Technical Recommendations
First, promote regional standardized technical packages. Local agricultural extension departments should formulate localized rapeseed high-yield and high-efficiency technical protocols according to cropping systems and climate, and deliver field training, on-site demonstrations, and machinery operation guidance to reduce the technology adoption threshold.

Second, support socialized agricultural machinery services. Subsidies should be directed to cooperatives and family farms to purchase precision seeders, combine harvesters, and plant protection drones, and promote shared machinery services across scattered smallholders to solve the problem of “small plots unsuitable for large machinery.”

Third, strengthen breeding of varieties suitable for mechanization and multi-purpose use, and integrate green, low-input cultivation technologies such as reduced fertilization and pesticide application to further reduce carbon emissions and production costs while improving product quality.

Fourth, improve the rapeseed price formation and premium mechanism, support the development of regional public brands of double-low rapeseed oil, and develop order-based production to connect growers with processing enterprises, so that farmers can share the value-added benefits of the industrial chain.

---

 4. Conclusion
Increasing rapeseed yield and growers’ income cannot rely on a single technical measure; it requires an integrated technical system that combines improved varieties, precision cultivation, scientific pest and nutrient management, full-process mechanization, and diversified value-chain development. Among these measures, mechanized precision direct seeding and full-process mechanization deliver the most significant cost-saving effects, while stress-tolerant high-quality cultivars and integrated field management underpin stable yield increases. Multi-purpose utilization and branded processing further expand income sources beyond seed sales. When adapted to local conditions and supported by extension services and policy subsidies, these technical packages can effectively narrow the yield gap, reduce labor and input costs, and substantially improve the economic returns of rapeseed cultivation, thereby supporting edible oil supply security and sustainable rural income growth.

---

 References
1. Chen, G., Zhou, W., & Yang, H. (2020). Effects of uniconazole on lodging resistance and yield of rapeseed under high-density planting. *Chinese Journal of Oil Crop Sciences*, 42(3), 412–419. (in Chinese with English abstract)
2. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. (2023). *FAOSTAT: Crops and livestock products database*. Retrieved from https://www.fao.org/faostat/
3. Liu, F., Zhao, X., & Wu, Y. (2023). Optimized fertilization improves nutrient use efficiency and seed yield of winter rapeseed in the Yangtze River Basin. *Field Crops Research*, 294, Article 108856.
4. National Agricultural Technology Extension and Service Center. (2022). *National rapeseed industry development and technology extension report*. China Agriculture Press. (in Chinese)
5. Wang, H., Guan, C., & Liu, S. (2022). Heterosis performance and industrial application of double-low hybrid rapeseed in China. *Oil Crop Science*, 7(2), 89–97.
6. Zhang, J., & Li, Y. (2021). No-till direct seeding technology improves rapeseed productivity and economic returns in rice–rapeseed rotation systems. *Agricultural Science & Technology*, 22(5), 45–52.

title: 生猪产业发展现状与对策
text:
Current Development Status and Countermeasures of the Global Hog Industry: A Short Empirical Analysis
*Journal of Agricultural and Resource Economics, Short Communication Section*  
Author Affiliation: Department of Agricultural Economics, College of Applied Economics, [Anonymous University], Beijing 100083, China  
Corresponding Author: [Researcher Name], E-mail: [corresponding@univ.edu.cn]  
Received: March 12, 2024; Accepted: April 8, 2024; Published: April 15, 2024

---

 Abstract
The hog industry serves as a core pillar of global livestock production and animal-derived food security, supplying over 35% of global meat consumption as of 2023 (FAO, 2024). In recent years, the sector has undergone accelerated structural transformation, while facing overlapping shocks from transboundary animal diseases, volatile input costs, supply chain disruptions, and tightening environmental regulations. This short paper synthesizes 2020–2024 industry data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and national agricultural statistics to systematically diagnose core operational bottlenecks, and proposes targeted, evidence-based countermeasures to support high-quality, resilient industry development. Findings indicate that large-scale, standardized production has become the dominant global trend, yet uneven productivity across regions, fragmented biosecurity systems, and weak market risk buffering capacity remain pervasive constraints. This study concludes that coordinated improvements in biosecurity governance, circular production models, value chain integration, and emergency response systems are critical to balancing stable supply, smallholder livelihood protection, and environmental sustainability.
Keywords: Hog Industry; Livestock Supply Chain; African Swine Fever; Agricultural Sustainability; Risk Resilience

---

 1. Introduction
Pork is the most widely consumed terrestrial animal protein worldwide, accounting for 36% of total global meat output in 2023, with per capita annual pork consumption reaching 15.2 kg (FAO, 2024). The hog industry not only supports the livelihoods of an estimated 72 million smallholder producers and upstream/downstream value chain actors globally, but also has significant spillover effects on feed grain markets, food price stability, and national macroeconomic performance, particularly in pork-dependent economies such as China, the European Union (EU), and the United States (USDA, 2023).
Since 2018, the global hog sector has experienced unprecedented volatility: the global spread of African Swine Fever (ASF) cut global pork output by 9.2% in 2019, and subsequent shocks from COVID-19 logistics disruptions, the 2022–2023 global feed grain price surge, and increasing carbon emission constraints have further exposed structural vulnerabilities in the sector. Existing scholarship has largely focused on single shock impacts (e.g., ASF transmission dynamics) or regional production trends, with limited systematic synthesis of cross-regional common challenges and replicable solutions. This study fills this gap by mapping the current state of global hog industry development, identifying core bottlenecks, and proposing actionable countermeasures for policymakers and industry stakeholders.

---

 2. Current Development Status of the Global Hog Industry
As of 2024, the global hog industry exhibits three dominant structural trends:
 2.1 Steady Rebound in Production Capacity with Gradual Concentration
Global pork production reached 114.2 million tonnes in 2023, recovering to 98% of pre-ASF (2018) levels, according to FAO data. Production has become increasingly concentrated in three core regions: the EU (22.1% of global output), China (47.8% of global output, with a 32% recovery in sow inventory since 2020), and the United States (10.3% of global output). Large-scale operations (defined as farms with >1,000 head annual slaughter capacity) now account for 62% of global production, up from 48% in 2018, as smallholder producers exited the market following repeated disease and price shocks (USDA, 2024). For example, in China, the share of large-scale hog farms rose from 54% in 2020 to 68% in 2023, while in the U.S. vertically integrated operations control over 90% of hog slaughter.
 2.2 Accelerated Technological Adoption Across Production Chains
Biosecurity, precision breeding, and smart farming technologies have seen rapid penetration since 2020. Closed-system all-in/all-out production, vehicle disinfection stations, and air filtration systems are now standard on 75% of large-scale farms globally, reducing ASF outbreak risk by an estimated 68% compared to open traditional systems (World Organisation for Animal Health [WOAH], 2023). Genomic selection for disease resistance and feed efficiency, as well as IoT-based real-time monitoring of pig health and feed intake, have increased average feed conversion ratio (FCR) efficiency by 11% in leading production regions, to 2.6 kg of feed per kg of live weight gain (National Pork Board, 2023).
 2.3 Rising Policy and Market Pressure for Green Transformation
Environmental regulations targeting manure pollution, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and antibiotic use have tightened across all major producing regions. The EU’s Farm to Fork Strategy mandates a 50% reduction in agricultural antibiotic use by 2030 and 30% reduction in livestock GHG emissions by 2030, while China’s 2021 Livestock Pollution Prevention Action Plan requires 90% of large-scale hog farms to implement manure recycling systems (European Commission, 2021; Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of China [MARA], 2021). Consumer demand for antibiotic-free, welfare-certified pork has grown at an annual rate of 8.7% since 2020, particularly in high-income markets, creating new incentives for production model upgrading.

---

 3. Core Bottlenecks Restricting Industry Development
Despite notable progress in production recovery and upgrading, the global hog industry faces four systemic constraints:
 3.1 Persistent Animal Disease Risks and Uneven Biosecurity Coverage
ASF remains endemic in 49 countries as of 2024, with no commercially available, broadly effective vaccine for all pig breeds. While large-scale farms have invested heavily in biosecurity, 38% of global hog production still comes from smallholder operations with limited disease prevention capacity, creating persistent reservoir risks for transboundary spread (WOAH, 2024). In 2023, for example, ASF outbreaks in Southeast Asia reduced regional pork output by 7.3%, driving up regional pork prices by 22% in six months. Routine diseases such as porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS) also cause an estimated $6.2 billion in annual global production losses.
 3.2 High Input Cost Volatility and Weak Risk Buffering Mechanisms
Feed costs account for 60–70% of total hog production costs, and the 2022–2023 global maize and soybean price spikes, driven by geopolitical conflicts and climate shocks, increased global average production costs by 28% between 2021 and 2023. Unlike crop sectors, most hog-producing regions lack targeted, inclusive price insurance or futures hedging mechanisms for small and medium producers, leading to repeated 2–3 year cycles of boom and bust in hog prices: for example, China’s hog price fell 56% between October 2022 and May 2023, pushing 18% of small and medium farms into loss-making territory (MARA, 2023).
 3.3 Tension Between Environmental Governance and Stable Production
The high pollution footprint of traditional hog production (manure runoff, ammonia emissions, and embedded feed grain emissions) has led to ad-hoc farm closures in environmentally sensitive zones in some regions, creating short-term supply gaps. At the same time, 42% of large-scale farms in middle-income countries have not yet installed cost-effective manure treatment and recycling systems, leading to an estimated 23% of hog manure being discharged without treatment, contributing to agricultural non-point source pollution (UN Environment Programme, 2023). The high upfront cost of green upgrading is prohibitive for 60% of small and medium producers, slowing sector-wide low-carbon transformation.
 3.4 Inadequate Livelihood Protection for Smallholder Producers
The rapid shift to large-scale production has displaced an estimated 9.3 million smallholder hog producers globally between 2018 and 2023, most of whom lack access to alternative livelihood training or inclusive value chain integration opportunities (FAO, 2024). Smallholders who remain in the sector are often locked out of high-value formal retail channels due to lack of certification, low product standardization, and weak bargaining power against large processors, trapping them in low-margin, high-risk production.

---

 4. Targeted Countermeasures for High-Quality Industry Development
To address the above bottlenecks and build a more resilient, sustainable, and inclusive hog industry, this study proposes four evidence-based countermeasures:
 4.1 Establish a Tiered, Collaborative Biosecurity Governance System
First, governments should roll out standardized, subsidized biosecurity upgrade programs for smallholder producers, including shared disinfection stations, free disease testing, and technical extension services, to close the biosecurity gap between small and large operations. Second, regional cross-border disease surveillance and information sharing platforms should be established, in partnership with WOAH, to enable early warning and rapid response to ASF and other transboundary diseases. Third, public and private R&D investment in safe, effective ASF vaccines and disease-resistant breeding should be scaled up, with targeted subsidies for producer adoption of new disease prevention technologies.
 4.2 Build an Inclusive Market Risk Stabilization Mechanism
For small and medium producers, governments should launch subsidized hog price and cost insurance programs, with premium contributions split between producers, processing enterprises, and public finance, to buffer against extreme price and input cost volatility. At the same time, regulated hog futures and spot markets should be developed to provide transparent price signals and hedging tools for industry actors. National and regional emergency pork reserve systems should be optimized, with dynamic stock adjustments to smooth extreme supply and demand fluctuations and reduce the amplitude of hog price cycles.
 4.3 Promote Circular, Low-Carbon Production Models
Policy incentives should be aligned to support the integration of hog farming with crop production, where treated manure is used as organic fertilizer to reduce chemical fertilizer use and lower pollution and GHG emissions. Subsidies and low-interest loans should be provided to farms of all sizes to install biogas digesters, manure composting systems, and precision feeding equipment that reduces feed waste and nitrogen excretion. A standardized green pork certification system should be established to create price premiums for low-carbon, antibiotic-free pork, aligning producer returns with environmental performance.
 4.4 Facilitate Inclusive Value Chain Integration of Smallholders
Contract farming models between large processing enterprises, cooperatives, and smallholder producers should be promoted, where enterprises provide smallholders with unified feed, breeding stock, technical guidance, and guaranteed purchase prices at set quality standards, reducing smallholder risk and improving product standardization. Targeted training programs should be offered to smallholders exiting the sector to support transition to downstream value chain roles (e.g., manure processing, retail, transport) or alternative agricultural livelihoods, to ensure structural transformation does not come at the cost of rural livelihoods.

---

 5. Conclusion
The global hog industry is at a critical juncture of post-shock recovery and structural transformation, with progress in large-scale production and technological adoption offset by persistent vulnerabilities in disease governance, risk buffering, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. A one-sided focus on scaling up production without addressing these structural gaps will lead to continued supply volatility, environmental damage, and inequitable outcomes for smallholder producers. The coordinated, multi-stakeholder countermeasures proposed in this study provide a pathway to build a hog industry that is not only productive and profitable, but also resilient to shocks, environmentally sustainable, and inclusive of the millions of actors that depend on the sector for their livelihoods. Future research should conduct quantitative cost-benefit analyses of these policy interventions across different regional contexts to identify context-specific optimal implementation strategies.

---

2. Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO]. (2024). *Global Livestock Market Review 2023/24*. Rome: FAO Livestock Information and Analysis Branch.
3. Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of China [MARA]. (2021). National Livestock and Poultry Pollution Prevention and Control 14th Five-Year Plan. Beijing: MARA Department of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services.
4. Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of China [MARA]. (2023). *2023 National Hog Industry Development Monitoring Report*. Beijing: China Agricultural Press.
5. National Pork Board. (2023). *U.S. Pork Industry Productivity Report 2023*. Des Moines, IA: National Pork Board.
6. United Nations Environment Programme [UNEP]. (2023). *Livestock Manure Pollution: Global Impacts and Solution Pathways*. Nairobi: UNEP Ecosystems Division.

title: 草莓水肥一体化技术应用
text:
Application of Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology in Strawberry Cultivation: Efficiency, Yield Response, and Sustainability Implications
*Running Title: Integrated Water-Fertilizer Management for Strawberry Production*

---

 Abstract
Strawberry (*Fragaria × ananassa* Duch.) is a high-value horticultural crop characterized by shallow root systems, high water and nutrient demand, and sensitivity to over-fertilization and water stress, which make conventional flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization practices inefficient and environmentally harmful. Integrated water and fertilizer (IWF, also termed fertigation) technology delivers dissolved nutrients directly to the root zone via pressurized irrigation systems, enabling precise, synchronous matching of water and nutrient supply to crop physiological demand. This paper evaluates the application performance of drip-based IWF systems in open-field and protected strawberry cultivation across subtropical and temperate production zones, drawing on 3 years of field trial data from commercial strawberry farms in Zhejiang Province, China, and peer-reviewed production data from North America and the European Union. Results indicate that compared to conventional management, optimized IWF regimes reduce irrigation water use by 32–41%, cut nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) fertilizer inputs by 28–35%, increase marketable strawberry yield by 17–24%, and reduce fruit nitrate content by 22% while improving soluble solid content by 1.2–1.8 °Brix. We further identify critical operational parameters: for protected June-bearing strawberry cultivars, a drip emitter flow rate of 1.6–2.2 L/h, irrigation threshold of -15 kPa soil matric potential, and a stage-specific N:P:K ratio of 1:0.4:1.2 during the fruit expansion stage deliver the highest economic returns. Key barriers to smallholder adoption, including high upfront equipment costs and lack of tailored nutrient formula guidance, are addressed with targeted policy and extension recommendations. This study confirms that IWF technology is a viable management practice to reconcile high strawberry productivity, improved fruit quality, and reduced agricultural non-point source pollution.

Keywords: Strawberry cultivation; Fertigation; Drip irrigation; Nutrient use efficiency; Water-saving agriculture; Protected horticulture

---

 1. Introduction
Global strawberry production reached 8.86 million tonnes in 2022, with 37% of output originating from protected cultivation systems where growers target high-value off-season market supply (FAO, 2023). As a shallow-rooted crop, 80% of strawberry roots are distributed in the 0–20 cm soil layer, leading to low tolerance for both waterlogging and drought, as well as high sensitivity to fluctuations in soil nutrient concentration (Zhang et al., 2021). Conventional strawberry management in most smallholder production systems relies on flood irrigation and broadcast application of compound fertilizers, which typically result in 60–70% of applied N fertilizer lost via leaching, runoff, and volatilization, with water use efficiency (WUE) as low as 1.2 kg/m³ (Wang et al., 2020). Excess fertilizer application not only increases production costs but also leads to secondary salinization of protected cultivation soils, elevated fruit nitrate levels, and downstream freshwater eutrophication (Liu et al., 2022).

Integrated water and fertilizer technology, defined as the combined application of water and soluble nutrients through pressurized irrigation networks, was first widely adopted in high-value horticultural production in Israel and California in the 1970s, and has been promoted as a core climate-smart agricultural practice by the Food and Agriculture Organization since 2010 (FAO, 2020). Unlike separate irrigation and fertilization, IWF allows for split, dose-adjusted delivery of nutrients across strawberry growth stages, reducing nutrient losses by matching supply to root uptake dynamics. While existing research has documented yield benefits of IWF for field crops, there remains a gap in stage-specific parameter optimization for strawberry cultivars across different production systems, as well as systematic assessment of tradeoffs between productivity, fruit quality, and environmental outcomes under on-farm (rather than experimental station) conditions.

This study addresses this gap by: (1) quantifying the water, fertilizer, yield, and quality responses of strawberry to optimized IWF management relative to conventional practices; (2) identifying evidence-based operational parameters for drip IWF systems in protected strawberry cultivation; and (3) analyzing adoption barriers and proposing actionable strategies for scaling.

---

 2. Materials and Methods
 2.1 Study Site and Experimental Design
Field trials were conducted across three consecutive growing seasons (2020–2023) at six commercial strawberry farms in Jiande City, Zhejiang Province (29.5°N, 119.3°E), a core protected strawberry production region in subtropical China, with supplementary meta-data collected from 42 published studies reporting IWF performance in strawberry production across temperate and subtropical zones. The experimental sites had loam soil with 2.3% organic matter, pH 5.8, 126 mg/kg alkali-hydrolyzable N, 38 mg/kg available P, and 142 mg/kg available K in the 0–20 cm layer, representative of major strawberry-growing soils in the region. The tested cultivar was *Hongyan*, the most widely grown June-bearing strawberry cultivar in China, planted in raised beds (30 cm height, 80 cm bed width, 30 cm furrow width) with black plastic mulch, at a planting density of 120,000 plants/ha, consistent with local commercial practices.

Two management treatments were applied across 12 paired 0.2-ha plots, arranged in a randomized complete block design with six replicates per treatment:
1.  Conventional management (CM): Flood irrigation every 10–15 days, with total fertilizer input of 450 kg N/ha, 220 kg P₂O₅/ha, and 420 kg K₂O/ha, 60% applied as basal fertilizer before planting, and 40% applied as topdressing via broadcast in three splits during the growing season, consistent with local smallholder practices.
2.  Optimized IWF management (IWF): Drip irrigation system with emitters spaced 20 cm apart, installed 5 cm from strawberry plant rows, connected to a proportional fertilizer pump for soluble nutrient delivery. Irrigation was triggered when soil matric potential at 15 cm depth reached -15 kPa, with irrigation amount set to raise soil water content to 85% of field capacity. Total fertilizer input was adjusted to 315 kg N/ha, 135 kg P₂O₅/ha, and 370 kg K₂O/ha, delivered in 12 split applications across growth stages (seedling establishment: 10% of total nutrients; vegetative growth: 20%; early flowering: 15%; fruit expansion: 40%; late harvest: 15%) using water-soluble N:P:K formulas tailored to each stage.

 2.2 Measurement Indicators
Across all growing seasons, we recorded total irrigation volume, total fertilizer input, marketable yield (fruit weight >12 g, no disease or mechanical damage), and unmarketable yield. WUE was calculated as marketable yield divided by total irrigation water plus growing-season precipitation. Fertilizer partial factor productivity (PFP) was calculated as marketable yield divided by total N+P₂O₅+K₂O input. Fruit quality indicators including soluble solid content (SSC, measured via handheld refractometer), vitamin C content (2,6-dichloroindophenol titration), and nitrate content (salicylic acid colorimetry) were measured on 30 randomly selected ripe fruit per plot at peak harvest. Soil residual mineral N content in the 0–60 cm layer was measured post-harvest to assess N leaching risk.

 2.3 Data Analysis
Independent sample t-tests were used to compare treatment means, with significance set at *p* < 0.05. Meta-data from published studies was synthesized to calculate weighted response ratios of yield, WUE, and nutrient use efficiency across production regions.

---

 3. Results
 3.1 Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency
Across three growing seasons, the IWF treatment delivered consistent reductions in resource input relative to CM (Table 1). Average irrigation water input under IWF was 2,140 m³/ha, 38% lower than the 3,450 m³/ha applied under CM, as the real-time soil moisture triggering avoided over-irrigation during rainfall events and slow growth stages. Total N, P₂O₅, and K₂O inputs under IWF were 30%, 39%, and 12% lower than CM, respectively, with P showing the largest reduction due to high residual P levels from long-term over-fertilization at the study sites. WUE under IWF reached 4.87 kg/m³, 77% higher than the 2.75 kg/m³ recorded under CM, while PFP of total nutrients was 25.6 kg/kg under IWF, 56% higher than the 16.4 kg/kg under CM. Post-harvest soil residual mineral N in the 0–60 cm layer was 68 kg/ha under IWF, 59% lower than the 166 kg/ha under CM, indicating a substantially reduced risk of N leaching into groundwater.

*Table 1. Resource use efficiency under conventional and integrated water-fertilizer management (2020–2023 mean)*
| Indicator | Conventional Management | Optimized IWF Management | Relative change (%) |
|-----------|--------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------|
| Total irrigation (m³/ha) | 3450 ± 210 | 2140 ± 120 | -38* |
| Total N input (kg/ha) | 450 ± 22 | 315 ± 12 | -30* |
| Total P₂O₅ input (kg/ha) | 220 ± 18 | 135 ± 8 | -39* |
| Total K₂O input (kg/ha) | 420 ± 15 | 370 ± 10 | -12 |
| Water use efficiency (kg/m³) | 2.75 ± 0.21 | 4.87 ± 0.28 | +77* |
| Nutrient partial factor productivity (kg/kg) | 16.4 ± 1.1 | 25.6 ± 1.5 | +56* |
| Post-harvest 0–60 cm residual mineral N (kg/ha) | 166 ± 19 | 68 ± 8 | -59* |
| *Note:  and * indicate significant difference between treatments at p<0.01 and p<0.001, respectively.* |

 3.2 Yield and Fruit Quality Response
Marketable strawberry yield under IWF averaged 21.1 t/ha, 21% higher than the 17.4 t/ha recorded under CM (Table 2). The yield gain was primarily driven by a 28% reduction in unmarketable fruit: under CM, frequent flood irrigation and uneven nutrient supply led to a 17.2% incidence of fruit cracking and botrytis rot, compared to 8.9% under IWF, where consistent root-zone moisture avoided sudden water uptake that causes cracking, and reduced canopy humidity lowered disease pressure. Average single fruit weight under IWF was 18.7 g, 12% higher than under CM.

Fruit quality metrics also improved under IWF. SSC, a key indicator of strawberry flavor, was 11.8 °Brix under IWF, 1.5 °Brix higher than under CM, where excess N application and water surplus promoted vegetative growth at the expense of sugar accumulation. Fruit vitamin C content was 62.3 mg/100g under IWF, 14% higher than CM, while nitrate content was 98 mg/kg, 24% lower than CM, well below the 300 mg/kg national food safety limit for fresh fruit. Meta-analysis of global strawberry IWF studies showed consistent yield (12–26%) and quality gains across cultivars and climate zones, with the largest benefits observed in protected cultivation systems where rainfall is excluded and root-zone conditions can be fully controlled.

*Table 2. Yield and fruit quality under conventional and integrated water-fertilizer management (2020–2023 mean)*
| Indicator | Conventional Management | Optimized IWF Management | Relative change (%) |
|-----------|--------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------|
| Marketable yield (t/ha) | 17.4 ± 0.9 | 21.1 ± 1.1 | +21* |
| Unmarketable fruit rate (%) | 17.2 ± 2.1 | 8.9 ± 1.2 | -48* |
| Average single fruit weight (g) | 16.7 ± 0.8 | 18.7 ± 0.6 | +12 |
| Soluble solid content (°Brix) | 10.3 ± 0.4 | 11.8 ± 0.3 | +15* |
| Vitamin C content (mg/100g) | 54.6 ± 2.7 | 62.3 ± 2.2 | +14 |
| Fruit nitrate content (mg/kg) | 129 ± 11 | 98 ± 7 | -24 |
| *Note:  and * indicate significant difference between treatments at p<0.01 and p<0.001, respectively.* |

 3.3 Optimized Operational Parameters for Strawberry IWF Systems
Synthesis of trial data and published literature identified three core parameters for maximum IWF performance in protected strawberry production:
1.  Drip system design: Emitter flow rates of 1.6–2.2 L/h, with emitter spacing of 20 cm along drip lines placed 5 cm from plant rows, to ensure wetted soil volume covers 70–80% of the root zone without surface runoff or deep percolation below 30 cm depth. Higher flow rates (>3 L/h) lead to surface waterlogging and elevated fruit rot risk, while lower flow rates (<1 L/h) fail to meet evapotranspiration demand during peak fruit expansion.
2.  Irrigation scheduling: Triggering irrigation at a soil matric potential of -10 to -15 kPa at 15 cm depth during the fruit expansion stage, and -20 to -25 kPa during seedling hardening and late harvest, avoids both water stress and excess moisture. Relative to fixed-interval irrigation, sensor-based scheduling reduces water input by an additional 15% without yield loss.
3.  Stage-specific nutrient formula: Seedling stage requires high P to promote root growth (N:P₂O₅:K₂O = 1:0.8:0.6), while fruit expansion stages require high K and reduced P to support sugar accumulation and fruit development (N:P₂O₅:K₂O = 1:0.3:1.4). Split application every 7–10 days during harvest, rather than 3–4 large fertilizer doses, reduces nutrient leaching and maintains stable soil nutrient concentrations.

---

 4. Discussion
 4.1 Mechanisms of IWF Benefits for Strawberry
The yield and quality gains observed under IWF are consistent with strawberry root physiology: the shallow, fibrous root system has limited nutrient and water storage capacity, requiring continuous, low-concentration supply of resources in the upper soil layer (Gao et al., 2021). Conventional flood irrigation creates alternating cycles of waterlogging and drought, which damages root hairs and reduces nutrient uptake capacity, while broadcast fertilization creates high, toxic salt concentrations in the root zone immediately after application, followed by nutrient deficiency as fertilizers leach below the root zone (Li et al., 2023). IWF maintains soil water potential and nutrient concentration within the optimal range for strawberry root function across the growing season, promoting consistent water and nutrient uptake, reducing physiological stress, and shifting dry matter partitioning toward fruit production rather than excess vegetative growth.

The reduced disease incidence under IWF is also a key contributing factor to yield gains: drip irrigation delivers water directly to the soil surface, avoiding wetting of strawberry leaves and fruit, which reduces canopy humidity and the spread of *Botrytis cinerea* and other airborne pathogens, cutting fungicide use by an estimated 25% in previous trials (Fernández et al., 2020).
 4.2 Adoption Barriers and Scaling Strategies
Despite demonstrated benefits, global adoption of IWF in strawberry production remains uneven: over 70% of strawberry farms in the U.S. and EU use fertigation systems, but adoption rates among smallholder producers in China and other middle-income countries are below 20% (FAO, 2023). Our survey of 120 smallholder strawberry growers in Zhejiang identified three core barriers: (1) high upfront equipment costs (approximately $2,200/ha for drip lines, filters, and fertilizer injectors, equivalent to 15% of annual strawberry production revenue for smallholders); (2) lack of tailored, crop-specific guidance on irrigation scheduling and nutrient formulas, leading many early adopters to over-apply water and soluble fertilizers, reducing expected benefits; (3) poor quality of low-cost drip equipment, which is prone to clogging and has a service life of only 1–2 years, compared to 5–7 years for high-quality systems.

Targeted strategies to address these barriers include: targeted equipment subsidies for smallholder producers to reduce upfront costs by 50–70%; development of simplified, low-cost soil moisture sensors and crop-specific nutrient formula guides distributed via local agricultural extension services; and quality certification standards for drip irrigation equipment to reduce clogging risk and extend system service life. Recent pilot programs in Zhejiang applying these strategies increased IWF adoption from 18% to 62% among strawberry growers between 2020 and 2023, with average net revenue gains of $7,800/ha for adopters due to higher yield, lower input costs, and premium prices for higher-quality fruit.
 4.3 Sustainability Implications
Beyond on-farm productivity and economic gains, widespread adoption of IWF in strawberry production has critical environmental co-benefits. The 30–40% reduction in N fertilizer input and 60% reduction in residual soil N observed in our trials would reduce agricultural N leaching by an estimated 50% in strawberry production regions, addressing a key driver of freshwater eutrophication in protected horticulture zones (Liu et al., 2022). The 38% reduction in irrigation water use is particularly critical for subtropical and Mediterranean strawberry production regions, where increasing drought frequency due to climate change has created competition for water between agriculture and urban use. When combined with biodegradable mulch and solar-powered drip pumps, IWF systems can reduce the carbon footprint of strawberry production by an estimated 32% relative to conventional management (Patanè et al., 2023).

---

 5. Conclusion
This study demonstrates that optimized drip-based integrated water and fertilizer technology delivers substantial multi-dimensional benefits for strawberry production: it cuts irrigation water use by more than a third, reduces fertilizer inputs by 28–35%, increases marketable yield by 21%, improves fruit flavor and nutritional quality, and reduces environmental pollution from nutrient leaching. The evidence-based operational parameters identified in this study—appropriate drip emitter specifications, soil-moisture-based irrigation scheduling, and stage-specific nutrient ratios—can guide growers to maximize benefits from IWF systems. While upfront costs and knowledge gaps limit smallholder adoption, targeted subsidies, extension support, and equipment quality standards can accelerate scaling. For high-value shallow-rooted horticultural crops like strawberry, IWF represents a critical management practice to reconcile agricultural productivity, farmer profitability, and environmental sustainability in the face of growing water scarcity and climate change.
