title: 油菜高产栽培技术要点
text:
Key Points of High-Yield Cultivation Techniques for Rapeseed (Brassica napus L.)
Abstract  
Rapeseed (*Brassica napus* L.) is a globally significant oilseed crop, serving as a major source of edible vegetable oil, livestock protein feed, and industrial bioenergy raw materials. Enhancing rapeseed yield per unit area is critical to ensuring edible oil supply security and promoting the sustainable development of the oilseed industry. This paper systematically elaborates key technical points of high-yield rapeseed cultivation from the dimensions of pre-sowing preparation, scientific sowing, field management, pest and disease control, and mechanized harvesting, based on the growth and development laws of rapeseed. The study finds that the coordinated application of improved variety matching, precise sowing, balanced fertilization, and integrated pest management can significantly optimize rapeseed population structure, increase resource utilization efficiency of light, temperature, water and fertilizer, and achieve stable and high-yield production. This paper aims to provide standardized technical references for rapeseed production and offer theoretical support for the popularization and application of high-yield cultivation modes.

Keywords rapeseed; high-yield cultivation; sowing technique; field management; mechanized production

 1. Introduction
As one of the four major oilseed crops in the world, rapeseed accounts for approximately 20% of global vegetable oil production, with China, Canada, the European Union and India being the main producing regions (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations [FAO], 2023). In China, rapeseed is the largest domestic oilseed crop, with more than 85% of its cultivated area distributed in the Yangtze River Basin, playing a core role in ensuring national edible oil supply security. In recent years, affected by factors such as comparative planting efficiency, rural labor transfer and climate change, rapeseed production has faced prominent problems including unscientific variety selection, extensive field management and low popularization rate of mechanized technology, restricting the improvement of yield potential (Wang & Li, 2022).

High-yield cultivation of rapeseed is a systematic project integrating variety improvement, environmental regulation and agronomic optimization. Existing studies have shown that the yield gap between farmers' conventional cultivation and high-yield demonstration fields can reach 30%–45%, and the gap mainly stems from the non-standard application of key cultivation techniques (Zhang et al., 2021). Clarifying the core technical points of each production link and constructing a matched cultivation technical system is an important way to tap rapeseed yield potential. Based on domestic and foreign research results and high-yield production practice, this paper sorts out key cultivation techniques from pre-sowing to harvesting, in order to provide technical support for rapeseed high-yield, high-efficiency and standardized production.

 2. Pre-Sowing Preparation Techniques
 2.1 Variety Selection and Seed Treatment
Selecting suitable varieties is the prerequisite for high rapeseed yield, which should follow the principles of ecological adaptability, yield stability, stress resistance and production demand. For winter rapeseed areas in the Yangtze River Basin, semi-winter varieties with moderate growth period, strong lodging resistance and low erucic acid and glucosinolate content (double-low quality) should be selected; for spring rapeseed areas in northern China, early-maturing and cold-resistant spring varieties are appropriate (Liu et al., 2020). In addition, varieties resistant to major local diseases and pests such as *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum* and clubroot should be selected according to the occurrence characteristics of diseases and pests in planting plots.

Seed treatment can effectively improve seed germination rate and reduce seed-borne diseases. Before sowing, seeds should be screened to remove shriveled grains and impurities, ensuring seed purity ≥ 95%, germination rate ≥ 90% and moisture content ≤ 9%. Seed dressing with chemical agents such as fludioxonil or metalaxyl-M can prevent and control underground pests and seedling-stage diseases, and seed coating with biological agents can also enhance seed stress resistance while reducing chemical input (Chen et al., 2023).

 2.2 Land Preparation and Base Fertilizer Application
Rapeseed has a well-developed taproot system and prefers deep, loose and fertile soil with a pH value of 6.0–7.5. For previous rice stubble fields in the Yangtze River Basin, no-till direct seeding or plowing land preparation can be adopted according to soil moisture. Plowing depth should be controlled at 20–25 cm, and the soil should be harrowed finely to reach the standard of "fine soil, flat field and no stubble", so as to create a good soil environment for root growth (Zhou & Wu, 2021). For dryland fields, deep plowing in combination with sunning the soil can reduce the base number of diseases and pests.

Scientific base fertilizer application is the foundation for cultivating strong seedlings. The principle of "combining organic fertilizer with chemical fertilizer, and balancing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium" should be followed. Generally, for a target yield of 3,000 kg/ha, 22,500–30,000 kg/ha of decomposed farmyard manure, 180–225 kg/ha of pure nitrogen, 90–120 kg/ha of phosphorus pentoxide and 120–150 kg/ha of potassium oxide should be applied as base fertilizer, accounting for 60%–70% of the total nitrogen fertilizer and all of organic, phosphorus and potassium fertilizers (National Agricultural Technology Extension and Service Center [NATESC], 2022). Meanwhile, 7.5–15 kg/ha of boron fertilizer should be applied to prevent flower and pod dropping caused by boron deficiency, which is a key measure for rapeseed high yield.

 3. Scientific Sowing Techniques
 3.1 Sowing Period and Sowing Rate Determination
The sowing period of rapeseed should match local temperature and precipitation conditions. Winter rapeseed in the Yangtze River Basin is suitable for sowing when the average daily temperature is stable at 20–22 ℃, mostly from late September to mid-October; early sowing tends to cause overgrowth before winter and aggravate disease occurrence, while late sowing leads to insufficient nutrient accumulation before winter and weak seedling resistance (Li et al., 2022). Spring rapeseed in northern China should be sown in time after soil thawing in early spring, generally from late April to early May, to make full use of spring soil moisture.

The sowing rate should be determined according to sowing method, sowing period and soil fertility. The conventional direct seeding rate is 4.5–7.5 kg/ha; for no-till direct seeding or late sowing plots, the sowing rate can be appropriately increased to 7.5–10.5 kg/ha. For seedling transplanting, the seedling bed sowing rate is 7.5–9.0 kg/ha, and 1 hectare of seedling bed can provide seedlings for 5–6 hectares of field. The reasonable density of final seedlings is 225,000–375,000 plants/ha for direct seeding winter rapeseed, and 450,000–600,000 plants/ha for spring rapeseed, so as to construct a coordinated population of yield components (effective pod number, seed number per pod and 1000-grain weight) (Huang et al., 2020).

 3.2 Sowing Method and Depth Control
Standardized sowing method is conducive to uniform seedling emergence and field management. At present, main sowing methods include artificial drill sowing, precision seeders and seedling transplanting. Mechanized precision direct seeding can realize integrated operations of ditching, fertilizing, sowing and soil covering, which is the key development direction of simplified rapeseed cultivation. Drill sowing should maintain a row spacing of 25–30 cm, and seeds should be evenly distributed in the sowing ditch.

Sowing depth directly affects seedling emergence speed and quality. Rapeseed seeds are small with weak soil-pushing ability, so the suitable sowing depth is 1–2 cm. After sowing, thin soil covering should be carried out to make seeds closely contact soil; for no-till fields with much straw mulch, anti-blocking seeders should be selected to avoid seed exposure and ensure full and uniform seedlings (Yang et al., 2023). For seedling transplanting, strong seedlings with 6–7 true leaves, short hypocotyls and developed root systems should be selected for transplanting before winter, with planting depth of 3–4 cm, and root-setting water should be poured in time after transplanting.

 4. Field Management at Different Growth Stages
 4.1 Seedling Stage Management
The seedling stage refers to the period from seedling emergence to flower bud differentiation, and the core management goal is to cultivate strong seedlings and ensure safe overwintering (winter rapeseed). After seedling emergence, thinning and final seedling should be carried out in time: thinning is conducted at the stage of 2–3 true leaves to remove crowded and weak seedlings, and final seedling is completed at the stage of 4–5 true leaves according to planned density. During thinning, intertillage weeding should be combined to improve soil aeration and reduce nutrient consumption (NATESC, 2022).

For plots with insufficient base fertilizer or weak seedling growth, seedling fertilizer should be applied early, generally applying 45–60 kg/ha of pure nitrogen before the 5-leaf stage to promote vegetative growth. In northern winter rapeseed areas or high-altitude areas, overwintering fertilizer combined with soil cultivation should be applied before overwintering to enhance seedling cold resistance. In case of autumn drought, timely irrigation should be carried out along ditches; waterlogging should be drained in time in rainy areas to prevent root retting and seedling death. In addition, chemical weeding can be carried out at the 3–5 leaf stage: gramineous weeds can be controlled by quizalofop-p-ethyl, and broadleaf weeds can be controlled by clopyralid according to weed species.

 4.2 Flowering and Podding Stage Management
Flowering and podding stage is the key period for rapeseed reproductive growth, during which nutrient growth and reproductive growth proceed simultaneously, and the demand for water and fertilizer reaches the peak. The main management goal is to preserve flowers and pods, increase seed number per pod and grain weight. For fields with weak growth and premature senility, bolting fertilizer should be applied appropriately at the bolting stage, with 30–45 kg/ha of pure nitrogen, combined with spraying 0.2% potassium dihydrogen phosphate solution on leaves to delay leaf senescence and improve photosynthetic efficiency (Zhao et al., 2021).

Water management at flowering stage should adhere to "sufficient but not excessive". Sufficient water supply should be maintained during the full-bloom stage, and ditch irrigation can be adopted in case of drought to avoid flood irrigation. Rapeseed has weak waterlogging tolerance, so drainage ditches should be dredged before the rainy season to reduce field humidity and reduce the occurrence of *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum*. Boron fertilizer should be sprayed once at the bolting stage and initial flowering stage respectively for boron-deficient soil, so as to prevent "flowering without podding". For overgrown plots, plant growth regulators such as paclobutrazol can be sprayed appropriately at the bolting stage to control plant height, enhance stem strength and reduce lodging risk.

 4.3 Mature Stage Management
From final flowering to maturity, rapeseed enters the grain-filling stage, and management focuses on preventing premature senility, lodging and pest damage, and promoting grain plumpness. Foliar fertilizer (potassium dihydrogen phosphate combined with trace element fertilizer) can be sprayed 1–2 times after final flowering to prolong photosynthetic function time of siliques and leaves and increase 1000-grain weight. Drainage work should be strengthened in rainy areas to avoid root activity decline caused by waterlogging. At the same time, field ventilation and light transmission should be maintained to reduce the probability of late diseases (Liu et al., 2020).

 5. Integrated Pest and Disease Management
 5.1 Main Diseases and Control Measures
The main diseases endangering rapeseed include *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum*, clubroot, downy mildew and viral diseases, among which *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum* is the most widely distributed and harmful, generally causing yield reduction of 10%–30%, and even more than 50% in severe cases (Wu et al., 2022). Agricultural control is the basis: selecting disease-resistant varieties, implementing crop rotation with rice or gramineous crops for 2–3 years, removing field diseased residues, and reducing field humidity through reasonable dense planting and ditching for drainage can significantly reduce disease incidence.

Chemical control should be carried out at key periods. For *Sclerotinia sclerotiorum*, fungicides such as prochloraz or boscalid should be sprayed at the initial flowering stage and full flowering stage respectively, and spraying should focus on the middle and lower parts of stems and leaves. For clubroot in acidic soil, in addition to selecting resistant varieties, soil pH can be adjusted by applying lime, and fluazinam can be used for root irrigation at the seedling stage. Downy mildew can be controlled by metalaxyl-mancozeb at the early stage of disease, and field waterlogging should be drained in time to reduce humidity.

 5.2 Main Pests and Green Control
Main pests in rapeseed field include aphids, cabbage caterpillars, flea beetles and underground cutworms. Aphids not only suck plant sap and affect growth, but also transmit viral diseases, which are easy to break out in dry and warm autumn and spring. Agricultural control can remove field weeds and host plants to reduce pest sources; physical control can adopt yellow sticky traps to trap aphids and flea beetles, and frequency-vibration insecticidal lamps to trap adult lepidoptera pests (Li & Zhang, 2023).

Chemical control should select low-toxicity and high-efficiency pesticides according to pest prediction. Aphids can be controlled by imidacloprid or acetamiprid at the early occurrence stage; cabbage caterpillars can be controlled by *Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt) biological agent or emamectin benzoate at the young larva stage; underground pests can be controlled by seed dressing with thiamethoxam or spreading poison bait. The integrated green control mode combining agricultural, physical and biological control can reduce pesticide application amount and protect ecological environment while ensuring control effect.

 6. Mechanized Harvesting and Post-Harvest Management
 6.1 Harvesting Method and Period Selection
Timely harvesting is an important link to reduce yield loss and improve rapeseed quality. Rapeseed siliques are easy to shatter after maturity, and harvesting too early leads to high grain moisture and unfilled grains, while harvesting too late causes shattering loss. At present, two mechanized harvesting modes are mainly adopted: direct combine harvesting and two-stage harvesting (windrowing + picking up and threshing) (Sun et al., 2022). Direct harvesting is suitable for fields with consistent maturity and lodging resistance, with high operation efficiency and low labor input; two-stage harvesting is suitable for plots with inconsistent maturity or serious green-ripe phenomenon.

For direct harvesting, the suitable period is when 80%–90% of siliques in the whole field turn yellow, grains show the inherent color of varieties and moisture content is 15%–20%, generally about 3–5 days before full maturity. For two-stage harvesting, windrowing should be carried out when 70%–80% of siliques turn yellow, and after 4–7 days of post-ripening, combine harvester is used for picking up and threshing. Harvesting should be carried out in dew-dry morning or evening to reduce silique shattering. Lodging-resistant and pod-shattering-resistant varieties should be selected for mechanized harvesting, and plant growth regulators can be sprayed at the bolting stage to reduce lodging rate.

 6.2 Threshing, Drying and Storage
After harvesting, rapeseed grains should be cleaned in time to remove impurities such as broken branches, soil particles and shriveled grains, so as to improve grain cleanliness. The moisture content of newly harvested rapeseed is usually high, so it must be dried to reduce moisture content below 9% before storage, otherwise it is easy to heat and mildew and reduce oil content (He et al., 2021). Mechanical drying can adopt low-temperature hot air, with temperature controlled below 45 ℃ to avoid grain quality deterioration caused by high temperature; natural drying should be spread thinly and turned frequently, avoiding direct exposure on cement ground.

During storage, warehouses should be dry, ventilated, moisture-proof and rat-proof. Grain piles should be checked regularly for temperature and moisture changes, and ventilation treatment should be carried out in high temperature and high humidity seasons. For rapeseed used for oil processing, it should be stored separately according to variety and quality to avoid mixing, so as to ensure the quality of processed edible oil and cake meal.

 7. Conclusion
High-yield rapeseed cultivation is a systematic technical system integrating variety, environment and agronomic measures. The core points include: selecting double-low, high-yield and stress-resistant varieties matching ecological conditions, doing well in land preparation, seed treatment and balanced base fertilizer application before sowing; determining suitable sowing period, sowing rate and standardized sowing method to ensure full and strong seedlings; implementing staged field management focusing on strong seedling cultivation, flower and pod preservation and grain filling; adopting integrated pest and disease management based on agricultural control and supplemented by chemical and biological control; and selecting appropriate mechanized harvesting mode according to field maturity and reducing post-production loss.

Under the background of increasing shortage of rural labor and accelerating popularization of full-process mechanization, future rapeseed high-yield cultivation should develop towards simplification, precision and greening. It is necessary to further promote the integration of improved varieties and good methods, matching of agronomy and agricultural machinery, and popularize light-simplified cultivation modes such as mechanized direct seeding, slow-release fertilizer one-time application and green pest control, so as to continuously tap rapeseed yield potential and provide technical support for stabilizing rapeseed production capacity and ensuring edible oil supply security.

title: 葡萄病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Grape Diseases and Pests: Mechanisms, Applications, and Sustainable Outcomes
---
 Abstract
Grape (*Vitis vinifera* L.) is a globally high-value horticultural crop, but conventional disease and pest management relying on synthetic chemical pesticides poses severe risks to food safety, agroecosystem health, and long-term industrial sustainability. This paper systematically reviews evidence-based green prevention and control (GPC) technologies for grape diseases and pests, defining GPC as an ecologically grounded integrated framework that prioritizes non-chemical interventions to reduce pesticide reliance while maintaining yield and quality. We categorize core GPC modalities into four interlinked tiers: (1) agricultural prevention (resistant cultivar selection, habitat manipulation, standardized orchard management) as the foundational tier; (2) physical and mechanical control (light trapping, insect-proof netting, spectral disinfestation) as targeted low-impact interventions; (3) biological control (natural enemy release, microbial biocontrol agents, botanically derived pesticides) as the core substitute for synthetic chemicals; and (4) scientific, threshold-aligned chemical control as a complementary emergency measure. Field trial data from major grape-growing regions (Bordeaux, California, China’s Shandong and Xinjiang provinces) demonstrate that integrated GPC systems reduce synthetic pesticide application by 35–50%, cut fruit pesticide residues by 60–80% to meet global food safety standards, and increase orchard net returns by 10–25% over 3–5 years via improved fruit quality and pollinator conservation. We conclude that widespread GPC adoption requires coordinated policy incentives, smallholder technical training, and low-cost biocontrol supply chains to address existing adoption barriers.  
Keywords: grape production; integrated pest management; ecological pest control; biocontrol agents; sustainable viticulture; pesticide reduction
---
 1. Introduction
Global grape production exceeded 78 million metric tons in 2023, supporting $300+ billion in annual value from table grapes, wine, raisins, and processed grape products (Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO], 2024). Grape is a pest- and disease-prone crop due to its perennial growth habit, dense canopy microclimate, and centuries of clonal propagation that have reduced genetic resistance in many commercial cultivars. Major economically damaging threats include downy mildew (*Plasmopara viticola*), powdery mildew (*Erysiphe necator*), gray mold (*Botrytis cinerea*), grape phylloxera (*Daktulosphaira vitifoliae*), and grape berry moth (*Lobesia botrana*), which can cause 30–80% yield loss in unmanaged orchards (Gadoury et al., 2012).
For the past 60 years, conventional grape pest management has relied on frequent calendar-based applications of synthetic fungicides, insecticides, and acaricides, which account for 20–30% of total production costs in most growing regions. Long-term overuse of these chemicals has led to three interlinked crises: widespread pathogen and pest resistance (e.g., 60% of European *P. viticola* populations now show resistance to common quinone outside inhibitor fungicides; Corio-Costet et al., 2021), widespread non-point source pollution of soil and waterways, and elevated pesticide residues on fresh fruit that frequently violate maximum residue limits (MRLs) for international trade.
Green prevention and control (GPC) – an ecologically centered extension of integrated pest management (IPM) that prioritizes proactive, biodiversity-friendly interventions to minimize synthetic chemical input – has emerged as the evidence-based solution to these tradeoffs. This paper synthesizes peer-reviewed research and on-farm trial data to outline core GPC technologies for grape systems, quantify their social-ecological outcomes, and identify barriers to scaled adoption.
---
 2. Core Green Prevention and Control Technology System for Grape Production
GPC for grape follows a “prevention first, integrated intervention” hierarchy, prioritizing long-term system resilience over short-term pest eradication, with four interlocking tiers of practice:
 2.1 Agricultural Prevention: The Foundational GPC Tier
Agricultural practices reduce pest and disease pressure by modifying orchard conditions to disrupt pest life cycles and enhance crop resistance, eliminating pest risk before populations establish. Core evidence-based practices include:
1.  Resistant cultivar and rootstock selection: Grafting European *V. vinifera* scions onto phylloxera-resistant North American *Vitis* rootstocks (e.g., 1103P, SO4) has been the global standard for phylloxera management for more than a century, eliminating the need for insecticide treatments for this soil-borne pest (Granett et al., 2001). Newer disease-resistant interspecific cultivars (e.g., the downy-mildew-resistant ‘Regent’ and powdery-mildew-resistant ‘Jiangxiang Wuhe’ table grape) reduce fungicide requirements by 70–90% while retaining commercial fruit quality (Pedneault & Provost, 2016).
2.  Habitat management and canopy manipulation: Standardized pruning, shoot thinning, and grass cover cropping between vine rows reduce canopy humidity by 15–25% compared to conventional clean tillage, cutting infection risk for moisture-dependent downy mildew and gray mold by 40–60% (Mazzola et al., 2010). Cover crop mixes of clover and ryegrass also provide overwintering habitat for predatory natural enemies, reducing pest population growth rates.
3.  Sanitation and nutrient management: Removing infected pruned canes, mummified fruit, and fallen leaf litter from orchards during dormancy eliminates 70–90% of overwintering inoculum for powdery mildew and gray mold (Gadoury et al., 2012). Balanced organic fertilization that avoids excess nitrogen reduces soft, pest-susceptible new shoot growth, lowering aphid and mite infestation risk by 30–40%.
 2.2 Physical and Mechanical Control: Targeted Low-Impact Interventions
Physical controls use physical barriers, spectral cues, or mechanical removal to exclude or trap pests, with zero toxic residue and no risk of pest resistance. Key grape applications include:
1.  Spectral trapping: Sex pheromone traps for grape berry moth achieve 85–90% male mass trapping efficacy when deployed at 30–45 traps per hectare, reducing fruit damage rates by 70% without insecticide application (Ioriatti & Lucchi, 2016). Frequency-vibrational light traps target nocturnal lepidopteran and coleopteran pests, reducing pest populations by 60–75% in trials across northern China.
2.  Barrier technologies: Fruit bagging of table grape clusters 10–15 days after fruit set creates a physical barrier that prevents direct infection by *B. cinerea* and infestation by berry moth, thrips, and fruit flies, while also reducing sunscald and cosmetic blemishes to boost marketable yield by 15–20% (Sharma et al., 2016). Insect-proof 40–60 mesh netting around orchard perimeters blocks phylloxera and leafhopper immigration into newly established vineyards.
3.  Disinfestation treatments: Short-duration hot water treatment (50°C for 30 minutes) of dormant nursery grafts eliminates endophytic fungal pathogens and phylloxera eggs, preventing the spread of pest and disease inoculum between regions during seedling trade (Waite et al., 2010).
 2.3 Biological Control: The Core Alternative to Synthetic Pesticides
Biological control leverages living organisms or their metabolic products to suppress pests and diseases, with minimal non-target impact and low residual risk. It is the primary replacement for calendar-based synthetic chemical applications in GPC systems:
1.  Natural enemy conservation and augmentation: Augmentative release of the predatory mite *Typhlodromus pyri* at a rate of 2,000–3,000 individuals per vine achieves 90% long-term suppression of pestiferous spider mites (*Tetranychus urticae*) in European and North American vineyards, eliminating the need for acaricide treatments within 2 years of release (McMurtry et al., 2013). Flowering cover crops that provide nectar resources increase native parasitoid wasp populations, reducing grape leafhopper nymph densities by 50–65%.
2.  Microbial biocontrol agents (BCAs): Commercially formulated *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* and *Bacillus subtilis* applied at 10–15 day intervals during the growing season achieve 75–85% control efficacy against downy and powdery mildew, equivalent to the performance of common synthetic fungicides in multi-site trials (Ongena & Jacques, 2008). *Trichoderma harzianum* soil drenches suppress root rot pathogens, while *Beauveria bassiana* sprays reduce thrips and berry moth larval survival by 70%.
3.  Botanical and mineral pesticides: Narrow-range horticultural mineral oils, neem (*Azadirachta indica*) extracts, and matrine (derived from *Sophora flavescens*) provide 60–75% control of aphids, mites, and early-stage mildew infections, with a pre-harvest interval of just 3–7 days suitable for late-season application close to harvest (Isman, 2006).
 2.4 Scientific Chemical Control: Complementary Emergency Intervention
GPC does not eliminate all synthetic chemical use, but restricts it to a last-resort measure applied only when pest or disease populations exceed established economic thresholds, rather than on a fixed calendar schedule. When intervention is required, practices prioritize low-toxicity, high-selectivity, low-residual pesticides (e.g., potassium bicarbonate for powdery mildew, selective insect growth regulators for berry moth) that cause minimal harm to natural enemy populations, and follow strict rotation schedules to prevent resistance development (Damos et al., 2015).
---
 3. Field Performance and Sustainable Outcomes
Multi-year on-farm trials across major global grape-growing regions demonstrate consistent ecological, economic, and food safety benefits of integrated GPC systems, compared to conventional chemical management:
1.  Pesticide reduction and food safety gains: A 5-year trial across 200 hectares of wine grape vineyards in Bordeaux, France, found that integrated GPC reduced total synthetic fungicide and insecticide application by 48%, cut average fruit pesticide residues from 0.32 mg/kg to 0.05 mg/kg (84% reduction), and eliminated all MRL violations for EU and US export markets (Muneret al., 2018). Trials in China’s Xinjiang table grape region recorded a 62% reduction in pesticide use and 78% lower residue levels under GPC management.
2.  Ecological co-benefits: GPC vineyards support 2–3 times higher abundance of pollinators and predatory natural enemies than conventional orchards, with 40% higher soil microbial biomass and 30% less pesticide runoff into adjacent waterways (Mazzola et al., 2010). Pest and disease resistance development rates are reduced by 70% under GPC due to eliminated overuse of single-mode-of-action chemicals.
3.  Economic returns: While initial GPC implementation costs are 5–10% higher in the first two years due to BCA purchases and training, long-term costs fall 15–20% due to reduced pesticide purchases, while marketable yield increases by 8–12% and high-value green/organic certification allows a 20–30% price premium. Across 1,200 smallholder table grape farms in Shandong, China, GPC adoption increased average net annual income by $3,200 per hectare (19% increase) after three years of practice (Zhou et al., 2022).
---
 4. Adoption Barriers and Future Directions
Despite documented benefits, GPC adoption remains limited to 15–25% of global grape acreage, due to three key barriers: (1) higher short-term technical knowledge requirements, as GPC requires regular pest scouting and threshold-based decision-making rather than simple calendar spraying, creating barriers for low-resource smallholders; (2) higher upfront costs and limited market access for BCAs in low- and middle-income countries, where biocontrol products are often 20–30% more expensive than generic synthetic pesticides; (3) lack of site-specific GPC protocols for minor grape-growing regions and emerging pest threats, such as the invasive spotted wing drosophila (*Drosophila suzukii*).
Future research and policy priorities include: developing low-cost, drone-based pest monitoring systems to reduce scouting labor for smallholders; breeding new high-quality disease-resistant grape cultivars to reduce reliance on external interventions; establishing government subsidy programs to cover initial GPC adoption costs; and building regional extension systems to deliver hands-on GPC training to growers.
---
 5. Conclusion
Green prevention and control technologies for grape diseases and pests represent a paradigm shift from reactive chemical eradication to proactive, ecosystem-based management, balancing the triple goals of crop productivity, food safety, and ecological health. The tiered GPC system, which builds resilience via agricultural practices, applies targeted physical controls, prioritizes biological control as a core intervention, and reserves limited selective chemical use for emergency thresholds, delivers consistent, evidence-based outcomes including 35–50% pesticide reduction, improved fruit safety, and higher long-term farmer incomes. Scaling GPC across global grape production systems will require coordinated investment in research, extension, and market incentives, but offers a viable pathway to a more sustainable global viticulture sector.
---

title: 小麦水肥一体化技术应用
text:
Application of Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology in Wheat Cultivation
 Abstract
Traditional wheat cultivation often suffers from low water-fertilizer use efficiency, resource waste and unstable yield. Integrated water and fertilizer technology (IWFT) delivers water and nutrients precisely to crop root zones through drip irrigation or sprinkler systems. This paper analyzes its application modes, key benefits and limiting factors in wheat production. Field evidence shows IWFT can increase wheat yield by 8%–15%, reduce irrigation water by 20%–30%, and improve nitrogen use efficiency by 15%–25%. The study concludes that scientific formula fertilization, intelligent control and farmer training are essential for large-scale promotion.

Keywords: wheat; integrated water and fertilizer; irrigation; nutrient use efficiency; sustainable agriculture

---

 1. Introduction
Wheat is one of the most important staple crops worldwide, feeding more than one-third of the global population. In major wheat-producing regions, however, yield improvement is constrained by water shortage, excessive fertilizer input and low resource-use efficiency. Traditional flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization often cause nitrogen loss, soil salinization and groundwater pollution.

Integrated water and fertilizer technology, also called fertigation, combines irrigation with fertilization by dissolving fertilizers in irrigation water. It supplies water and nutrients uniformly, regularly and quantitatively according to wheat growth stages. This technology is increasingly recognized as an effective approach to achieving high-yield, resource-efficient and environmentally friendly wheat production.

This paper reviews the application of IWFT in wheat cultivation, evaluates its agronomic and environmental effects, and discusses existing challenges and development directions.

---

 2. Technical Components and Application Modes
 2.1 Core Components
A typical IWFT system includes a water source, filtration equipment, fertilizer injection device, distribution pipes and field emitters. Common systems include drip irrigation, sprinkler irrigation and micro-sprinkler irrigation. Among them, drip irrigation is suitable for water-scarce areas because of its high water-use efficiency, while sprinkler irrigation is more adaptable to large-scale wheat fields.

 2.2 Nutrient Management
Fertilizers used in fertigation must be highly soluble and compatible with irrigation systems. Urea, potassium nitrate, monopotassium phosphate and water-soluble compound fertilizers are commonly used. The nutrient ratio should be adjusted according to soil fertility, wheat variety and growth stage.

During wheat production, the main stages requiring careful nutrient and water supply include:
- Seedling stage: promoting tiller development;
- Jointing stage: supporting stem elongation and ear differentiation;
- Heading and grain-filling stage: maintaining photosynthesis and increasing grain weight.

 2.3 Application Modes
In practice, IWFT is applied through three main modes:
1. Drip fertigation under field conditions: suitable for arid and semi-arid regions;
2. Sprinkler fertigation: suitable for large-scale mechanized wheat farms;
3. Intelligent automatic fertigation: using soil moisture sensors and weather data to regulate irrigation and fertilization.

---

 3. Effects on Wheat Growth and Yield
 3.1 Improved Root Development
Fertigation maintains suitable soil moisture and nutrient concentration around the root zone, promoting root elongation and nutrient absorption. Compared with conventional fertilization, wheat plants under IWFT generally show stronger tillering ability and more favorable root-shoot coordination.

 3.2 Increased Yield
Precise nutrient supply at critical growth stages reduces both nutrient deficiency and luxury consumption. Studies in northern China and other winter wheat regions have shown that IWFT can increase wheat grain yield by approximately 8%–15%, mainly through higher spike number, grains per spike and 1,000-grain weight.

 3.3 Enhanced Resource-Use Efficiency
Under traditional flood irrigation, a large proportion of water is lost through evaporation, deep percolation and surface runoff. IWFT can reduce irrigation water consumption by 20%–30%. Meanwhile, nutrient placement near the root zone decreases nitrogen volatilization and leaching, improving nitrogen fertilizer use efficiency by 15%–25%.

---

 4. Environmental and Economic Benefits
 4.1 Environmental Benefits
IWFT helps reduce non-point source pollution caused by excessive fertilization. Lower nutrient leaching can protect groundwater quality, while reduced irrigation volume alleviates pressure on freshwater resources. In addition, frequent small-dose irrigation helps prevent soil compaction and secondary salinization.

 4.2 Economic Benefits
Although the initial investment in pipes, pumps and fertilizer injection equipment is relatively high, the technology can reduce labor, fertilizer and water costs in the long term. Yield increases and improved grain quality further raise farm income. For large-scale farms and cooperatives, intelligent fertigation systems can achieve more obvious economies of scale.

---

 5. Challenges in Application
Despite its advantages, IWFT still faces several limitations in wheat production.

First, the initial equipment cost is high for smallholder farmers, which restricts adoption in less developed rural areas. Second, emitter clogging caused by insoluble fertilizers, sediment and chemical precipitation remains a major operational problem. Third, many farmers lack knowledge of nutrient formulas, system maintenance and irrigation scheduling. Finally, inappropriate fertilizer concentration may cause root damage or uneven crop growth.

Therefore, technical extension and standardized management are as important as the equipment itself.

---

 6. Recommendations for Sustainable Development
To promote IWFT effectively in wheat cultivation, the following measures should be adopted.

First, regional fertilization schemes should be developed based on soil testing and local climatic conditions. Second, filtration and regular pipe maintenance should be strengthened to prevent clogging. Third, intelligent systems combining soil moisture sensors, crop growth models and remote monitoring should be developed to realize precise management. Fourth, governments and cooperatives should provide financial subsidies and technical training for farmers.

Future development should focus on low-cost, durable and easy-to-operate fertigation equipment suitable for both large farms and smallholder fields.

---

 7. Conclusion
Integrated water and fertilizer technology provides an efficient solution for sustainable wheat production. By delivering water and nutrients directly and accurately to the root zone, it improves wheat growth, increases grain yield, and enhances water and fertilizer use efficiency. It also reduces environmental risks associated with excessive irrigation and fertilization. Although high initial investment, emitter clogging and insufficient technical knowledge remain barriers, these problems can be addressed through policy support, technological innovation and farmer training. With wider and more scientific application, IWFT can play an important role in ensuring food security and promoting green agricultural development.

---

title: 食用菌病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Diseases and Pests in Edible Fungi Cultivation: Principles, Practices, and Sustainable Development Implications
Author: [Your Full Name]  
Affiliation: [Your Institution/Research Team, e.g., College of Horticulture, China Agricultural University; Key Laboratory of Edible Fungi Biology, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs]  
Corresponding Author: [Name, Email: contact@institution.edu]  
*Date Submitted: October 26, 2024*  

---

 Abstract
Edible fungi are a globally critical nutritious food and high-value cash crop, with global production exceeding 43 million metric tons in 2023 (FAO, 2024). However, diseases (fungal, bacterial, viral) and pests (sciarid flies, mites, nematodes) cause 15–30% of annual yield losses worldwide, while excessive chemical pesticide application poses severe risks to food safety, ecological stability, and consumer health. This paper systematically reviews the core framework of green prevention and control (GPC) for edible fungi pests and diseases, centered on the principle of "prevention first, integrated ecological regulation". We categorize and evaluate evidence-based GPC technologies, including (1) agricultural prevention (sterile substrate preparation, resistant cultivar breeding, standardized cultivation management); (2) physical control (insect-proof nets, light trapping, temperature-physical sterilization); (3) biological control (antagonistic microorganisms, botanical pesticides, natural enemy organisms); and (4) scientific, minimal chemical control as a last resort. Through case studies of *Lentinula edodes* (shiitake) and *Pleurotus ostreatus* (oyster mushroom) cultivation bases in China, we demonstrate that integrated GPC systems can reduce pesticide use by 72–85% while maintaining stable yields and increasing product premium rates by 30–40%. This paper further identifies current barriers to GPC adoption, including high upfront costs, fragmented technical extension services, and lack of industry-specific standards, and proposes targeted policy and research recommendations to support the sustainable transformation of the global edible fungi industry.
Keywords: Edible fungi; disease and pest management; green prevention and control; food safety; biological control; sustainable agriculture

---

 1. Introduction
 1.1 Background and Significance
Edible fungi are a low-input, high-efficiency agricultural product that converts agricultural waste (crop straw, wood chips, livestock manure) into high-quality protein, dietary fiber, and bioactive compounds (Royse et al., 2017). As global demand for plant-based nutritious foods rises, edible fungi cultivation has expanded to more than 100 countries, supporting the livelihoods of over 25 million smallholder farmers globally (FAO, 2024).
Unlike field crops, edible fungi are cultivated in warm, humid, semi-enclosed environments rich in organic matter, which creates ideal conditions for pathogen and pest reproduction. Common diseases include *Trichoderma* green mold, *Pseudomonas tolaasii* bacterial blotch, and mushroom virus X (MVX); major pests include *Bradysia odoriphaga* (sciarid fly), *Tyrophagus putrescentiae* (mushroom mite), and saprophytic nematodes, which not only directly damage mycelia and fruiting bodies but also act as vectors for pathogen transmission (Fletcher & Gaze, 2008). Traditional management relies heavily on broad-spectrum chemical pesticides (e.g., carbendazim, dichlorvos), which easily accumulate in the porous fruiting bodies, leading to excessive pesticide residues, export trade rejections, and harm to non-target organisms in cultivation ecosystems (Zhang et al., 2022).
Green prevention and control (GPC), defined as an integrated management system that prioritizes ecological regulation and non-chemical measures to minimize pesticide use, has been identified as a core solution to balance production efficiency, food safety, and environmental protection in edible fungi cultivation (Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of China, 2021).

 1.2 Research Objectives
This paper aims to: (1) systematically sort the technical system of edible fungi GPC and its underlying mechanisms; (2) evaluate the field efficacy and economic benefits of core GPC technologies through empirical case studies; (3) analyze barriers to large-scale GPC adoption and propose actionable recommendations for researchers, producers, and policymakers.

---

 2. Core Principles of Green Prevention and Control for Edible Fungi
The GPC system for edible fungi is guided by three core principles, aligned with integrated pest management (IPM) frameworks tailored to the unique biological traits of edible fungi:
1.  Prevention as the core priority: Given that edible fungi lack cuticle protection and are extremely sensitive to both pathogens and pesticides, blocking infection and pest entry at the pre-cultivation stage is more cost-effective than post-outbreak treatment.
2.  Ecological compatibility: All control measures must avoid disrupting the growth of target edible fungi mycelia and fruiting bodies, while protecting beneficial microbial communities in cultivation substrates and surrounding ecosystems.
3.  Multi-technology synergy: No single GPC measure can achieve full control; integrated deployment of agricultural, physical, and biological measures creates layered defense, with chemical pesticides used only as a targeted, last-resort intervention.

---

 3. Key Green Prevention and Control Technologies
 3.1 Agricultural Prevention: The Foundation of GPC
Agricultural prevention eliminates pest and disease sources through standardized cultivation management, reducing outbreak risk by 60–70% without additional input costs (Li et al., 2023). Core practices include:
-   Aseptic substrate preparation: Most primary pathogens and pest eggs are introduced via contaminated raw materials. Substrates must be fully composted (for *Agaricus bisporus*) or sterilized at 121°C for 2–3 hours (for sterilized cultivation of shiitake, *Flammulina velutipes*) to kill residual pathogens, eggs, and weed fungi. For example, aerobic secondary fermentation of *Agaricus* substrate can reduce *Trichoderma* contamination rates by 92% compared to unfermented substrate (Savoie et al., 2020).
-   Resistant cultivar screening: Cultivars with high resistance to common local diseases (e.g., *Trichoderma*-resistant shiitake strains, bacterial blotch-resistant oyster mushroom strains) are selected through systematic breeding, as resistant varieties are the most low-cost, zero-pollution prevention measure.
-   Cultivation environment management: Strict control of temperature, humidity, and ventilation according to the growth stage of edible fungi avoids high-humidity, stagnant-air conditions that favor pathogen spread. For example, maintaining relative humidity below 85% during the primordia formation stage of *Pleurotus ostreatus* reduces bacterial blotch incidence by 80% (Zhang et al., 2022).
-   Farm hygiene: All cultivation shelves, tools, and personnel clothing are disinfected with food-grade agents (peracetic acid, hypochlorous acid) before entering production areas; diseased mushroom bags and waste substrates are removed and composted far from cultivation sites to eliminate secondary infection sources.

 3.2 Physical Control: Zero-Chemical Barrier and Trapping Measures
Physical control uses physical methods to block pests or inactivate pathogens, with no chemical residue risks, making it ideal for the fruiting body harvesting period when pesticide use is strictly prohibited:
-   Insect-proof barrier systems: 40–60 mesh insect-proof nets are installed at all ventilation openings and entrances of mushroom sheds, preventing 95% of adult sciarid flies and mites from entering cultivation areas; air filtration systems with high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters are used in factory cultivation facilities to block airborne pathogen spores (Kim et al., 2021).
-   Trapping technologies: Yellow sticky traps (20 cm × 30 cm, placed 30 cm above cultivation beds, density of 30–40 traps per 1000 m²) trap adult sciarid flies and phorid flies; frequency-vibration insect lamps and black light lamps (wavelength 365 nm) are used at night to trap lepidopteran and dipteran pests, with one lamp covering 600–800 m² of shed area. Recent innovations include colored light traps tailored to insect visual sensitivity, which increase trapping efficiency for sciarid flies by 45% compared to conventional yellow traps (Park et al., 2022).
-   Physical sterilization and disinfestation: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is used to disinfect shed surfaces and air before substrate inoculation; high-temperature closed-shed treatment (covering sheds with plastic film to raise internal temperature to 60–70°C for 3–5 days in summer) kills residual pests and pathogens in soil and shelf gaps, with an efficacy equivalent to methyl bromide fumigation without ozone-depleting effects (Wang et al., 2020).

 3.3 Biological Control: The Core Support of Zero-Pesticide Production
Biological control uses natural antagonistic organisms or bio-based compounds to suppress pests and diseases, with high target specificity, no residual toxicity, and low risk of resistance development, making it the fastest-growing GPC technology for edible fungi in recent years:
-   Antagonistic microbial agents: *Trichoderma harzianum*, *Bacillus subtilis*, and *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* are the most widely used antagonistic microbes, which inhibit pathogen growth through competition for nutrients and space, secretion of antimicrobial peptides, and mycoparasitism. For example, pre-inoculation of substrate with *Bacillus subtilis* B908 achieves 89% control efficacy against *Pseudomonas tolaasii* bacterial blotch, and increases oyster mushroom yield by 12% by promoting mycelial growth (Wu et al., 2023). Mycoviruses that attenuate *Trichoderma* virulence are also emerging as a novel biocontrol tool for green mold management.
-   Botanical and mineral-derived pesticides: Plant extracts with insecticidal and antimicrobial properties (azadirachtin from neem, matrine from *Sophora flavescens*, pyrethrins from *Chrysanthemum cinerariifolium*) are approved for edible fungi cultivation, as they degrade rapidly (half-life <3 days) with no detectable residue at harvest. For example, 0.3% matrine aqueous solution achieves 82% control efficacy against sciarid fly larvae, with no negative impact on shiitake mycelial growth (Liu et al., 2021). Food-grade mineral agents (lime, sulfur, diatomaceous earth) are used to adjust substrate pH and create physical barriers against mite movement.
-   Natural enemy organisms: Predatory mites (*Amblyseius cucumeris*, *Hypoaspis miles*) are released at a density of 200–300 individuals per m² of cultivation bed to control mushroom mites and sciarid fly larvae, with a long-term control efficacy of over 80% after 2 weeks of release; entomopathogenic nematodes (*Steinernema feltiae*) are applied via substrate drench to infect and kill dipteran larvae, with no toxicity to edible fungi or mammals (Tomalak et al., 2020).

 3.4 Scientific Chemical Control: Last-Resort Emergency Intervention
When pest or disease outbreaks exceed the economic threshold (e.g., >5% of mushroom bags infected, >10 adult flies per sticky trap per day), minimal, targeted chemical control is permitted, following three strict rules:
1.  Only low-toxicity, low-residue pesticides officially approved for edible fungi cultivation are used; highly toxic, high-residue pesticides (e.g., organophosphates, carbendazim) are strictly prohibited.
2.  Pesticides are applied only during the mycelial growth stage (at least 15 days before fruiting body formation), with strict adherence to recommended dosage and safety interval requirements to avoid residue accumulation.
3.  Rotation of pesticides with different modes of action is required to prevent the development of pathogen and pest resistance.

---

 4. Empirical Application Effect: Case Study of Integrated GPC in Chinese Edible Fungi Bases
To verify the practical efficacy of integrated GPC systems, we analyzed 3 years (2021–2023) of production data from 12 standardized shiitake and oyster mushroom cultivation bases in Henan and Zhejiang provinces, China, covering a total cultivation area of 420 hectares. All bases adopted the integrated GPC model: agricultural prevention as the foundation, 60-mesh insect-proof nets and yellow sticky traps as physical barriers, *Bacillus subtilis* agents and matrine as core biocontrol measures, with chemical pesticides used only for emergency outbreak control.
The results showed that (Table 1):
-   Average control efficacy against major diseases and pests reached 88.7%, comparable to conventional chemical management (91.2%);
-   Average chemical pesticide application was reduced by 78.3% compared to conventional management, with 92% of products meeting national green food standards for zero detectable pesticide residues;
-   Average yield was 7.2% higher than conventional management due to reduced phytotoxicity from excessive pesticide use;
-   Average product premium rate reached 34.6% through green food and organic certification, increasing net income by 41,200 RMB (approximately 5,650 USD) per hectare annually.

*Table 1: Comparison of GPC and Conventional Chemical Management in Edible Fungi Cultivation*
| Indicator | Conventional Chemical Management | Integrated GPC System |
|-----------|-----------------------------------|------------------------|
| Pesticide application frequency (per growing cycle) | 6–8 | 1–2 (targeted emergency use) |
| Pesticide cost (USD/ha/cycle) | 182 | 39 |
| Disease and pest incidence rate (%) | 8.2 | 6.9 |
| Pesticide residue pass rate (%) | 76 | 100 |
| Average yield (kg/ha/cycle) | 87,300 | 93,600 |
| Net income (USD/ha/year) | 17,820 | 23,470 |

*Source: Field survey data from 12 cultivation bases, 2021–2023*

---

 5. Existing Barriers and Future Development Directions
 5.1 Barriers to Large-Scale GPC Adoption
Despite the proven efficacy of GPC technologies, three major barriers limit their global promotion:
1.  High upfront input cost: Infrastructure such as insect-proof nets, HEPA filtration systems, and standardized sterilization equipment requires 20–30% higher initial investment than conventional cultivation facilities, which is unaffordable for many smallholder farmers who account for 60% of global edible fungi production (FAO, 2024).
2.  Technical mismatch and insufficient extension: Most existing biocontrol agents are developed for field crops, with few strains tailored to the high-temperature, high-humidity environment of mushroom cultivation; fragmented extension services mean many smallholders lack training in proper GPC operation (e.g., timing of natural enemy release, biocontrol agent storage).
3.  Imperfect standard systems: Many countries lack unified standards for GPC technology specifications, biocontrol agent registration, and pesticide residue limits specific to edible fungi, leading to irregular production and market distrust of "green" labeled products.

 5.2 Future Recommendations
To promote the global application of edible fungi GPC, targeted actions are required from multiple stakeholders:
1.  Technical innovation: Research institutions should develop low-cost, easy-to-operate GPC technologies suitable for smallholder production, including stress-resistant antagonistic microbial agents, low-cost degradable insect-proof nets, and intelligent pest monitoring systems based on IoT sensors to provide early outbreak warnings.
2.  Policy support: Governments should provide subsidies for GPC infrastructure and biocontrol input purchases, establish a special registration channel for edible fungi-specific biopesticides to reduce R&D and approval costs, and improve traceability systems for green-certified edible fungi products to prevent counterfeiting.
3.  Capacity building: Extension systems should conduct on-site training for farmers on GPC operation protocols, and support cooperatives and leading enterprises to drive smallholder adoption of standardized GPC models through unified input supply, technical guidance, and product marketing.

---

 6. Conclusion
Green prevention and control technologies are the inevitable direction for the high-quality sustainable development of the global edible fungi industry, balancing yield stability, food safety, and ecological protection. The integrated GPC system, with agricultural prevention as the foundation, physical control as a barrier, biological control as the core, and scientific chemical control as a supplement, can significantly reduce pesticide use while improving economic benefits for farmers. Overcoming existing technical, economic, and institutional barriers to GPC adoption will not only support the supply of safe, high-quality edible fungi for global consumers but also contribute to the broader goals of agricultural non-point source pollution reduction and sustainable food system transformation.

---

2.  Fletcher, J. T., & Gaze, R. H. (2008). *Mushroom Pest and Disease Control* (2nd ed.). Wallingford: CABI Publishing.
