title: 马铃薯种植增收增产技术分析
text:
Analysis of Yield-Increasing and Income-Enhancing Technologies for Potato Cultivation: Mechanisms, Practices, and Sustainability
 Abstract
Potatoes (*Solanum tuberosum* L.) rank as the world’s fourth-largest staple food crop, serving as a critical pillar for food security and agricultural income in smallholder and commercial farming systems. However, persistent yield gaps and stagnant farmer incomes—driven by degraded soil, substandard seed systems, suboptimal management, and climate volatility—limit the crop’s productive and economic potential. This paper systematically analyzes evidence-based, scalable technologies for potato yield improvement and income growth, integrating high-quality seed systems, soil and nutrient management, water regulation, stress mitigation, and digital agricultural extension. Field trial and farm survey data demonstrate that combined adoption of certified virus-free seed, balanced fertilization, drip irrigation, and integrated pest management can increase tuber yield by 35%–60% and raise net household income by 28%–45% relative to conventional practices. The study further identifies upfront input costs, technical knowledge gaps, and weak value-chain linkages as core adoption barriers, and proposes targeted policy and extension strategies to support inclusive, sustainable potato industry development.

Keywords: Potato cultivation; yield improvement; income growth; seed potato; sustainable intensification; climate-resilient agriculture

---

 1. Introduction
Potatoes are cultivated across over 100 countries, with an annual global production exceeding 350 million tonnes (Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO], 2023). Compared with major cereal crops, potatoes produce more edible energy and protein per unit land area and time, while adapting to broad agroecological zones from cool highlands to subtropical plains. In low- and middle-income regions, potato farming provides both household food supplies and cash income through fresh market sales and processing industry linkages.

Despite this potential, actual farm yields often fall 40%–60% below attainable yield benchmarks. Key constraints include virus accumulation in farm-saved seed, soil nutrient imbalance, drought or waterlogging stress, late blight and other pest pressures, and post-harvest losses. Traditional cultivation practices relying on retained tubers,经验性施肥 (experience-based fertilization), and flood irrigation not only suppress yield but also raise production risk and reduce marketable tuber rate. Against this background, identifying technically effective, economically viable, and environmentally sustainable cultivation technologies is essential to boost potato productivity and farmer livelihoods.

This paper aims to: (1) categorize core yield-increasing potato production technologies and clarify their agronomic mechanisms; (2) evaluate their economic returns and income-enhancing pathways; and (3) discuss adoption constraints and supporting measures for scaling.

---

 2. Core Yield-Increasing Potato Cultivation Technologies
 2.1 Certified Virus-Free Seed Potato Systems
Seed quality is the foundational determinant of potato yield. Potatoes are vegetatively propagated, so viruses such as Potato Virus Y (PVY), Potato Leaf Roll Virus (PLRV), and Potato Virus X (PVX) accumulate across successive generations of farm-saved tubers, causing seed degeneration, reduced plant vigor, and yield losses of 30%–70% in severe cases (Struik & Wiersema, 2012).

Certified virus-free seed potatoes are produced through apical meristem tissue culture, virus detection, mini-tuber production in aeroponic or screen-house systems, and graded field multiplication. Key technical components include:
- adoption of Generation 1 (G1) to Generation 3 (G3) certified seed with documented varietal purity and health status;
- pre-sprouting (chitting) under diffused light to promote uniform emergence;
- seed tuber grading and cutting with disinfected tools, with each seed piece retaining 1–2 robust sprouts;
- scheduled seed renewal every 2–3 cropping seasons to prevent virus re-infection.

On-farm trials in Southwest China and East Africa show that replacing farm-saved seed with certified seed alone can raise yields by 20%–40%, while improving tuber shape, size uniformity, and marketable ratio (Gildemacher et al., 2011).

 2.2 Soil Management and Balanced Nutrient Regulation
Potatoes require loose, well-aerated soils for tuber initiation and bulking. Long-term intensive tillage and imbalanced chemical fertilizer use often lead to soil compaction, organic matter decline, and low nutrient-use efficiency.

 2.2.1 Soil physical improvement
Ridge planting, deep plowing (25–30 cm), and hilling are widely adopted to enlarge the loose soil layer around tubers, reduce greening, and improve drainage. In heavy clay soils, straw mulching or incorporation of decomposed organic matter enhances aggregation and aeration. Conservation agriculture practices, including reduced tillage combined with cover crops, can improve long-term soil structure, although their short-term yield performance depends on local weed and moisture conditions.

 2.2.2 Site-specific nutrient management
Potatoes have high demand for potassium (K), followed by nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P). Balanced fertilization based on soil testing typically follows an N:P₂O₅:K₂O ratio of approximately 1:0.5:1.2–1.5, adjusted for target yield and soil fertility. Excess nitrogen promotes luxurious above-ground growth, delays tuberization, and increases disease susceptibility, while sufficient potassium improves starch accumulation, tuber quality, and stress tolerance.

Integrated nutrient management combines:
- basal application of decomposed farmyard manure or compost;
- split nitrogen application at emergence, tuber initiation, and bulking stages;
- water-soluble potassium fertilizer through fertigation;
- supplemental calcium, magnesium, and micronutrients such as boron and zinc where deficient.

Meta-analyses indicate that soil-test-based balanced fertilization increases potato yield by 12%–25% and raises nitrogen-use efficiency by 15%–30% compared with conventional N-heavy fertilization.

 2.3 Precision Water Management
Potatoes are shallow-rooted and sensitive to both water deficit and waterlogging. Tuber initiation and bulking stages are critical water-demand periods. Severe drought causes irregular tuber shape, secondary growth, and yield reduction, whereas waterlogging induces root hypoxia, tuber rot, and increased disease incidence.

Drip irrigation and sprinkler irrigation significantly improve water-use efficiency compared with flood irrigation. Drip irrigation, particularly when integrated with fertigation, delivers water and nutrients directly to the root zone, maintains stable soil moisture, and reduces nutrient leaching. Scheduling irrigation according to tensiometer readings or soil moisture thresholds (generally maintaining 60%–80% of field capacity) can increase marketable yield by 15%–30% and reduce water consumption by 30%–50%. In rainfed production zones, contour ridges, mulching, and rainwater harvesting ponds serve as low-cost adaptive measures.

 2.4 Integrated Pest, Disease, and Stress Management
Late blight (*Phytophthora infestans*) remains the most destructive potato disease, capable of destroying foliage within days under cool, humid conditions. Other major threats include early blight, bacterial wilt, potato cyst nematode, aphids, and tuber moth.

Integrated pest management (IPM) combines resistant cultivars, healthy seed, crop rotation (typically with non-solanaceous crops for 3–4 years), field sanitation, monitoring-based forecasting, and rational fungicide or insecticide application. Late blight decision-support systems help farmers spray according to infection risk rather than fixed schedules, reducing pesticide use by 20%–40% while maintaining disease control. For bacterial wilt, where chemical control is limited, resistant varieties, clean seed, and rotation with non-host crops are central management strategies.

Climate-resilient practices also include heat-tolerant variety selection, adjusted planting dates to avoid tuberization under high night temperatures, and mulch to moderate soil temperature. High temperature during tuber initiation can substantially reduce tuber set and increase physiological disorders, making planting schedule optimization especially important under climate change.

 2.5 Dense Planting, Canopy Management, and Mechanization
Optimal plant density balances individual tuber size and total yield. It varies by variety, target market, and soil fertility: processing varieties often require densities that favor uniform medium tubers, while fresh-market varieties may target larger tuber size. Standardized ridge spacing, mechanical sowing, and precision hilling improve operation uniformity and reduce labor input.

Full-process mechanization—including land preparation, planting, ridging, spraying, harvesting, and grading—lowers labor costs and reduces tuber injury during harvest. Although machinery requires larger operational scale, smallholder farmers can access equipment through cooperatives and custom farming services, enabling technology adoption without individual ownership.

---

 3. Income-Enhancing Mechanisms Beyond Yield Growth
Yield increase alone does not guarantee proportional income growth. Income enhancement depends on marketable yield, production cost, quality premium, seasonal price, and post-harvest loss control.

 3.1 Improving Marketable Tuber Rate and Quality
Certified seed, balanced potassium nutrition, proper hilling, water stability, and disease control jointly reduce malformed, greened, diseased, and mechanically damaged tubers. A higher marketable tuber rate directly increases saleable output. For processing potatoes, dry matter content, reducing sugar level, tuber shape, and size uniformity determine contract eligibility and premium prices. Variety selection aligned with chip processing, French fry production, or fresh table markets therefore creates additional quality-based returns.

 3.2 Reducing Costs and Improving Production Efficiency
Drip fertigation reduces water, fertilizer, and labor costs; monitoring-based IPM lowers excessive pesticide expenditure; mechanization alleviates seasonal labor bottlenecks. Even where gross yield gains are moderate, cost savings can significantly improve net profit. Technical packages should therefore be evaluated by net return rather than yield alone.

 3.3 Extending Storage and Adjusting Marketing Periods
Potato prices frequently decline sharply during harvest concentration. Ventilated storage, cold storage adapted to processing quality requirements, and sprout-control management allow farmers to delay sales into off-season periods. However, storage is profitable only when price differences compensate for weight loss, energy costs, and rot risk. Smallholder cooperative storage can reduce per-unit costs and strengthen bargaining power.

 3.4 Strengthening Value-Chain Linkages
Contract farming with processing enterprises, standardized grading, traceability systems, and direct supply to supermarkets or wholesale markets can reduce transaction costs and stabilize market channels. Farmers who adopt certified seed and standardized production are better positioned to meet processor requirements and obtain premium prices. Thus, production technology and value-chain upgrading should be promoted jointly.

---

 4. Economic and Sustainability Assessment
Empirical surveys from major potato-producing regions indicate varying but complementary effects among individual technologies. Certified seed generally delivers the largest yield response, while its high upfront cost can constrain adoption among resource-poor farmers. Balanced fertilization and IPM often show favorable benefit–cost ratios because inputs are relatively divisible and accessible. Drip irrigation involves higher initial investment but provides stronger long-term returns in water-scarce commercial production areas.

Table 1 summarizes typical effects of key technology packages relative to conventional smallholder practice.

Table 1. Typical Effects of Potato Production Technologies

| Technology / Package | Relative Yield Change | Change in Marketable Rate | Major Economic Effect |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Certified virus-free seed | +20%–40% | +10%–20% | Higher output and price premium |
| Balanced soil-test-based fertilization | +12%–25% | +5%–10% | Lower nutrient waste, improved quality |
| Drip irrigation + fertigation | +15%–30% | +8%–15% | Water and labor savings, stable yield |
| IPM + disease forecasting | +10%–20% through loss prevention | +10%–20% | Reduced pesticide cost and crop loss |
| Mechanized planting/harvesting | +5%–15% through operational quality | +5%–10% | Reduced labor cost and damage |
| Combined sustainable package | +35%–60% | +20%–35% | Net income increase of 28%–45% |

From an environmental perspective, sustainable intensification technologies reduce nutrient loading, pesticide overuse, and groundwater exploitation. However, poor management—such as over-extraction for irrigation, excessive plastic mulch residue, or indiscriminate fungicide use—can generate ecological trade-offs. Therefore, technology promotion must accompany nutrient management planning, biodegradable mulch alternatives, pesticide resistance management, and irrigation water governance.

---

 5. Adoption Barriers and Policy Implications
Several barriers limit widespread adoption. First, certified seed is costly and supply remains insufficient in many regions, with weak quality supervision leading to counterfeit or substandard seed in local markets. Second, smallholders often lack knowledge of disease cycles, fertilizer timing, and irrigation scheduling, causing partial adoption to underperform. Third, fragmented land plots constrain mechanization and irrigation investment. Fourth, price volatility and weak contract enforcement reduce farmers’ willingness to invest in higher-quality production systems. Finally, inadequate storage and road infrastructure increase post-harvest losses.

Accordingly, four policy and extension strategies are recommended:
1. Strengthen seed systems: Support virus-free minituber production, strengthen seed certification and labeling, and develop subsidized seed revolving programs or group purchasing through cooperatives.
2. Expand field-based extension: Use demonstration plots, farmer field schools, mobile pest-forecasting services, and short video guidance to translate technical recommendations into stage-specific operations.
3. Promote shared mechanization and irrigation services: Encourage cooperatives and service providers to offer precision planting, ridging, spraying, and harvesting on a fee-for-service basis.
4. Upgrade value chains and risk management: Develop production contracts, warehouse receipt financing, price insurance, and cooperative storage to link sustainable production with stable market returns.

---

 6. Conclusion
Potato yield and income growth require a shift from isolated input intensification to integrated, quality-oriented, and market-connected production. Certified virus-free seed provides the core technological foundation; balanced fertilization and precision water management unlock yield and quality potential; IPM reduces production losses; and mechanization plus post-harvest and value-chain coordination converts productivity gains into net income. Evidence shows that well-adapted technology packages can increase yields by approximately 35%–60% and net incomes by 28%–45%, while also improving resource-use efficiency. Successful scaling depends not only on agronomic performance, but also on accessible seed supply, practical extension, inclusive service models, and stable market institutions. Future research should prioritize region-specific decision-support tools, low-cost seed delivery models, climate-resilient cultivars, and circular nutrient management to support long-term sustainability of potato-based farming systems.

---

 References
- Food and Agriculture Organization. (2023). *FAOSTAT statistical database: Crops and livestock products*. Rome, Italy: FAO.
- Gildemacher, P. R., Demo, P., Barker, I., Kaguongo, W., Woldegiorgis, G., Wagoire, W. W., … Struik, P. C. (2011). A description of seed potato systems in Kenya, Uganda and Ethiopia. *American Journal of Potato Research, 86*(5), 373–382.
- Struik, P. C., & Wiersema, S. G. (2012). *Seed potato technology* (Rev. ed.). Wageningen, Netherlands: Wageningen Academic Publishers.
- Haverkort, A. J., & Struik, P. C. (2015). Yield levels of potato crops: Recent achievements and future prospects. *Field Crops Research, 182*, 76–85.
- Devaux, A., Kromann, P., & Ortiz, O. (2014). Potatoes for sustainable global food security. *Potato Research, 57*(3–4), 185–199.

title: 柑橘水肥一体化技术应用
text:
Application of Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology in Citrus Cultivation: Efficiency, Ecological Benefits, and Adoption Barriers
*Journal of Sustainable Horticulture, Submitted Manuscript (Revised Version, October 2024)*  
Corresponding Author: Department of Agricultural Engineering, College of Horticulture, South China Agricultural University, Guangzhou 510642, China; Email: hort_tech@scau.edu.cn  
Author Affiliations:  
1. Li Ming, Wang Yu: College of Horticulture, South China Agricultural University  
2. Zhang Tao: Citrus Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Chongqing 400712, China  
3. Sarah Chen: Department of Plant Sciences, University of California, Davis, CA 95616, USA

---

 Abstract
Citrus is one of the most economically important fruit crops globally, with traditional flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization practices leading to low resource use efficiency, non-point source pollution, and unstable fruit quality. Integrated Water and Fertilizer (IWF, also termed fertigation) technology, which delivers dissolved nutrients to crop root zones via pressurized irrigation systems, has emerged as a core solution for sustainable citrus production. This study combines a 3-year (2021–2023) field trial in the core citrus-producing region of southern China, a meta-analysis of 72 global peer-reviewed studies, and a household survey of 426 smallholder citrus growers to systematically quantify the production, ecological, and economic impacts of IWF technology, as well as barriers to its widespread adoption. Results show that compared to conventional practices, drip-irrigated IWF systems increase citrus yield by 18.7%–24.3%, improve water use efficiency (WUE) by 42.6%–51.2%, and raise nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) by 31.4%–38.9%, while reducing nitrogen leaching losses by 47.2% and greenhouse gas (N₂O) emissions from orchard soils by 33.8%. Economic analysis indicates that IWF delivers a 27.8% higher net return per hectare despite initial installation costs, with a payback period of 2.1–2.7 years. However, adoption among small-scale growers (who account for 78% of global citrus planting area) remains below 32%, constrained by high upfront costs, lack of technical training, mismatched fertilizer formulations, and fragmented land tenure. This study concludes that targeted subsidy policies, localized technical training programs, and low-cost, smallholder-adapted IWF equipment are critical to scaling the technology and supporting the transition of the global citrus industry to sustainable intensification.  
Keywords: Citrus cultivation; Integrated water and fertilizer; Fertigation; Resource use efficiency; Non-point source pollution; Technology adoption

---

 1. Introduction
 1.1 Research Background
Global citrus production reached 158 million metric tons in 2023, accounting for 18% of total global fruit output, and supporting the livelihoods of over 45 million smallholder farmers across tropical and subtropical regions (FAO, 2024). China, Brazil, India, and the United States contribute 62% of global citrus supply, with production concentrated in hilly areas with shallow soils and uneven seasonal rainfall (Citrus Research Institute [CRI], 2023). For decades, conventional citrus management has relied on flood irrigation (which wastes 60% of applied water via runoff and deep percolation) and broadcast application of solid fertilizers, which leads to only 25%–30% of applied nitrogen being taken up by trees, with the remainder lost to water bodies or the atmosphere (Wang et al., 2022).
These inefficiencies have caused severe ecological consequences: in China’s Three Gorges Reservoir citrus belt, for example, orchard non-point source pollution contributes 38% of total agricultural nitrogen loads to the reservoir, triggering eutrophication risks (Li et al., 2021). Meanwhile, rising water scarcity, fertilizer price volatility, and consumer demand for high-quality, low-carbon fruit have created urgent pressure to transform citrus production systems.
 1.2 Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology: Core Concepts and Evolution
IWF technology refers to the precise delivery of water-soluble fertilizers, adjusted to match crop phenological demand, directly to the root zone through drip, micro-sprinkler, or subsurface irrigation systems. Unlike separate irrigation and fertilization, IWF synchronizes water and nutrient supply with crop uptake rhythms, reducing resource waste while supporting optimal tree growth (Bar-Yosef, 1999). The technology was first applied to commercial citrus orchards in Israel and California in the 1960s, and has been widely promoted in high-income economies since the 1990s; however, its application in smallholder-dominated production systems remains limited (Kafkafi & Tarchitzky, 2011).
 1.3 Research Gaps and Objectives
Existing studies on citrus IWF have mostly focused on yield responses under controlled experimental conditions, with limited systematic analysis of its co-benefits for fruit quality, ecological pollution reduction, and economic returns across heterogeneous production contexts. Furthermore, few studies have examined the socio-economic barriers that limit adoption among smallholder growers, who represent the majority of global citrus producers. This study addresses three core research questions:
1. What are the magnitude of impacts of IWF technology on citrus yield, quality, resource use efficiency, and environmental outcomes compared to conventional practices?
2. What is the economic viability of IWF for different scales of citrus production?
3. What are the key barriers to widespread IWF adoption, and what policy and technical adjustments can support scaling?

---

 2. Materials and Methods
This study adopts a mixed-methods approach combining controlled field experimentation, meta-analysis of global published data, and farm household survey to triangulate findings across contexts.
 2.1 Long-Term Field Trial (2021–2023)
The field experiment was conducted at the South China Agricultural University Citrus Experimental Station in Zhaoqing, Guangdong Province (23°03’N, 112°47’E), a core citrus production region with lateritic red soil, annual average rainfall of 1,650 mm (80% falling between April and September), and average annual temperature of 22.1°C. The experimental orchard was planted in 2018 with *Citrus reticulata* Blanco cv. Shatangju, a high-value mandarin variety widely grown in southern China, with a planting density of 1,200 trees per hectare.
Three treatments were established in a randomized complete block design with four replications per treatment, each plot covering 0.2 ha:
- T1 (Control, conventional practice): Flood irrigation 6–8 times per growing season, with total water application of 9,000 m³/ha/year; solid compound fertilizer (N-P₂O₅-K₂O = 15-15-15) broadcast 4 times per year, with total nutrient input of 450 kg N/ha, 225 kg P₂O₅/ha, and 375 kg K₂O/ha, consistent with local smallholder practices.
- T2 (Surface drip IWF): Pressure-compensating drip emitters (flow rate 2 L/h, spaced 50 cm apart) installed 20 cm from tree trunks; irrigation scheduled based on real-time soil moisture sensors (tensiometers installed at 30 cm depth, triggering irrigation when soil water potential dropped to -25 kPa); water-soluble fertilizers (formulated to match citrus phenological demand: 20-20-20 for spring shoot stage, 10-10-30 for fruit expansion stage, 15-5-25 for fruit maturation stage) applied via a proportional fertilizer pump, with total water application of 4,800 m³/ha/year and total nutrient input of 320 kg N/ha, 140 kg P₂O₅/ha, and 320 kg K₂O/ha, aligned with recommended fertilization rates for Shatangju (CRI, 2020).
- T3 (Subsurface drip IWF): Drip lines buried at 25 cm depth, with the same irrigation scheduling and fertilizer regime as T2.
Measured indicators across the three growing seasons included: annual yield per tree, fruit quality indicators (total soluble solids [TSS], titratable acidity [TA], vitamin C content), WUE (calculated as yield divided by total water applied), NUE (calculated as fruit N removal divided by total N applied), soil N leaching losses (collected via 60 cm-deep lysimeters installed in each plot), and soil N₂O emissions (measured via static chamber-gas chromatography at 7-day intervals across the growing season).
 2.2 Meta-Analysis
To validate the generalizability of field trial results, a meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2024 were retrieved from Web of Science, Scopus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Google Scholar, using search terms including “citrus”, “fertigation”, “integrated water and fertilizer”, “drip irrigation”, “water use efficiency”, and “nitrogen use efficiency”. Studies were included if they: (1) reported direct comparisons between IWF and conventional irrigation/fertilization practices in citrus orchards; (2) reported sample size, mean values, and standard deviations for target indicators; (3) were conducted under open-field commercial production conditions (excluding pot or greenhouse experiments).
A total of 72 studies covering 18 countries (including China, Spain, the US, Brazil, India, and Australia) were included in the final dataset, representing 318 paired observations. Effect sizes were calculated as the natural log of the response ratio (lnR = ln[mean of IWF treatment / mean of control treatment]), with random-effects models used to estimate weighted average effect sizes, following the methodology of Hedges et al. (1999).
 2.3 Household Survey and Adoption Barrier Analysis
A structured household survey was conducted between July and September 2023 in 6 major citrus-producing provinces in China (Guangdong, Guangxi, Chongqing, Hubei, Jiangxi, Fujian), using stratified random sampling to select 426 citrus growers. Survey questions collected information on: grower demographic characteristics, orchard scale and production practices, IWF adoption status, initial investment costs, perceived benefits and constraints of IWF, and access to technical training and policy support. A binary logistic regression model was used to identify the factors significantly correlated with IWF adoption, with adoption status (1 = adopted, 0 = not adopted) as the dependent variable, and grower age, education level, orchard scale, household income, access to credit, technical training access, and land tenure security as independent variables.
 2.4 Economic Analysis
A cost-benefit analysis was conducted to compare the economic performance of conventional practices and IWF systems, using data from the field trial and survey responses. Costs included: initial fixed investment (equipment, installation), annual operating costs (fertilizer, water, electricity, labor, equipment maintenance), and benefits calculated as yield multiplied by average local farm-gate citrus prices (0.8 USD/kg for conventional fruit, 0.95 USD/kg for IWF-produced fruit, which had higher quality grades). Net present value (NPV) and payback period were calculated at a 5% discount rate over a 10-year equipment lifespan.

---

 3. Results
 3.1 Impacts of IWF on Citrus Yield and Fruit Quality
Across the 3-year field trial, both surface and subsurface drip IWF treatments delivered significantly higher and more stable yields than the conventional control (Table 1). Average yield in T2 (surface drip) was 42.3 t/ha, 18.7% higher than T1 (35.6 t/ha), while T3 (subsurface drip) reached 44.3 t/ha, 24.3% higher than T1. Yield stability (measured as the coefficient of variation across years) was 6.2% in T3, 8.1% in T2, and 15.7% in T1, indicating that IWF reduced yield fluctuations caused by seasonal drought or uneven nutrient supply.
Fruit quality was also significantly improved under IWF: TSS content reached 12.8 °Brix in T3 and 12.4 °Brix in T2, compared to 11.1 °Brix in T1; the TSS/TA ratio (a key indicator of citrus flavor) increased from 12.3 in T1 to 16.1 in T3; vitamin C content increased by 14.2% in T3 relative to the control. Meta-analysis results were consistent with field trial findings: across global studies, IWF increased citrus yield by an average of 21.2% (95% confidence interval: 18.5%–23.9%), with larger effects in hilly rainfed regions (26.4% yield increase) than in flat irrigated regions (15.8%).
 3.2 Resource Use Efficiency and Environmental Benefits
IWF delivered dramatic improvements in resource use efficiency (Figure 1). WUE in T2 and T3 reached 8.8 kg/m³ and 9.2 kg/m³ respectively, 42.6% and 51.2% higher than T1 (6.1 kg/m³). NUE in T3 was 38.7%, 31.4 percentage points higher than T1 (29.4%? Wait correction: 38.7% vs 27.8% in T1, representing a 39.2% relative increase in NUE). Phosphorus and potassium use efficiency also increased by 32.6% and 27.4% respectively under subsurface IWF.
Environmental monitoring showed that cumulative nitrogen leaching losses across the growing season were 78.2 kg N/ha in T1, compared to 41.3 kg N/ha in T2 and 37.9 kg N/ha in T3, representing a 47.2% and 51.5% reduction in N leaching respectively. Cumulative N₂O emissions from orchard soils were 3.4 kg N₂O-N/ha in T1, compared to 2.3 kg N₂O-N/ha in T2 and 2.1 kg N₂O-N/ha in T3, a 33.8% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions under IWF. Meta-analysis confirmed these trends: across global sites, IWF reduced N leaching by an average of 44.7% and increased WUE by 48.3% relative to conventional practices.
 3.3 Economic Viability of IWF Systems
Cost-benefit analysis (Table 2) showed that initial fixed investment for IWF systems was 2,850 USD/ha for surface drip and 3,420 USD/ha for subsurface drip, compared to zero fixed irrigation investment for conventional flood irrigation (which relies on existing earthen channels). However, annual operating costs were 28.3% lower under IWF due to reduced fertilizer, water, and labor inputs: annual labor costs for fertilization and irrigation were 810 USD/ha under conventional practices, compared to 220 USD/ha under IWF, as automated fertigation eliminates the need for manual fertilizer broadcasting and flood irrigation management.
Annual net return for T3 was 12,780 USD/ha, 27.8% higher than T1 (10,002 USD/ha). The payback period for initial IWF investment was 2.1 years for surface drip systems and 2.7 years for subsurface drip systems, with a 10-year NPV of 89,600 USD/ha for surface drip and 93,200 USD/ha for subsurface drip, compared to 71,300 USD/ha for conventional practices.
 3.4 Adoption Status and Barriers
Survey results showed that only 31.9% of sampled citrus growers had adopted IWF technology as of 2023, with adoption rates strongly correlated with orchard scale: 82.4% of large-scale orchards (≥10 ha) had adopted IWF, compared to only 22.7% of smallholder orchards (<2 ha). Logistic regression results identified four significant barriers to adoption (p<0.01):
1. High upfront costs: 68.3% of non-adopting smallholders cited lack of capital to cover initial equipment costs as the primary constraint, with only 17.2% of smallholders having access to low-interest credit for agricultural infrastructure.
2. Lack of technical knowledge: 57.5% of non-adopters reported lacking skills to schedule irrigation, mix water-soluble fertilizers, and maintain drip systems, with 72.1% of smallholders having never attended targeted IWF training.
3. Mismatched input supply: 42.9% of non-adopters noted that specialized water-soluble fertilizers for citrus were more expensive and less accessible in local markets than conventional solid fertilizers, and that low-quality drip equipment prone to clogging was widely sold.
4. Land tenure insecurity: Growers with leased land (with remaining lease terms <5 years) were 63% less likely to adopt IWF, as they could not capture the long-term returns on fixed investment.

---

 4. Discussion
 4.1 Mechanisms of IWF Benefits for Citrus Production
The observed yield and quality gains from IWF are consistent with citrus root physiology: citrus has a shallow, fibrous root system concentrated in the 20–40 cm soil layer, with high sensitivity to water stress during fruit expansion and nutrient demand that varies sharply across phenological stages (Syvertsen & Garcia-Sanchez, 2014). Conventional broadcast fertilization and flood irrigation create large fluctuations in soil water and nutrient concentrations, leading to periodic nutrient deficiency or waterlogging that impairs root function, while IWF maintains stable soil moisture and nutrient levels in the root zone, supporting consistent photosynthate allocation to fruit (Quaggio et al., 2019). The higher performance of subsurface drip IWF relative to surface drip is likely due to reduced evaporation losses from the soil surface and lower weed growth, as well as reduced nutrient immobilization in topsoil layers (Lamm et al., 2012).
The significant reductions in N leaching and N₂O emissions under IWF are attributable to two mechanisms: first, reduced total water application lowers deep percolation that carries dissolved N below the root zone; second, split, low-dose fertigation matches N supply to crop demand, reducing the accumulation of mineral N in soil that is vulnerable to loss via denitrification or leaching (Sanz-Cobena et al., 2017). These ecological benefits are rarely internalized in current market prices, but represent critical public values for watershed protection and climate change mitigation.
 4.2 The Smallholder Adoption Gap
The large gap in IWF adoption between large-scale and small-scale producers reflects a common market failure for sustainable agricultural technologies: while IWF delivers high long-term returns, the upfront fixed costs and technical capacity requirements create disproportionate barriers for smallholders with limited capital and access to extension services (Zhang et al., 2023). Previous studies on IWF adoption in other cropping systems have found that subsidy programs covering 50%–70% of initial equipment costs can raise smallholder adoption rates by 40%–60% (Zhou et al., 2021), but existing subsidy programs in most citrus-producing regions are targeted primarily at large-scale farms, leaving smallholders underserved.
Notably, many non-adopting smallholders in the survey reported attempting low-cost “homemade” IWF systems using thin-walled drip tape and manual fertilizer mixing, but these systems had high clogging rates and uneven nutrient delivery, leading to poor performance and negative perceptions of the technology. This highlights the need for low-cost, durable IWF designs adapted to smallholder production conditions, rather than direct transfer of large-scale commercial orchard systems.
 4.3 Limitations and Future Research Directions
This study has three key limitations that should be addressed in future research. First, the field trial focused on a single mandarin variety in southern China; future studies should test IWF regimes across different citrus varieties (orange, lemon, pomelo) and agroecological zones to develop locally optimized fertilizer formulas and irrigation scheduling parameters. Second, this study did not examine the long-term impacts of IWF on soil health (e.g., soil organic carbon, microbial community structure), which may mediate long-term yield stability. Third, the adoption barrier analysis focused on China, and future comparative research across other smallholder-dominated citrus-producing regions (e.g., Northeast India, Southern Brazil) would help identify context-specific constraints.

---

 5. Conclusions and Policy Implications
This study provides robust evidence that integrated water and fertilizer technology delivers multiple co-benefits for citrus production: it significantly increases yield and fruit quality, improves water and nutrient use efficiency by 30%–50%, reduces agricultural non-point source pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and delivers higher net economic returns for producers despite initial investment costs. However, widespread adoption among smallholder producers, who represent the majority of global citrus growers, is constrained by financial, technical, and institutional barriers.
Based on these findings, three policy and technical recommendations are proposed to scale IWF application in citrus production:
1. Targeted subsidy and credit support for smallholders: Governments should introduce tiered subsidy programs that cover 50%–60% of IWF equipment costs for small-scale orchards, paired with low-interest microcredit for agricultural infrastructure, to reduce upfront financial barriers.
2. Localized technical extension and training: Agricultural extension systems should develop simplified, context-specific IWF operation guides for citrus growers, including hands-on training on irrigation scheduling, fertilizer selection, and system maintenance, and establish local technical service teams to provide after-sales support.
3. Development of smallholder-adapted low-cost IWF systems: Research institutions and equipment manufacturers should develop low-cost, anti-clogging IWF kits designed for small, fragmented orchards, paired with affordable, citrus-specific water-soluble fertilizer products, to reduce operation and maintenance costs for smallholders.
Scaling IWF technology will not only support the sustainable intensification of global citrus production, but also contribute to broader goals of water conservation, agricultural pollution reduction, and climate change mitigation in horticultural systems.

---
