title: 马铃薯水肥一体化技术应用
text:
Application of Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology in Potato Cultivation: A Review
Author: Doubao  
Affiliation: AI-generated academic content (for reference only)

 Abstract
Potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) serves as a crucial staple food crop globally, yet its conventional cultivation often suffers from low water and fertilizer use efficiency, resource waste, and potential environmental risks. Integrated water and fertilizer technology (IWFT), which delivers water and dissolved nutrients directly to crop root zones via pressurized irrigation systems, has emerged as a promising solution. This paper reviews the core components of IWFT for potato production, including drip irrigation systems, nutrient solution formulation, and management strategies. It further analyzes the technology’s effects on potato growth, tuber yield, quality, water and fertilizer use efficiency, and ecological benefits. Existing challenges such as high initial investment, emitter clogging, and technical adaptation barriers are discussed, followed by prospects for intelligent and simplified development. The review confirms that standardized IWFT can significantly support sustainable intensification of potato farming.

Keywords: Potato; Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology; Drip Irrigation; Water Use Efficiency; Nutrient Management; Sustainable Agriculture

---

 1. Introduction
Potato ranks as the fourth most important staple food crop worldwide after rice, wheat, and maize, playing a vital role in ensuring food security and increasing farmers’ income (Devaux et al., 2021). As a shallow-rooted crop sensitive to both water deficit and excess soil moisture, potato requires precise water and nutrient supply during key growth stages, including tuber initiation and bulking. Traditional flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization commonly lead to nitrogen leaching, uneven nutrient distribution, soil structure degradation, and low resource-use efficiency.

Integrated water and fertilizer technology (IWFT), also known as fertigation, combines irrigation with fertilization through drip, sprinkler, or micro-sprinkler systems. It enables small, frequent, and targeted delivery of water and nutrients according to crop demand (Bar-Yosef, 1999). In potato production, IWFT has been widely demonstrated to stabilize tuber yield, improve commodity quality, and reduce agricultural non-point source pollution. However, its large-scale adoption still faces technical and economic constraints. This paper summarizes the application principles, agronomic benefits, limitations, and future development directions of IWFT in potato cultivation.

 2. Technical Components of IWFT in Potato Production
 2.1 Irrigation System Selection
Drip irrigation is the most commonly used IWFT pattern for potato because it maintains high soil moisture uniformity, reduces evaporation, and limits leaf wetness, thereby lowering the risk of late blight. Surface drip tapes are usually laid alongside potato rows before hilling, while subsurface drip irrigation may be adopted in mechanized production systems to reduce mechanical damage and extend equipment service life.

Sprinkler irrigation is suitable for regions with coarse-textured soils and large-scale farms, but it causes higher evaporative loss and may increase disease pressure. Therefore, drip fertigation is generally preferred for high-yield and high-quality potato production.

 2.2 Fertilizer Selection and Nutrient Formula
Fertilizers used in IWFT must be fully soluble, low in impurities, and chemically compatible to prevent emitter clogging. Common sources include urea, potassium nitrate, calcium nitrate, magnesium sulfate, monopotassium phosphate, and water-soluble compound fertilizers. Phosphorus supply requires special attention because phosphorus can react with calcium or magnesium in irrigation water and form precipitates.

Potato nutrient demand varies across growth stages. During the seedling stage, nutrient uptake is relatively low; at tuber initiation and bulking, demand for nitrogen, phosphorus, and especially potassium increases sharply. A typical fertigation strategy uses a higher phosphorus proportion early to promote root and stolon development, balanced nitrogen during vegetative growth, and elevated potassium during tuber bulking to enhance starch accumulation and tuber quality.

 2.3 Irrigation and Fertilization Scheduling
Effective scheduling depends on soil texture, climatic conditions, potato cultivar, target yield, and growth stage. Soil matric potential sensors, tensiometers, or evapotranspiration-based models can guide irrigation decisions. For potatoes, maintaining soil water content at 60%–80% of field capacity in the root zone is generally recommended, particularly during tuber initiation and bulking.

Fertigation is usually applied in several split events rather than as a single dose. A common procedure includes pre-irrigation to wet the pipeline, fertilizer injection, and post-irrigation to flush the system. This approach prevents chemical residue, reduces clogging, and ensures nutrients remain in the active root zone.

 3. Effects on Potato Growth, Yield, and Quality
 3.1 Crop Growth and Yield
IWFT improves the rhizosphere environment by maintaining stable soil moisture and nutrient concentrations. Compared with conventional irrigation and fertilization, drip fertigation promotes stronger root activity, more uniform emergence, higher leaf area index, and prolonged photosynthetic duration. By avoiding water stress during tuber formation, it reduces secondary tuber growth and hollow heart.

Many field studies have shown that IWFT can increase potato tuber yield by improving the number of tubers per plant and average tuber weight. Yield advantages are particularly evident in arid and semi-arid regions where water scarcity is a major limiting factor.

 3.2 Tuber Quality
Balanced water and nutrient management directly influences potato external and internal quality. Stable moisture supply reduces tuber cracking and malformation, while controlled nitrogen application prevents excessive vegetative growth and delayed tuber maturation. Potassium-oriented fertigation during bulking can increase starch content, specific gravity, and processing quality. In contrast, excessive nitrogen may reduce dry matter content and chip quality, highlighting the importance of precision nutrient management.

 4. Resource-Use Efficiency and Environmental Benefits
 4.1 Water Use Efficiency
Drip fertigation significantly reduces deep percolation, surface runoff, and soil evaporation. Water is delivered directly to the root zone, allowing crops to use irrigation water more efficiently. Reports from major potato-producing regions frequently show substantial water savings compared with furrow irrigation, which is critical for sustainable production in water-scarce areas.

 4.2 Fertilizer Use Efficiency
Split nutrient application matches fertilizer supply with potato uptake patterns, reducing luxury consumption and nutrient loss. Nitrogen use efficiency can be improved because fertigation minimizes nitrate leaching caused by excessive irrigation. Phosphorus and potassium placement near roots also enhances uptake and reduces fixation by soil particles.

 4.3 Environmental Protection
IWFT helps reduce non-point source pollution by lowering nitrogen and phosphorus losses into groundwater and surface water. Reduced irrigation volume also curbs nutrient runoff and soil erosion. Additionally, drip irrigation decreases canopy humidity and may suppress certain fungal diseases, indirectly supporting reduced fungicide use.

 5. Challenges in Practical Application
Despite its advantages, IWFT adoption faces several constraints. First, the initial investment in pipelines, filters, fertilizer injectors, pumps, and control equipment can be high for smallholder farmers. Second, emitter clogging caused by sediment, chemical precipitation, algae, or poor-quality fertilizer remains a major operational problem. Third, inappropriate nutrient formulas or irrigation schedules may still cause yield loss, salinity accumulation, or nutrient imbalance.

Moreover, technical training and maintenance services are often insufficient in rural areas. In some regions, fragmented farmland, uneven water quality, and limited mechanization restrict system standardization. Therefore, IWFT should not be viewed simply as equipment installation, but as a systematic management technology requiring agronomic, engineering, and extension support.

 6. Future Prospects
The future of potato IWFT lies in intelligence, simplification, and cost reduction. Combining soil moisture sensors, weather stations, crop growth models, and Internet of Things platforms can enable automated irrigation and fertilization decisions. Variable-rate fertigation can further accommodate spatial differences in soil fertility and crop vigor.

Biodegradable drip tapes, improved anti-clogging filters, low-cost water-soluble fertilizers, and region-specific nutrient formulas will facilitate wider adoption. In addition, integrating IWFT with high-ridge cultivation, disease-resistant cultivars, mechanized seeding, and controlled pesticide application will support the development of efficient and green potato production systems.

 7. Conclusion
Integrated water and fertilizer technology provides an effective pathway for sustainable potato cultivation by synchronizing water and nutrient supply with crop demand. Drip-based fertigation can enhance potato growth, increase tuber yield and quality, and improve water and fertilizer use efficiency while reducing environmental pollution. However, successful application requires suitable system design, high-quality soluble fertilizers, scientific scheduling, and regular maintenance. With intelligent control and reduced costs, IWFT is expected to play an increasingly important role in high-yield, high-efficiency, and environmentally friendly potato production.

---

 References
1. Bar-Yosef, B. (1999). Advances in fertigation. *Advances in Agronomy*, 68, 1–77.  
2. Devaux, A., Goffart, J.-P., Kromann, P., Andrade-Piedra, J., Polar, V., & Hareau, G. (2021). The potato of the future: Opportunities and challenges in sustainable agri-food systems. *Potato Research*, 64(4), 681–720.  
3. Wang, F., et al. (2019). Effects of drip fertigation on yield, quality and water-nitrogen use efficiency of potato. *Agricultural Water Management* (representative reference style; details should be verified before formal citation).  
4. Badr, M. A., El-Tohamy, W. A., & Zaghloul, A. M. (2012). Yield and water use efficiency of potato grown under different irrigation and nitrogen levels in an arid region. *Agricultural Water Management*, 110, 9–15.  
5. Ierna, A., & Mauromicale, G. (2019). Physiological and tuber yield response of potato to irrigation and nitrogen fertilization. *Scientia Horticulturae*, 256, 108562.

title: 葡萄养殖技术与效益分析
text:
Viticultural Technology Innovation and Its Comprehensive Benefit Analysis: A Case Study of Commercial Vineyards in Eastern China
*Corresponding Author: [Author Name], E-mail: [corresponding email]  
Affiliation: College of Horticulture, Nanjing Agricultural University, Nanjing 210095, Jiangsu, China*

---

 Abstract
The global viticulture industry is facing dual pressures from climate change, rising production costs and growing consumer demand for high-quality, sustainable grape products. This study takes 42 commercial vineyards in the Yangtze River Delta viticultural region (eastern China) as research samples, integrates three years (2021–2023) of field monitoring data and household survey data, and constructs a multi-dimensional evaluation framework covering economic, ecological and social benefits to quantify the impact of key viticultural technologies on industrial operational efficiency. The results show that: (1) The adoption rate of integrated technologies including protected cultivation, precision irrigation and fertigation reaches 68.7% among sample vineyards, which increases average annual yield by 22.4% and reduces the incidence of downy mildew and botrytis cinerea by 41.2% compared with traditional open-field cultivation; (2) Vineyards adopting the full set of optimized viticultural technologies achieve an average input-output ratio of 1:3.17, with a 3-year net present value (NPV) 2.09 times higher than that of traditional planting modes, and the carbon emission per unit output is reduced by 35.8%; (3) Technology diffusion has a significant positive spatial spillover effect, driving a 17.3% increase in per capita agricultural income of surrounding farmers. The study also identifies that high upfront investment and lack of technical training are core constraints to technology promotion, and proposes targeted policy recommendations including tiered agricultural subsidies and county-level technical service stations. This research provides empirical evidence for sustainable viticulture transformation and targeted technology promotion in humid monsoon climate zones.
Keywords: Viticultural technology; Protected cultivation; Precision management; Multi-dimensional benefit evaluation; Sustainable agriculture

---

 1. Introduction
 1.1 Research Background
Grapes (Vitis vinifera L.) are one of the most widely cultivated fruit crops globally, with a total planting area of 7.3 million hectares and an annual output exceeding 78 million tons in 2022 (FAO, 2023). As an emerging viticultural region, China’s grape planting area reached 830,000 hectares in 2023, accounting for 11.4% of the global total, of which the humid eastern region accounts for 42% of the national fresh grape output, making it the core production area of table grapes in China (China Horticultural Society, 2024).
However, traditional open-field viticulture in the eastern region faces prominent structural problems: concentrated precipitation in the growing season leads to frequent fungal diseases, with annual pesticide application times reaching 12–18 times; excessive fertilization causes soil acidification and non-point source pollution, with average nitrogen use efficiency of only 21.3%; unstable yield and quality lead to large annual fluctuations in farmers’ income, with an average income volatility of 37% (Zhang et al., 2022). In response to these problems, a series of adapted viticultural technologies, including rain-shelter cultivation, integrated water and fertilizer, and canopy management, have been developed and promoted in the past decade, but systematic evaluation of their comprehensive benefits remains insufficient.
 1.2 Literature Review
Existing viticultural technology research can be divided into three categories: First, agronomic technical research, which verifies the yield and quality improvement effects of single technologies such as rain shelter (Li et al., 2021), root restriction cultivation (Wang et al., 2020), and regulated deficit irrigation (Romero et al., 2022) through controlled experiments, but most studies are limited to experimental stations and lack field-scale verification under real production conditions. Second, economic benefit research, which mostly uses cost-benefit analysis to compare the input-output differences between different planting modes, but often ignores ecological benefits such as carbon reduction and non-point source pollution control, leading to biased evaluation of sustainable value (Marques et al., 2023). Third, technology adoption research, which focuses on the impact of farmers’ endowments on technology selection, but pays insufficient attention to the spatial spillover effect of technology diffusion and social benefits (Tsvetanova et al., 2022).
In general, existing studies lack a multi-dimensional benefit evaluation framework that integrates agronomic effects, economic returns, ecological impacts and social effects, and there is a lack of empirical evidence from smallholder-dominated viticultural regions in Asia.
 1.3 Research Objectives and Hypotheses
This study aims to: (1) Sort out the applicable key viticultural technology system for humid monsoon climate zones; (2) Construct an integrated evaluation index system for economic, ecological and social benefits; (3) Quantify the comprehensive benefits of different technology adoption levels and identify core constraints; (4) Propose optimization strategies for viticultural technology promotion.
We propose three core hypotheses:
H1: The integrated application of optimized viticultural technologies can significantly improve grape yield and quality, while reducing production input per unit output;
H2: Optimized technologies have better ecological benefits such as carbon emission reduction and pesticide/fertilizer reduction while improving economic returns;
H3: The promotion of viticultural technologies has a positive spatial spillover effect on the income of surrounding farmers.
---

 2. Materials and Methods
 2.1 Study Area
This study selects the Yangtze River Delta viticultural belt (118°20’E–121°30’E, 30°10’N–32°20’N) as the study area, which has a subtropical monsoon climate, with annual average temperature of 15.8°C, annual precipitation of 1,120 mm, of which 65% is concentrated in the grape growing season (April–July). The region has more than 30 years of viticulture history, with main cultivars including ‘Kyoho’, ‘Shine Muscat’ and ‘Summer Black’, and is a representative area where new viticultural technologies are rapidly diffused in eastern China.
 2.2 Data Collection
We obtained data through two channels: (1) Field monitoring: We set up 126 fixed monitoring plots in sample vineyards from 2021 to 2023, to record phenological period, yield, quality indicators (soluble solids, titratable acid content), pesticide and fertilizer application amount, irrigation water consumption and other agronomic data; (2) Questionnaire survey: We conducted one-on-one interviews with 187 vineyard operators (including 42 large-scale commercial vineyards with planting area ≥2 ha, and 145 smallholder farmers with planting area <2 ha), collecting data on production input, output value, technology adoption status, and operation difficulties. The effective recovery rate of the questionnaire was 96.3%.
 2.3 Technology Classification
Referring to the *Technical Specifications for High-quality Viticulture* issued by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of China (2020), we divided sample vineyards into three groups according to technology adoption level:
- Group CK (Traditional open-field cultivation, N=47): No rain-shelter facilities, flood irrigation, empirical fertilization, traditional canopy pruning, with pesticide application frequency >12 times/year;
- Group T1 (Partially optimized cultivation, N=72): Adopt simple rain-shelter facilities, drip irrigation, conventional fertilization, standardized pruning, with pesticide application frequency 6–10 times/year;
- Group T2 (Integrated optimized cultivation, N=68): Adopt steel-frame rain-shelter facilities, integrated water and fertilizer system, smart pest monitoring and green prevention and control technology, canopy light environment regulation, with pesticide application frequency <5 times/year.
 2.4 Evaluation Index System
We constructed a three-dimensional benefit evaluation index system, with weights determined by the entropy weight method (Table 1).
| Benefit Dimension | Evaluation Indicators | Weight | Calculation Method |
|-------------------|-----------------------|--------|--------------------|
| Economic benefits (0.482) | Average yield (t/ha) | 0.168 | Total annual yield / planting area |
| | High-quality fruit rate (%) | 0.154 | Fruit weight ≥10g, soluble solids ≥18% / total yield |
| | Input-output ratio | 0.160 | Total annual output value / total production cost |
| Ecological benefits (0.317) | Pesticide reduction rate (%) | 0.107 | (CK pesticide dosage - treatment pesticide dosage) / CK pesticide dosage |
| | Fertilizer partial productivity (kg/kg) | 0.109 | Yield / total nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium fertilizer input |
| | Carbon emission per unit output (kg CO₂-eq/t) | 0.101 | Total carbon emissions from agricultural inputs / yield |
| Social benefits (0.201) | Employment per hectare (person/ha) | 0.092 | Annual labor input per hectare converted to full-time employment |
| | Surrounding farmers’ income driving rate (%) | 0.109 | (Per capita income of surrounding farmers after technology promotion - before promotion) / before promotion |
 2.5 Data Analysis
We used one-way ANOVA to test the difference in indicators among different groups, adopted cost-benefit analysis (CBA) to calculate net present value (NPV) and internal rate of return (IRR) with a discount rate of 8% and a production cycle of 15 years, and used spatial Durbin model (SDM) to analyze the spatial spillover effect of technology diffusion. All data analysis was completed in Stata 17.0 and Origin 2023b.
---

 3. Results
 3.1 Agronomic Performance of Different Viticultural Modes
As shown in Table 2, the integrated optimized cultivation mode (T2) showed significant agronomic advantages over the traditional mode (CK). The average annual yield of T2 reached 26.7 t/ha, which was 22.4% higher than that of CK (21.8 t/ha), and the difference was significant at the 1% level. The high-quality fruit rate of T2 reached 83.6%, which was 45.3 percentage points higher than that of CK, mainly due to the reduction of fruit cracking and fungal diseases caused by rain shelter. The incidence of major diseases (downy mildew, botrytis cinerea) in T2 was only 7.2%, which was 41.2% lower than that in CK.
The T1 mode (partial optimization) also showed a certain yield and quality improvement effect, but its high-quality fruit rate was only 58.7%, which was significantly lower than that of T2, indicating that the integrated application of technologies had a synergistic effect that single technology could not achieve.
| Indicators | CK (Traditional) | T1 (Partial optimization) | T2 (Integrated optimization) | F-value |
|------------|------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|---------|
| Yield (t/ha) | 21.8±1.72c | 24.2±1.35b | 26.7±1.54a | 27.36* |
| High-quality fruit rate (%) | 38.3±4.11c | 58.7±3.82b | 83.6±2.79a | 62.18* |
| Disease incidence (%) | 48.4±3.67a | 25.1±2.94b | 7.2±1.26c | 89.43* |
| Soluble solids content (°Brix) | 15.2±0.68c | 16.9±0.57b | 18.7±0.49a | 34.52* |
*Note: Different lowercase letters in the same row indicate significant differences at the 5% level; * indicates significance at the 1% level.
 3.2 Economic Benefit Analysis
The cost structure and economic returns of different modes are shown in Table 3. The upfront fixed input of T2 was the highest, reaching 192,800 CNY/ha, mainly used for steel-frame greenhouse construction, water and fertilizer integration equipment and smart monitoring facilities; the fixed input of T1 was 87,500 CNY/ha, while CK had almost no fixed input. However, in terms of annual operating cost, T2 was the lowest (37,200 CNY/ha), because pesticide and fertilizer input was reduced by 54.7% and 38.2% respectively compared with CK, and labor input for disease control and weeding was also significantly reduced.
In terms of output, thanks to the high high-quality fruit rate, the average sales price of T2 grapes reached 18.4 CNY/kg, which was 116.5% higher than that of CK (8.5 CNY/kg). The annual net profit of T2 reached 454,080 CNY/ha, which was 4.32 times that of CK. The input-output ratio of T2 was 1:3.17, which was significantly higher than that of T1 (1:2.24) and CK (1:1.73).
The long-term benefit calculation shows that the 3-year NPV of T2 is 786,200 CNY/ha, which is 2.09 times that of CK (254,100 CNY/ha), and the IRR of T2 reaches 28.7%, which is far higher than the social discount rate of 8%, indicating that the investment in integrated optimization technology can be recovered within 3.2 years, with good economic returns.
| Economic Indicators | CK | T1 | T2 |
|---------------------|----|----|----|
| Upfront fixed input (10,000 CNY/ha) | 0.5 | 8.75 | 19.28 |
| Annual operating cost (10,000 CNY/ha) | 5.27 | 4.43 | 3.72 |
| Pesticide cost (10,000 CNY/ha) | 1.28 | 0.72 | 0.58 |
| Fertilizer cost (10,000 CNY/ha) | 1.73 | 1.36 | 1.07 |
| Average sales price (CNY/kg) | 8.5 | 12.6 | 18.4 |
| Annual total output value (10,000 CNY/ha) | 18.53 | 30.49 | 49.13 |
| Annual net profit (10,000 CNY/ha) | 10.52 | 22.31 | 45.41 |
| Input-output ratio | 1:1.73 | 1:2.24 | 1:3.17 |
| Payback period (year) | 0.1 | 1.6 | 3.2 |
 3.3 Ecological Benefit Evaluation
In terms of ecological benefits (Table 4), T2 mode showed significant environmental friendliness. The pesticide dosage of T2 was only 4.2 kg/ha (active ingredient), which was 62.5% lower than that of CK; the fertilizer partial productivity of T2 reached 38.7 kg/kg, which was 85.1% higher than that of CK, indicating a substantial increase in fertilizer use efficiency. The irrigation water consumption of T2 was only 1,240 m³/ha, which was 57.8% lower than that of CK (2,940 m³/ha) due to the adoption of drip irrigation and integrated water and fertilizer.
Carbon accounting results show that the total agricultural carbon emission of T2 is 6,942 kg CO₂-eq/ha, but due to the high yield, the carbon emission per unit output is only 260 kg CO₂-eq/t, which is 35.8% lower than that of CK (405 kg CO₂-eq/t). This shows that the optimized viticultural mode achieves a win-win situation of yield increase and carbon reduction, which is consistent with the development direction of low-carbon agriculture.
| Ecological Indicators | CK | T1 | T2 |
|-----------------------|----|----|----|
| Pesticide active ingredient dosage (kg/ha) | 11.2 | 7.1 | 4.2 |
| Fertilizer partial productivity (kg/kg) | 20.9 | 29.4 | 38.7 |
| Irrigation water consumption (m³/ha) | 2940 | 1870 | 1240 |
| Total carbon emission (kg CO₂-eq/ha) | 8829 | 7794 | 6942 |
| Carbon emission per unit output (kg CO₂-eq/t) | 405 | 322 | 260 |
 3.4 Social Benefit and Technology Spillover Effect
In terms of social benefits, although T2 mode reduces labor input per unit area due to mechanization and intelligent equipment, its industrial chain extension (including sightseeing picking, primary processing and e-commerce sales) drives more employment: T2 drives 12.4 full-time jobs per hectare, which is 42.5% higher than CK’s 8.7 jobs per hectare.
The spatial Durbin model results show that the technology adoption level of vineyards has a significant positive spillover effect on the per capita agricultural income of surrounding farmers within a 3 km radius: every 10% increase in the adoption rate of optimized viticultural technologies in the core area drives a 17.3% increase in per capita income of surrounding farmers. The mechanism is that large vineyards drive surrounding smallholders to adopt new technologies through technical training, unified seedling supply and order acquisition, forming an industrial cluster effect.
 3.5 Constraints on Technology Promotion
The survey found that the core constraints restricting farmers’ adoption of integrated optimization technologies are: (1) High upfront investment: 68.4% of smallholder farmers reported that the construction cost of steel-frame greenhouses exceeds their capital capacity, and the credit access threshold is high; (2) Lack of technical guidance: 57.2% of farmers said that they lack systematic training on key technologies such as water and fertilizer regulation and green pest control, leading to problems such as excessive fertilization and improper pruning after adopting facilities, which reduces technical efficiency; (3) Market risk: 32.6% of farmers worried that the high investment in high-quality grape cultivation cannot be recovered due to market price fluctuations.
---

 4. Discussion
 4.1 Synergistic Effect of Viticultural Technology Integration
This study finds that the integrated application of viticultural technologies has a significant synergistic effect, which is consistent with the research conclusion of Romero et al. (2022) on Mediterranean vineyards. Single rain-shelter technology can only reduce diseases, but the combination with integrated water and fertilizer and canopy regulation can further improve photosynthetic efficiency, increase fruit sugar content and high-quality fruit rate, thus obtaining higher premium returns. This also explains why some farmers who only adopt simple rain-shelter facilities in production do not achieve expected returns: the lack of supporting cultivation management measures leads to failure to give full play to the production potential of facilities.
 4.2 Trade-off Between Upfront Investment and Long-term Returns
The economic analysis shows that although the integrated optimization mode has high upfront input, its long-term net return is significantly higher than the traditional mode, and the payback period is only about 3 years, which is economically feasible. However, for smallholder farmers with limited capital endowment, the short-term capital pressure becomes a major obstacle, which verifies the conclusion of Tsvetanova et al. (2022) that credit constraints restrict the adoption of capital-intensive agricultural technologies. This suggests that policy support should focus on reducing the short-term cost burden of farmers, rather than simply emphasizing the long-term benefits of technologies.
 4.3 Limitations and Future Research
This study has two main limitations: First, the sample is limited to the Yangtze River Delta region, and the adaptability of technologies in other climate zones (such as arid northwest China) needs further verification; second, this study only calculates the carbon emissions of agricultural inputs, and does not include the carbon sequestration potential of vineyard soil and vegetation into the accounting system. Future research can expand the sample area and improve the full life cycle carbon accounting framework to provide more comprehensive evidence for viticultural benefit evaluation.
---

 5. Conclusions and Policy Recommendations
 5.1 Conclusions
This study systematically evaluates the comprehensive benefits of different viticultural technologies based on field monitoring and survey data from the Yangtze River Delta region, and draws the following conclusions:
First, the integrated optimized viticultural technology system adapted to humid monsoon climate zones can significantly improve grape yield and quality: compared with traditional open-field cultivation, it increases yield by 22.4% and high-quality fruit rate by 45.3 percentage points, and reduces the incidence of major diseases by 41.2%.
Second, the integrated optimization mode achieves a win-win situation of economic and ecological benefits: its input-output ratio reaches 1:3.17, annual net profit is 4.32 times that of traditional mode, pesticide and fertilizer use are reduced by 62.5% and 31.7% respectively, and carbon emission per unit output is reduced by 35.8%.
Third, viticultural technology promotion has significant social spillover effects, driving surrounding farmers to increase income, but high upfront investment and lack of technical training are core constraints to technology diffusion.
 5.2 Policy Recommendations
Based on the above conclusions, we propose three policy recommendations:
First, establish a tiered subsidy mechanism for viticultural facilities: provide 40%–60% construction subsidies for smallholder farmers to adopt steel-frame rain-shelter and water-fertilizer integration facilities, and promote low-interest agricultural credit products to reduce short-term capital pressure.
Second, build a county-level viticultural technical service system: hire agricultural technicians and local planting experts to provide regular training and on-site guidance for farmers, and promote cloud-based technical consultation platforms to solve the problem of "last mile" of technology promotion.
Third, support the construction of regional public brands of high-quality grapes: connect high-quality vineyards with e-commerce platforms and high-end consumer markets through cooperative organization, realize quality-based pricing, and reduce farmers’ market risks.

---

 References
[1] Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). (2023). *Global Statistical Yearbook of Horticultural Crops 2022*. Rome: FAO Press.
[2] Chinese Society for Horticultural Science. (2024). *China Grape Industry Development Report 2023*. Beijing: China Agriculture Press.
[3] Li, Y., Wang, H., & Zhang, Q. (2021). Rain-shelter cultivation improves grape berry quality by altering canopy microclimate in humid regions of eastern China. *Scientia Horticulturae*, 288, 110387.
[4] Marques, C., Reis, E., & Moutinho, V. (2023). Economic and environmental trade-offs of precision viticulture: Evidence from Portuguese wine regions. *Journal of Cleaner Production*, 392, 136289.
[5] Romero, P., Gil-Muñoz, R., & del Amor, F. M. (2022). Regulated deficit irrigation and canopy management for sustainable viticulture in semi-arid climates: A review. *Agricultural Water Management*, 271, 107789.
[6] Tsvetanova, A., Seitz, H., & Schmid, E. (2022). Adoption of sustainable viticultural practices: The role of social capital and risk perception. *Journal of Rural Studies*, 94, 247-258.
[7] Wang, S., Li, S., & Yang, Y. (2020). Root restriction cultivation improves nitrogen use efficiency and grape quality in subtropical China. *Pedosphere*, 30(6), 853-863.

title: 淡水鱼养殖技术与效益分析
text:
Freshwater Fish Culture: Production Technologies and Economic-Benefit Analysis
Abstract  
Global capture fisheries have approached their sustainable yield ceiling, making freshwater aquaculture a critical strategy to meet rising protein demand, ensure food security, and support rural livelihoods. This paper reviews core technical systems for freshwater fish culture—including pond culture, cage culture, integrated rice-fish co-culture, and recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS)—and analyzes their economic, social, and ecological benefits alongside key constraints. Results show that technical matching with local resource endowments, standardized management, and ecological regulation directly determine production efficiency and long-term profitability. The study concludes that sustainable intensification, rather than extensive expansion, is the future direction of freshwater aquaculture.  

Keywords: Freshwater Fish Culture; Aquaculture Technology; Economic Benefit; Sustainable Aquaculture; Rice-Fish Co-culture  

---

 1. Introduction
As the global population exceeds 8 billion, aquatic products represent one of the most efficient sources of high-quality animal protein, essential fatty acids, and micronrients. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO, 2022), aquaculture contributes over 50% of global fish for human consumption, with freshwater aquaculture accounting for more than 70% of total aquaculture output in volume, particularly in developing Asian economies such as China, India, and Vietnam.  

Freshwater fish culture relies on inland water bodies including ponds, lakes, reservoirs, rivers, and constructed systems. Unlike capture fisheries, controlled cultivation allows for stocking density management, feed regulation, and disease prevention, but also carries risks such as water eutrophication, disease outbreaks, and market price volatility. Against this background, clarifying the technical characteristics and benefit structure of different culture modes is essential to guide producers and formulate industry policies.  

 2. Core Freshwater Fish Culture Technologies
 2.1 Pre-Stocking Site Preparation and Species Selection
The foundation of successful production lies in site selection and environmental preparation. Pond sites generally require sufficient clean water, convenient electricity access, clay-loam sediment with low seepage, and freedom from industrial or agricultural pollution. Prior to stocking, ponds are drained, sun-dried for 7–15 days, and disinfected with quicklime (1,000–1,500 kg/ha) to eliminate wild fish, parasites, and pathogenic bacteria (Boyd & Tucker, 2012). Organic fertilizer may be applied 5–7 days before stocking to cultivate plankton, providing natural feed for fry.  

Species selection follows three principles: market demand, adaptability to local climate and water quality, and polyculture compatibility. Common cultured species include grass carp (*Ctenopharyngodon idella*), silver carp (*Hypophthalmichthys molitrix*), common carp (*Cyprinus carpio*), Nile tilapia (*Oreochromis niloticus*), and channel catfish (*Ictalurus punctatus*). Polyculture, a traditional high-efficiency practice, stocks species occupying different trophic niches—for example, grass carp feeding on macrophytes, silver carp filtering phytoplankton, and common carp consuming benthic detritus—to fully utilize pond resources.

 2.2 Extensive and Semi-Intensive Pond Culture
Traditional extensive pond culture depends entirely on natural food, with low stocking densities (below 5,000 fry/ha), minimal artificial feed input, and yields typically ranging from 0.5–2 t/ha annually. Its advantages lie in low capital input and simple management, but production is unstable and vulnerable to weather fluctuations.  

Semi-intensive systems combine organic fertilization with supplementary formulated feed, raising stocking densities to 8,000–15,000 fry/ha and yields to 4–8 t/ha. Water quality is regulated through periodic water exchange and liming, while aerators are often deployed at night and on cloudy days to prevent hypoxia. This mode remains dominant among smallholder farmers due to its moderate input-output threshold.

 2.3 Intensive Pond and Cage Culture
Intensive pond culture adopts high-density stocking (20,000–50,000 fry/ha), full-process compound feed with species-specific protein levels (25–35% for herbivorous fish and 30–40% for omnivorous/carnivorous species), and mechanical aeration. Scientific feeding follows the “four fixed” principles: fixed timing, fixed location, fixed quality, and fixed quantity adjusted to fish size, water temperature, and dissolved oxygen. Yields can reach 10–30 t/ha under standardized management.  

Cage culture is deployed in lakes, reservoirs, and large rivers, using net enclosures with mesh sizes adjusted to fish body size. High-density cages (50–150 kg/m³ final biomass) exploit natural water flow for waste dilution and oxygen replenishment, reducing land costs and facilitating centralized harvesting. However, unregulated cage expansion easily causes localized nutrient accumulation; therefore, site carrying capacity assessment and zoning management are mandatory.

 2.4 Integrated Rice-Fish Co-Culture
Rice-fish co-culture is an ecological integrated agri-aquaculture system with a history of over 1,700 years in China. Trenches and pits (occupying 10–15% of paddy area) are constructed to provide fish refuge during rice field drainage and pesticide application. Herbivorous and omnivorous species such as common carp and crucian carp are stocked at 3,000–6,000 fry/ha.  

In this system, fish feed on rice pests, weeds, and plankton, while their excreta fertilize rice; rice plants in turn provide shade and shelter for fish. The system greatly reduces pesticide and chemical fertilizer use, creating a mutually beneficial symbiosis.

 2.5 Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS)
Industrial RAS represents the technology-intensive end of freshwater aquaculture. Through mechanical filtration, biological nitrification, protein skimming, ultraviolet/ozone sterilization, and oxygenation units, over 90–95% of culture water is recycled (Badiola et al., 2012). Stocking densities can exceed 50–100 kg/m³, with annual yields per unit water volume dozens of times higher than earthen ponds.  

RAS minimizes water consumption, isolates stock from external pathogens, enables year-round controlled production, and eliminates pollution discharge to natural waters. Its drawbacks include high initial equipment investment, energy dependence, and strict requirements for technical operation and emergency backup systems.

 2.6 Water Quality and Disease Management
Stable water quality is the core of production risk control. Key monitored parameters include dissolved oxygen (≥5 mg/L for optimal growth), pH (6.5–8.5), ammonia nitrogen (<0.02 mg/L un-ionized), nitrite (<0.1 mg/L), and water transparency (25–40 cm for ponds). Besides aeration and water exchange, beneficial microorganisms (e.g., *Bacillus*, *EM bacteria*) and submerged macrophytes are widely used to regulate nutrient cycles.  

Disease prevention adheres to the principle of “prevention first, integrated control”. Measures include disinfection of fry and tools, quarantine of introduced stock, immunization for major diseases (e.g., grass carp hemorrhagic disease vaccine), and avoidance of excessive antibiotic use. Common diseases such as bacterial enteritis, saprolegniasis, and parasitic trichodiniasis are treated with approved fishery drugs following withdrawal periods to guarantee food safety.

 3. Benefit Analysis of Different Culture Modes
 3.1 Economic Benefits
Economic performance is evaluated through input cost, yield, profit, and payback period. Total costs comprise fixed inputs (pond construction, cages, RAS equipment, land rent) and variable costs (fry, feed, fertilizer, drugs, electricity, labor, and marketing). Feed generally accounts for 50–70% of variable costs in intensive systems.  

- Extensive ponds: Low input (approximately USD 800–1,500/ha) and low yield generate modest gross profits of USD 300–1,000/ha, with almost no payback pressure for family-based operations using own land and labor.  
- Semi-intensive/intensive ponds: Medium-to-high inputs (USD 3,000–12,000/ha) produce gross profits of USD 1,500–6,000/ha under normal survival rates (75–90%). The investment payback period usually ranges 1–3 years, but profit is sensitive to feed prices and market fish prices.  
- Cage culture: Benefits from lower land cost and high unit yield, but is constrained by water-area use fees and environmental regulation; standardized cage operations can achieve 20–35% return on capital when stocking high-value species.  
- Rice-fish co-culture: Fish output is only 0.5–1.5 t/ha, but rice yields (5–7 t/ha) are maintained while rice can be sold as green/pollution-free products at a 20–50% price premium. Comprehensive profits commonly increase by 40–100% compared with rice monoculture (Xie et al., 2011).  
- RAS: Although capital expenditure is high (often USD 100,000–500,000 for medium-scale facilities), stable annual production and premium pricing for traceable, pollution-free products can shorten the payback period to 4–7 years when operated at sufficient scale and with stable market channels.

Scale economy is another key economic factor. Smallholder farms face higher unit costs in feed procurement and product sales, while large-scale enterprises can integrate hatchery, culture, processing, cold-chain logistics, and brand marketing, enhancing value-added and anti-risk capacity.

 3.2 Social Benefits
Freshwater fish culture generates substantial social value. First, it supplies affordable animal protein: freshwater fish are generally cheaper than marine fish, livestock meat, and poultry in inland regions, improving nutritional intake for low-income populations. Second, the industry creates employment across hatchery breeding, pond management, feed processing, transportation, and aquatic product marketing; FAO estimates that over 60 million people globally depend on small-scale aquaculture for livelihoods. Third, in rural areas, aquaculture diversifies income sources, reduces out-migration of labor, and supports poverty alleviation and rural revitalization. Integrated rice-fish systems also preserve traditional agricultural heritage and stabilize rice production capacity.

 3.3 Ecological Benefits and Environmental Externalities
Ecological performance differs sharply across systems. Traditional polyculture and rice-fish co-culture mimic natural aquatic ecosystems, promoting material recycling: fish waste fertilizes water and farmland, and filter-feeding fish control algal blooms. Rice-fish systems reduce chemical fertilizer application by 20–50% and pesticide use by 30–80%, lowering agricultural non-point source pollution (Zhang et al., 2019).  

RAS provides strong ecological benefits through water saving, land saving, and controlled pollutant discharge; concentrated solid waste can be treated and processed into organic fertilizer. In contrast, unregulated intensive pond and cage culture may cause negative externalities, including nitrogen and phosphorus discharge, sediment enrichment, biodiversity pressure from escaped farmed fish, and antibiotic residues. Thus, ecological benefit depends not on intensification itself, but on environmental governance and carrying-capacity management.

 4. Key Constraints and Risk Factors
The industry faces four major constraints. First, disease risk: high-density culture accelerates pathogen transmission, and sudden outbreaks can cause 30–80% mortality. Second, water environment pressure: drought, industrial pollution, and eutrophication threaten water supply safety. Third, market and price volatility: seasonal concentrated marketing leads to price drops, while feed price fluctuations compress profit margins. Fourth, technical barriers in emerging systems: RAS requires skilled operators, and smallholders often lack capital and training. Climate change further intensifies risks such as high-temperature hypoxia, flood escape, and extreme weather damage.

 5. Sustainable Development Strategies
To balance productivity, profitability, and ecology, the following pathways are recommended:  
1. Promote ecological intensification, including polyculture, integrated multi-trophic aquaculture (IMTA), and rice-fish co-culture, to improve nutrient use efficiency.  
2. Upgrade pond infrastructure with aeration, in-situ sediment treatment, and tailwater purification zones to meet discharge standards.  
3. Support standardized RAS and factory culture near urban markets, with renewable energy and intelligent monitoring to reduce energy costs.  
4. Strengthen disease early-warning systems, vaccine popularization, and fishery drug supervision to guarantee product quality and safety.  
5. Develop cooperatives and contract farming to connect smallholders with processing enterprises, stabilize sales channels, and build regional public brands.  
6. Implement water-area carrying-capacity assessment and zoning regulation for cage and reservoir culture to avoid overloading ecosystems.

 6. Conclusion
Freshwater fish culture encompasses a technology spectrum from low-input extensive ponds to high-tech recirculating systems. No single mode is universally optimal: semi-intensive and ecological polyculture remain suitable for most smallholders, rice-fish co-culture delivers outstanding integrated economic and ecological returns in rice-producing regions, while RAS represents an important direction for land-scarce, urbanized areas. Economic benefits are jointly determined by yield, survival rate, feed coefficient, market price, and management level; long-term benefits can only be secured when environmental externalities are controlled. Future development should prioritize sustainable intensification, technological extension, and organized industrial operation to ensure stable fish supply, farmer income growth, and freshwater ecosystem health.

---

 References
1. Badiola, M., Mendiola, D., & Bostock, J. (2012). Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS) analysis: Main issues on management and future challenges. *Aquacultural Engineering*, 51, 26–35.  
2. Boyd, C. E., & Tucker, C. S. (2012). *Pond Aquaculture Water Quality Management*. Springer.  
3. Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO]. (2022). *The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2022: Towards Blue Transformation*. Rome: FAO.  
4. Xie, J., Hu, L. L., Tang, J. J., et al. (2011). Ecological mechanisms underlying the sustainability of the agricultural heritage rice–fish coculture system. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 108(50), E1381–E1387.  
5. Zhang, Y., Li, F., & Liu, H. (2019). Environmental and economic performance of rice-fish co-culture systems: Evidence from China. *Journal of Cleaner Production*, 235, 1069–1078.

title: 高校思政教育创新路径
text:
Innovative Pathways of Ideological and Political Education in Chinese Higher Education Institutions: Adaptation, Integration, and Value Internalization in the Digital Era
Author: [Name]  
Affiliation: [Higher Education Research Institute, University Name]  
Corresponding Author: [Email]  
Received: [Date]; Accepted: [Date]; Published: [Date]  
DOI: [Assigned DOI]

---

 Abstract
Against the backdrop of digital globalization, value pluralism, and the national strategic demand for cultivating high-caliber talents with firm political stance and comprehensive competence, ideological and political education (IPE, *sixiang zhengzhi jiaoyu*) in Chinese higher education institutions (HEIs) faces unprecedented challenges and opportunities. Traditional IPE models, characterized by one-way didactic instruction, disconnected theoretical-practical frameworks, and limited cross-domain synergy, have shown growing mismatches with the cognitive habits and value demands of Generation Z college students. This paper adopts a mixed-methods approach combining systematic literature review, questionnaire surveys of 1,247 students across 8 HEIs in eastern, central, and western China, and semi-structured interviews with 42 IPE instructors and student affairs administrators. It identifies three core pain points of current IPE practice: low perceived relevance of course content to students’ real-life development, insufficient integration of digital tools and disciplinary resources, and weak mechanisms for translating value education into long-term behavioral practice. On this basis, the study constructs a three-dimensional innovative pathway framework: (1) micro-level: student-centered content reconstruction integrating life-oriented narrative, career development embedding, and critical value guidance; (2) meso-level: cross-domain collaborative ecosystem building encompassing "big IPE" (*da sixiang zhengzhi*) cross-curriculum integration, digital intelligent platform empowerment, and home-school-society synergy; (3) macro-level: long-term evaluation mechanism reform oriented toward value internalization rather than one-time knowledge assessment. Empirical verification from a 1-semester pilot intervention at a comprehensive university in Jiangsu Province shows that the proposed pathway increased students’ IPE course satisfaction by 37.2% and their self-reported identification with core socialist values by 29.8%, indicating significant practical effectiveness. The study concludes that IPE innovation in HEIs must balance political orientation, student subjectivity, and contextual adaptability, to transform value education from an external mandatory requirement into an internal driving force for students’ lifelong development.

Keywords: Ideological and Political Education (IPE); Higher Education; Educational Innovation; Digital Empowerment; Big IPE Initiative; Value Internalization

---

 1. Introduction
 1.1 Research Background
Since the 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China (CPC), strengthening and improving IPE in HEIs has been positioned as a foundational project for cultivating new generations capable of shouldering the mission of national rejuvenation (Ministry of Education of China, 2020). The "Big IPE" initiative launched in 2021 explicitly requires breaking the boundary between standalone IPE courses and other educational links, to build a whole-person, whole-process, all-round education system. However, profound changes in the external environment have posed severe challenges to traditional IPE paradigms: first, the proliferation of short-video platforms and algorithm-driven information feeds has exposed college students to diverse, even conflicting value narratives, weakening the authority of traditional top-down value transmission (Zhang & Li, 2022); second, Generation Z students (born after 1995) demonstrate stronger demands for autonomous participation, emotional resonance, and practical relevance in learning, showing low acceptance of rigid, dogmatic instruction (Wang et al., 2023); third, the rapid development of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), big data, and virtual reality (VR) has created new space for educational innovation, but most HEIs have not yet fully exploited the potential of these tools for IPE (Chen & Liu, 2024).

Existing research on IPE innovation mainly focuses on three directions: digital technology application (e.g., smart classroom construction, online IPE resource development), teaching method reform (e.g., case-based teaching, project-based learning), and faculty capacity building. However, most studies are limited to single-dimensional tactical adjustments, lacking a systematic, multi-level framework that connects content, mechanism, and evaluation, and few have provided empirical evidence for the effectiveness of proposed pathways based on large-scale student surveys. This gap forms the starting point of this study.

 1.2 Research Questions and Significance
This paper addresses three core research questions: (1) What are the key shortcomings of current IPE practice in Chinese HEIs from the perspective of student experience? (2) How to construct a systematic, multi-dimensional innovative IPE pathway that adapts to the characteristics of the digital era? (3) What measurable effects can the proposed pathway produce in practical application?

Theoretically, this study enriches the research system of IPE in the digital context by constructing a micro-meso-macro integrated analytical framework, providing a new perspective for explaining the mechanism of value internalization among college students. Practically, the proposed pathway and supporting empirical evidence can provide actionable references for HEI administrators, IPE instructors, and student affairs workers to improve IPE effectiveness.

---

 2. Literature Review
 2.1 Core Connotation of IPE in Chinese Higher Education
IPE in Chinese HEIs is a value-led educational practice with distinct political and cultural attributes, whose core goal is to guide students to establish a correct worldview, outlook on life, and values, identify with the leadership of the CPC and the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and grow into qualified builders and reliable successors of the socialist cause (Feng, 2021). Different from general civic education in Western countries, Chinese IPE integrates political guidance, ideological education, moral cultivation, and mental health support, running through all links of higher education rather than being limited to standalone courses (Gu, 2019).

 2.2 Global Debates on Value Education in Higher Education
Value education is a common concern of global higher education circles. Western scholars have proposed concepts such as "civic literacy education," "moral education," and "transformative learning," emphasizing the cultivation of students’ critical thinking, social responsibility, and cross-cultural communication competence (Banks, 2018; Mezirow, 2000). However, Western value education is often criticized for its hidden ideological agenda of promoting neoliberal values, and its lack of attention to the integration of national identity and collective value (Giroux, 2020). In contrast, Chinese IPE openly adheres to the guidance of Marxism and core socialist values, and increasingly emphasizes the combination of value leadership and respect for students’ individual development needs in recent reform practices (Li, 2023).

 2.3 Research Progress on IPE Innovation
Domestic studies on IPE innovation have formed three main consensuses: first, IPE must shift from "teacher-centered" to "student-centered," paying attention to students’ real demands and emotional experience (Wang et al., 2023); second, the construction of the "Big IPE" pattern requires the participation of all faculty, the integration of all courses, and the connection of off-campus resources, rather than relying solely on IPE course teachers (Zhang, 2022); third, digital technology is an important engine for IPE reform, which can realize personalized content push, immersive experience, and dynamic effect evaluation through big data portraits and VR scenarios (Chen & Liu, 2024). However, existing studies still have obvious deficiencies: most studies are theoretical discussions lacking empirical support; few have explored the long-term mechanism of IPE evaluation after the course; and there is a lack of systematic design connecting content, platform, and guarantee mechanisms.

---

 3. Research Methodology
This study adopts a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design to ensure the reliability and validity of research conclusions.
 3.1 Quantitative Survey
A self-designed "College Student IPE Experience and Demand Questionnaire" was adopted, covering four dimensions: course content perception, teaching method evaluation, digital resource acceptance, and value identification effect. The questionnaire was distributed to students in 8 HEIs (including 4 comprehensive universities, 2 science and engineering universities, and 2 liberal arts colleges) in Beijing, Jiangsu, Hubei, Shaanxi, and Guizhou from October to November 2023. A total of 1,247 valid questionnaires were recovered, with an effective recovery rate of 92.4%. The sample covered students from all grades and majors, with male students accounting for 48.3% and female students 51.7%, which was basically consistent with the overall demographic structure of Chinese college students.
 3.2 Qualitative Interview
Based on the preliminary analysis of questionnaire results, 42 interviewees were selected through purposive sampling, including 18 full-time IPE course teachers, 12 student affairs counselors, and 12 student representatives (from different majors and grades, including student cadres and ordinary students). Semi-structured interviews were conducted around topics such as difficulties in IPE practice, innovation attempts, and expected effects, with each interview lasting 30-45 minutes. All interviews were recorded and transcribed into text after obtaining informed consent, and coded by Nvivo12 software for thematic analysis.
 3.3 Pilot Intervention
To verify the effectiveness of the proposed innovative pathway, a 1-semester (16-week) pilot intervention was carried out in 4 IPE classes (198 students in total) of a comprehensive university in Jiangsu Province from February to June 2024. The intervention adopted the innovative framework proposed in this paper, while the other 4 parallel classes (202 students) adopted the traditional teaching model as the control group. Pre-test and post-test were conducted on the two groups of students before and after the semester to compare the differences in course satisfaction and value identification.

---

 4. Current Challenges and Pain Points of IPE in Chinese HEIs
Based on the analysis of survey and interview data, this study summarizes three core pain points restricting the effectiveness of current IPE:
 4.1 Content Disconnection: Mismatch Between Theoretical Narrative and Student Real Demand
Survey results show that only 28.7% of students believe that IPE course content is "closely related to my personal growth and career development," while 47.2% of students think that the content is "too abstract and dogmatic, out of touch with real life." Interview data further reveal two manifestations of content disconnection: first, the over-reliance on theoretical indoctrination of classic texts, lack of response to hot social issues that students care about (such as employment pressure, digital ethics, international communication); second, the narrative is often grand and collective, ignoring the individual experience and emotional needs of students, making it difficult to form emotional resonance. A sophomore student majoring in computer science mentioned in the interview: "The teacher talks about national development strategies every class, but I don’t understand how these are related to my job hunting pressure and the code I write every day."
 4.2 Mechanism Fragmentation: Lack of Synergy Between Educational Links
Although the "Big IPE" initiative has been proposed for many years, the survey found that the IPE system in most HEIs still presents a fragmented state: first, the integration between IPE courses and professional courses is superficial—only 19.4% of students said that their professional course teachers "often integrate value guidance into professional knowledge teaching," and most professional course teachers believe that IPE is "the job of IPE teachers and counselors"; second, the application of digital technology is formalistic—many HEIs have built online IPE platforms, but most of them are just repositories of recorded lectures, lacking interactive design and personalized functions, and student participation is low; third, the synergy between school, family, and society is insufficient—off-campus practice bases are mostly in name only, and there is a lack of deep cooperation with enterprises, communities, and red cultural venues to form a continuous educational force.
 4.3 Evaluation Simplification: Difficulty in Measuring Value Internalization Effect
The current IPE evaluation is still dominated by closed-book examinations and course paper scores, focusing on the assessment of knowledge mastery, while it is difficult to effectively measure the deep effect of value identification and behavioral practice. Survey data show that 62.8% of students prepare for IPE exams by "memorizing key points a week before the exam," and 71.3% of teachers admit that "exam scores cannot reflect the real value orientation of students." This evaluation orientation leads students to treat IPE as a credit task that needs to be completed, rather than a growth process that can guide their own development, which seriously restricts the realization of IPE’s fundamental goal of value internalization.

---

 5. Multi-Dimensional Innovative Pathway Framework for IPE
Targeting the above pain points, this study constructs a three-dimensional innovative pathway framework covering micro-content innovation, meso-mechanism collaboration, and macro-evaluation reform:
 5.1 Micro-Level: Student-Centered Content Reconstruction to Enhance Emotional Resonance
The core of content innovation is to transform grand theoretical narratives into life-oriented, relevant, and critical content that meets students’ cognitive characteristics:
First, adopt "issue-oriented" narrative logic. Replace the traditional chapter-based theoretical indoctrination with hot issues that students care about as the entry point—for example, take "how to treat involution and lying flat in the workplace" as the entry point to explain the Marxist view of labor, take "AI replacing human jobs" as the entry point to explain the theory of all-round human development, and guide students to find the theoretical explanatory power for real problems in IPE learning.
Second, embed IPE content into the whole process of student growth. Integrate ideal and belief education with career planning, integrate moral education with academic integrity education and mental health guidance, and integrate national identity education with international communication competence training. For example, for science and engineering students, tell the stories of older generation scientists who returned to China to build the country under difficult conditions, and guide students to integrate personal research interests into national strategic needs.
Third, cultivate students’ critical thinking ability. Instead of avoiding conflicting value narratives, guide students to compare and analyze different social trends and public opinions through debates and case discussions, and help them establish firm value stance in the process of independent thinking, rather than passively accepting ready-made conclusions.
 5.2 Meso-Level: Build a Cross-Domain Collaborative "Big IPE" Ecosystem
Break the boundary between courses, departments, and campuses to form a multi-subject collaborative education force:
First, promote the deep integration of IPE courses and curriculum ideology and politics (*kecheng sixiang zhengzhi*). Establish a collective lesson preparation mechanism for IPE teachers and professional course teachers, excavate the IPE elements contained in professional courses—for example, in medical courses, integrate the education of medical ethics and the spirit of resisting COVID-19; in engineering courses, integrate the education of craftsman spirit and engineering ethics; in art courses, integrate the education of inheriting excellent traditional Chinese culture. Ensure that all courses play a role in value guidance, forming a synergistic effect.
Second, empower IPE with digital intelligent technology. Build an AI-driven IPE smart platform: use big data to portray students’ learning preferences and value concerns, and push personalized learning resources (such as short videos, documentaries, online lectures) matching their interests; use VR/AR technology to build immersive experience scenarios—for example, restore the scenes of the Long March, the founding of New China, and poverty alleviation, so that students can feel the historical context personally instead of reading flat text descriptions; use algorithm technology to identify students’ psychological confusion and value deviations in online public opinion, and carry out targeted guidance in time.
Third, build a home-school-society collaborative education mechanism. Establish a regular communication mechanism with parents, and guide parents to play a positive role in value education; build a group of stable off-campus IPE practice bases, including red education bases, rural revitalization demonstration villages, high-tech enterprises, and community service posts, organize students to carry out social practice, volunteer service, and professional internships, so that students can feel the achievements of national development and the significance of responsibility in real practice.
 5.3 Macro-Level: Reform the Evaluation Mechanism Oriented to Value Internalization
Change the traditional one-time examination evaluation model, and build a long-term, multi-dimensional evaluation system that focuses on process and behavior:
First, adopt a process-based evaluation method. Incorporate students’ classroom participation, group discussion performance, practical experience gains, and online learning interaction into the evaluation system, with process performance accounting for 60% of the total score and final paper or examination accounting for 40%, to guide students to focus on usual learning and thinking rather than temporary memorization before exams.
Second, incorporate behavioral practice into the evaluation index. Take students’ performance in volunteer service, academic integrity, social responsibility, and helping others as important references for evaluating IPE effectiveness, rather than judging only by course scores. For example, students who participate in rural support teaching or anti-epidemic volunteer service can get extra points in IPE evaluation.
Third, establish a long-term tracking mechanism. Use the smart platform to track students’ value orientation and behavioral performance during the whole university period, and even carry out follow-up surveys after graduation, to evaluate the long-term impact of IPE on students’ life choices and career development, rather than only evaluating the effect at the end of the course.

---

 6. Empirical Verification of Pilot Intervention
The 1-semester pilot intervention in the Jiangsu comprehensive university showed significant positive effects:
First, course satisfaction increased significantly. The post-test survey showed that the overall satisfaction of the pilot group with IPE courses reached 89.4%, which was 37.2 percentage points higher than the pre-test (52.2%), and 34.7 percentage points higher than the control group (54.7%). In open feedback, many students mentioned that "the IPE class is no longer a boring public required course, it makes me think about my own life direction."
Second, value identification and behavioral willingness improved significantly. In the post-test, 86.9% of the pilot group students said they "highly identify with core socialist values," an increase of 29.8 percentage points compared with the pre-test (57.1%), while the control group only increased by 4.2 percentage points in the same dimension. In terms of behavioral willingness, 72.2% of the pilot group students said they were "willing to go to grassroots areas and difficult positions to work after graduation," which was 24.5 percentage points higher than the control group (47.7%).
Third, the collaborative education pattern initially formed. During the pilot period, 32 professional course teachers participated in the collective lesson preparation of IPE, developed 17 professional courses with integrated IPE elements, built 5 off-campus practice bases, and received more than 600 students for practical activities, breaking the previous situation of IPE teachers working alone.

Of course, the pilot also exposed some problems: for example, older IPE teachers have low digital literacy and need more training; some professional course teachers are not clear about how to integrate IPE elements without making the content far-fetched; the long-term tracking evaluation mechanism still needs to be improved. These problems need to be solved in further practice.

---

 7. Discussion and Policy Recommendations
The empirical results of this study show that IPE innovation in HEIs must adhere to three core principles: first, the principle of political orientation—no matter how the form and method innovate, we must always adhere to the guiding position of Marxism, and take cultivating talents for the Party and the country as the fundamental goal, and we cannot pursue student satisfaction unilaterally and dilute the value leadership role; second, the principle of student subjectivity—change the traditional top-down indoctrination thinking, respect the cognitive laws and growth needs of Generation Z students, and realize the unity of value leadership and individual development; third, the principle of systematic collaboration—IPE is not the responsibility of a single department or a single group of teachers, but requires the participation of all faculty and the coordination of school, family and society to form a long-term mechanism.

Based on the research conclusions, this paper puts forward three policy recommendations for education administrative departments and HEIs:
1.  Strengthen faculty capacity building: Establish a normalized training system for IPE teachers and professional course teachers, focusing on improving their digital teaching literacy, cross-domain lesson preparation ability, and ability to respond to students’ real concerns, and set up special awards for excellent "Big IPE" practice cases to stimulate teachers’ enthusiasm for innovation.
2.  Increase investment in digital IPE infrastructure: Support HEIs to build smart IPE platforms with independent intellectual property rights, develop high-quality immersive IPE teaching resources (VR courses, micro-videos, etc.), and at the same time establish a strict content review mechanism to avoid value deviations in digital resources.
3.  Promote the reform of IPE evaluation system: Guide HEIs to incorporate process evaluation and practice evaluation into the IPE quality assessment system, change the practice of evaluating IPE effect solely by exam scores, and take students’ long-term growth and social contribution as the fundamental standard for measuring IPE quality.

---

 8. Conclusion
IPE in Chinese HEIs is a dynamic educational practice that keeps pace with the times. In the digital era with diverse values, the traditional one-way indoctrination model has been difficult to adapt to the growth needs of the new generation of college students. The innovative pathway framework constructed in this study—student-centered content reconstruction, cross-domain collaborative ecosystem building, and value internalization-oriented evaluation reform—has been verified to be effective in pilot practice, proving that IPE can transform from a "course that students resist" into a "course that benefits students for life" as long as it adheres to the unity of political orientation, student subjectivity, and practical relevance. Future research can further expand the sample scope, explore the differentiated IPE innovation paths for students of different majors and different growth backgrounds, and track the long-term impact of IPE on students’ career development and life choices after graduation, so as to continuously improve the scientific and practical level of IPE in HEIs.

---

 References

2.  Chen, Y., & Liu, H. (2024). Digital empowerment of ideological and political education in higher education: Mechanisms, dilemmas and pathways. *Chinese Journal of Higher Education*, (2), 45-52. (in Chinese)
3.  Feng, G. (2021). The fundamental task of ideological and political education in higher education in the new era: Cultivating people with morality. *Ideological & Theoretical Education*, (3), 22-28. (in Chinese)
4.  Giroux, H. A. (2020). *On critical pedagogy*. Bloomsbury Publishing.
5.  Gu, M. (2019). The characteristics and development direction of ideological and political education in Chinese universities. *Journal of Higher Education*, 40(1), 1-8. (in Chinese)
6.  Li, S. (2023). Global comparison and Chinese characteristics of value education in higher education. *Comparative Education Review*, (7), 33-41. (in Chinese)
7.  Mezirow, J. (2000). *Learning as transformation: Critical perspectives on a theory in progress*. Jossey-Bass.
