title: 淡水鱼高效种植模式与经济效益分析
text:
Efficient Freshwater Fish Culture Models and Economic Benefit Analysis  
 Abstract  
With the global demand for high-quality aquatic protein continuing to rise and the constraints of freshwater aquaculture resources becoming increasingly tight, exploring efficient freshwater fish farming models is of great significance for ensuring food security and improving aquaculture economic returns. This study takes three mainstream efficient farming models—integrated rice-fish farming, pond recirculating aquaculture system (RAS), and pond cage culture—as research objects, and compares their production performance, cost composition, and economic benefits through field surveys, cost-benefit accounting, and comparative analysis. The results show that all three efficient models outperform traditional extensive pond farming in yield per unit area and resource utilization efficiency. The integrated rice-fish farming model has the lowest input cost and strongest ecological synergy, with an input-output ratio of 1:2.38; the RAS model achieves the highest fish yield per unit area and strongest production controllability, with an input-output ratio of 1:1.72, but has high upfront infrastructure and energy costs; the pond cage culture model balances yield and management convenience, with an input-output ratio of 1:2.05. Further analysis indicates that factors including fry quality, feed conversion ratio (FCR), water environment management, and market sales channels directly affect the economic benefits of farming. This study suggests that farmers should select appropriate farming models based on regional resource endowments, capital strength, and market conditions, and the government should increase support for ecological and efficient aquaculture technologies to promote the sustainable development of the freshwater aquaculture industry.  

Keywords: Freshwater fish; Efficient aquaculture model; Economic benefit; Input-output ratio; Sustainable aquaculture  


 1. Introduction  
Freshwater aquaculture is a key component of global food supply systems, providing a large amount of high-quality animal protein for human society. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO, 2022), global freshwater aquaculture output exceeded 54 million tons in 2020, accounting for more than 60% of total aquaculture output, and plays an important role in ensuring global food security and reducing poverty in rural areas. China is one of the earliest countries in the world to carry out freshwater aquaculture, with a long history of fish farming such as carp and grass carp. In recent decades, China’s freshwater aquaculture industry has developed rapidly, but it also faces problems such as excessive reliance on water and land resources, extensive production methods, frequent water quality pollution, and unstable economic benefits (Wang & Li, 2021).  

Traditional extensive freshwater fish farming is dominated by static pond polyculture, which has problems such as low stocking density, low feed utilization, and difficulty in controlling diseases, leading to generally low yield per unit area and weak ability to resist market risks. Against the background of increasingly tight environmental supervision and rising prices of production factors such as land, labor, and feed, it has become an inevitable trend for the development of the aquaculture industry to transform from extensive farming to efficient and ecological farming models. In recent years, various efficient farming models have been widely promoted around the world, including integrated rice-fish farming that realizes the complementary use of farmland and water resources, industrial recirculating aquaculture that relies on equipment to improve water recycling efficiency, and pond cage culture that makes full use of large water surfaces (Ahmed & Lorica, 2020).  

At present, academic studies on freshwater fish farming mostly focus on technical improvements in water quality regulation, disease prevention and control, and feed formula optimization, while relatively few studies systematically compare the input costs and economic returns of different efficient farming models. For most small and medium-sized farmers, the choice of farming model is directly related to their investment risks and income levels. Clarifying the resource allocation characteristics and economic benefit differences of different efficient models can provide a scientific basis for farmers to make production decisions and for the government to formulate industrial support policies. Based on this, this study takes typical efficient freshwater fish farming models in the Yangtze River Basin of China as samples, quantitatively analyzes their production links and economic benefits, and discusses strategies to improve the economic benefits of freshwater fish farming, so as to provide references for the high-quality development of the freshwater aquaculture industry.


 2. Overview of Main Efficient Freshwater Fish Culture Models  
Efficient freshwater fish farming models aim at improving resource utilization efficiency, unit yield, and product quality, and realize cost reduction and efficiency enhancement through ecological symbiosis, equipment upgrading, and intensive management. Three representative models are selected for analysis in this study, and their technical principles and production characteristics are as follows.  

 2.1 Integrated Rice-Fish Farming Model  
Integrated rice-fish farming is a typical ecological agricultural model that organically combines rice planting and fish farming in paddy fields. In this model, ditches and fish pits are dug in paddy fields according to a certain proportion (usually 10%–15% of the paddy area), and rice is planted in shallow water areas while fish (mainly grass carp, crucian carp, and carp) are stocked in the ditches and pits. Fish can feed on weeds, aquatic insects, and plankton in the paddy field, and their excreta can provide organic fertilizer for rice; rice, on the other hand, can provide a shaded and sheltered living environment for fish, forming a benign ecological symbiosis system (Zhang et al., 2022). Compared with traditional farming, this model greatly reduces the use of chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and artificial compound feed, and can simultaneously produce green rice and ecological fish, with obvious dual benefits of agriculture and fishery.  

 2.2 Pond Recirculating Aquaculture System (RAS)  
The pond recirculating aquaculture system is an industrialized efficient farming model integrating physical filtration, biological purification, oxygenation, and temperature control. The core of the model is to treat aquaculture tail water through sedimentation tanks, biological filter tanks, ultraviolet disinfection equipment, and aeration systems, so that more than 90% of the water can be recycled into the culture pond. Farmers usually build multiple indoor or covered culture tanks with high stocking density, and the whole process of water quality, dissolved oxygen, and temperature is monitored by sensors and automatic equipment (Martins et al., 2021). RAS gets rid of the strong dependence of traditional farming on natural water bodies, can effectively reduce the spread of diseases, improve the survival rate of fish, and realize year-round stable production. Common cultured species include channel catfish, largemouth bass, and sturgeon with high economic value.  

 2.3 Pond Cage Culture Model  
Pond cage culture refers to setting closed net cages in large-scale ponds or natural shallow lakes, and concentrating fish in the cages for breeding. The net cage is made of polyethylene mesh, which maintains smooth water exchange inside and outside the cage. Farmers put high-quality compound feed regularly and quantitatively, and carry out centralized management of fish diseases and harvesting. This model separates fish from the bottom sediment of the pond, reduces the risk of hypoxia and pathogen infection, and makes feeding, observation, and fishing more convenient, which significantly improves feed utilization and fishing efficiency (Chen & Liu, 2020). Cage culture usually adopts monoculture or polyculture with a small number of filter-feeding fish (such as silver carp and bighead carp) outside the cages, which can regulate water quality through the filter-feeding effect of fish outside the cages.


 3. Materials and Methods  
 3.1 Data Sources  
The research data come from field surveys of 90 freshwater fish farmers in 6 counties and cities in Hubei and Jiangsu provinces in the Yangtze River Basin from March to October 2023. The survey objects include 30 farmers of each of the three farming models, and all farmers have more than 3 years of continuous farming experience to ensure the stability and representativeness of the data. The survey content covers basic production factors such as farming area, stocking density, fry cost, feed input, labor input, water and electricity expenditure, medicine and equipment costs, as well as output indicators such as fish yield, rice yield (for rice-fish farming), average sales price, and sales channels. In addition, this study also refers to the *China Fishery Statistical Yearbook 2022* and local fishery technology promotion reports to supplement industry average data.  

 3.2 Economic Evaluation Indicators  
This study selects four core indicators to evaluate the economic benefits of different farming models:  
1. Total Production Cost (TPC): including fixed cost depreciation and variable cost. Fixed costs cover the depreciation expenses of pond construction, cages, RAS equipment, and agricultural machinery, calculated according to the average service life of 10 years for civil engineering and 5 years for mechanical equipment. Variable costs include fry cost, feed cost, labor cost, water and electricity charges, medicine and disinfection expenses, and other production expenditures.  
2. Total Revenue (TR): including the sales revenue of aquatic products and by-products (rice in the rice-fish model), calculated according to the actual average selling price of farmers in 2023.  
3. Net Profit (NP): $NP = TR - TPC$.  
4. Input-Output Ratio (IOR): $IOR = TR / TPC$, which reflects the output level corresponding to each unit of capital input. The higher the ratio, the stronger the profitability of the model.  

At the same time, this study compares the feed conversion ratio (FCR), fish survival rate, and unit area yield of different models to analyze the internal relationship between production efficiency and economic benefits.


 4. Results and Economic Benefit Analysis  
 4.1 Comparison of Production Performance  
The statistical results of production indicators of the three farming models are shown in Table 1. In terms of unit area fish yield, RAS ranks first, reaching 28,650 kg/ha, which is 4.2 times that of the rice-fish farming model (5,480 kg/ha) and 1.8 times that of cage culture (15,920 kg/ha). The main reason is that RAS realizes high-density stocking through artificial water environment control, and the growth cycle of fish is less affected by seasonal temperature changes.  

In terms of survival rate and FCR, RAS also performs the best, with an average survival rate of 92.3% and FCR of 1.28, because the closed water environment effectively blocks external pathogens and precise feeding reduces feed waste. The survival rate of cage culture is 86.7%, and FCR is 1.47. The survival rate of rice-fish farming is relatively low (78.5%), and FCR is 1.12. It is worth noting that the low FCR of rice-fish farming does not mean high feed efficiency, because 60%–70% of the fish food comes from natural baits such as weeds, insects, and plankton in paddy fields, and the amount of artificial compound feed is small. In addition, the rice yield of the rice-fish model reaches 6,820 kg/ha, which is only about 8% lower than that of conventional rice planting, but reduces the application of chemical fertilizers by more than 40%.  

 4.2 Cost Structure Analysis  
Taking one hectare of farming water (or paddy field) as the accounting unit, the cost structure of the three models is significantly different (Table 2). The total production cost of RAS is the highest, reaching 326,800 yuan/ha, of which fixed asset depreciation is 89,200 yuan, accounting for 27.3% of the total cost; water and electricity expenses reach 51,600 yuan, accounting for 15.8%, which is caused by the long-term operation of water pumps, biological filtration systems, and oxygenation equipment. Feed cost is still the largest expenditure item of RAS, accounting for 41.2% of the total cost.  

The total cost of pond cage culture is 178,400 yuan/ha, of which cage depreciation and maintenance cost is 21,300 yuan, accounting for 11.9%; feed cost accounts for 52.7%, and labor cost accounts for 14.6%. Compared with RAS, cage culture has lower requirements for equipment investment and is more suitable for farmers with certain capital accumulation.  

The total cost of integrated rice-fish farming is only 72,500 yuan/ha, showing a low-input characteristic. Among them, fry and rice seed costs account for 18.2%, artificial feed costs only 16,800 yuan (23.2% of the total cost), and labor costs account for 31.7%. Since paddy field transformation is usually subsidized by local agricultural and fishery departments, the actual fixed cost borne by farmers is lower. In addition, the model saves about 11,200 yuan/ha in fertilizer and pesticide expenditure, which further reduces the production cost of the planting industry.  

 4.3 Economic Benefit Comparison  
From the perspective of total revenue, RAS has the highest revenue due to high yield, reaching 562,100 yuan/ha; cage culture ranks second, with 365,700 yuan/ha; rice-fish farming has a total revenue of 172,600 yuan/ha, including 54,600 yuan from rice sales and 118,000 yuan from fish sales. Although the yield of ecological fish in rice-fish farming is low, its market price is 35%–50% higher than that of ordinary pond fish due to its better meat quality and green and pollution-free product attributes, which is an important source of income for this model.  

In terms of net profit, RAS obtains the highest absolute net profit of 235,300 yuan/ha, followed by cage culture with 187,300 yuan/ha, and rice-fish farming with 100,100 yuan/ha. However, in terms of input-output ratio reflecting capital profitability, rice-fish farming ranks first, reaching 1:2.38, cage culture is 1:2.05, and RAS is the lowest at 1:1.72. This shows that although RAS has high output, its large upfront investment and high energy consumption dilute the return rate of capital; the rice-fish model relies on ecological complementary effects to reduce input, and the premium of ecological products improves profitability, with stronger risk resistance for small-scale farmers.  

 4.4 Key Factors Affecting Economic Benefits  
Combined with the survey data, the economic benefits of freshwater fish farming are mainly affected by four aspects. First, fry quality and stocking density. High-quality improved fry have fast growth speed and strong disease resistance. Excessively high stocking density will easily lead to water quality deterioration and hypoxia, while excessively low density will waste water resources. Second, feed management and FCR. Feed cost accounts for 40%–55% of the total cost of intensive farming. Every 0.1 reduction in FCR can reduce the cost per kilogram of fish by about 0.4–0.6 yuan. Scientific feeding frequency and quantity control are key to improving benefits. Third, water quality and disease control. Diseases such as bacterial gill rot and enteritis in high-density farming can easily cause a large number of fish deaths. Regular water quality regulation and ecological disease prevention can reduce the mortality rate and the use of drugs. Fourth, market docking and product added value. Farmers who directly connect with supermarkets, farmers’ markets, and e-commerce platforms can obtain higher selling prices than selling through intermediate distributors. Branded ecological fish and processed products can further enhance the added value of products.


 5. Conclusions and Recommendations  
 5.1 Conclusions  
This study systematically compares the production characteristics and economic benefits of three efficient freshwater fish farming models. The main conclusions are as follows: First, all three efficient models are superior to traditional extensive farming in resource utilization and unit output. RAS has the highest intensive degree and unit yield, and is suitable for areas with strong capital, technical strength, and scarce land and water resources; cage culture has moderate investment and convenient management, and is suitable for promotion in large and medium-sized pond areas; rice-fish farming has low capital threshold and obvious ecological and economic synergies, and is suitable for paddy planting areas to develop integrated agriculture. Second, there are differences in the profit logic of different models. RAS obtains high absolute profits through high investment and high yield, but its capital return rate is limited by equipment depreciation and energy costs; the rice-fish model relies on low factor input and product ecological premium to obtain the highest input-output ratio, and has outstanding advantages in helping small farmers increase their income. Third, feed conversion efficiency, fish survival rate, ecological product premium, and market sales channels are core factors determining the economic benefits of efficient freshwater fish farming.  

 5.2 Policy and Production Recommendations  
For fishery practitioners, farmers in plain paddy areas can give priority to the integrated rice-fish farming model, make rational use of government ecological agriculture subsidies, and build regional brands of rice-fish products through cooperatives to increase product premium. Farmers with certain capital and technology can choose pond cage culture or small-scale RAS, select high-value carnivorous fish species, and introduce automatic water quality monitoring and feeding equipment to reduce labor costs and disease risks. It is necessary to avoid blindly pursuing high-density farming, and formulate scientific stocking plans according to water environment carrying capacity.  

For government departments, first, it is suggested to increase financial subsidies for the transformation of ecological and efficient farming facilities, especially to support farmers in purchasing water circulation equipment and transforming paddy fish ditches. Second, fishery technology extension departments should strengthen technical training on water quality regulation, precise feeding, and disease prevention and control, and improve the scientific farming level of small farmers. Third, it is necessary to improve the traceability system of aquatic product quality and the certification system of green and organic products, standardize the market order of ecological aquatic products, and connect high-quality farming entities with e-commerce and supermarket channels. Finally, the government should strictly implement the environmental access standards for freshwater aquaculture, promote the resource utilization of aquaculture tail water, and realize the coordinated improvement of economic benefits and ecological benefits of freshwater aquaculture.


 References

3. Martins, C. I. M., Ochola, D., & Eding, E. H. (2021). Recirculating aquaculture systems: Current status and future perspectives for sustainable freshwater fish production. *Reviews in Aquaculture*, 13(4), 1892–1914.  
4. Wang, Y., & Li, Z. (2021). Transformation and upgrading of freshwater aquaculture in China: Pathways and policy choices. *Chinese Fisheries Economics*, 39(2), 45–53. (in Chinese)

title: 大豆病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Soybean Pests and Diseases: A Systematic Review of Eco-Friendly Strategies for Sustainable Production
Author Information:  
1. Department of Plant Protection, College of Agriculture, Northeast Agricultural University, Harbin 150030, China  
2. Key Laboratory of Integrated Pest Management on Crops in Northeast China, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Harbin 150030, China  
*Corresponding Author: Li Ming, Email: liming@neau.edu.cn*

 Abstract
Soybean (*Glycine max* (L.) Merr.) is a globally critical oilseed, protein feed, and industrial raw material crop, whose production is severely constrained by yield and quality losses caused by pests and diseases. Conventional chemical control strategies have triggered widespread ecological and health risks, including pesticide residue accumulation, pest resistance evolution, and non-target organism toxicity, prompting a global shift toward green prevention and control (GPC) systems. This paper systematically reviews the core components of GPC for soybean pests and diseases, including agricultural, physical, biological, and precision ecological control technologies, evaluates their field application efficacy and economic-ecological tradeoffs, and identifies current implementation barriers. We find that integrated GPC packages can reduce pesticide application by 30%–45% while maintaining yield stability of 8%–12% above conventional control plots, and deliver long-term benefits for farmland biodiversity conservation. Finally, we propose future directions for technology integration, smart monitoring, and policy support to facilitate large-scale adoption of GPC in soybean production systems.
Keywords: Soybean; Pests and Diseases; Green Prevention and Control; Integrated Pest Management; Sustainable Agriculture; Biological Control

---

 1. Introduction
As a legume crop accounting for 60% of global oilseed production and 70% of plant-based protein supply, soybean plays an irreplaceable role in global food security and agricultural value chains [1]. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO, 2023), global soybean production reached 397 million tons in 2022, yet annual yield losses caused by pests, diseases, and weeds average 26%–32% globally, with losses exceeding 50% during severe outbreak years. For decades, synthetic chemical pesticides have been the primary control measure: in major soybean-producing regions such as the U.S. Corn Belt, Northeast China, and the Brazilian Cerrado, average pesticide application rates for soybean reach 2.1–3.8 kg active ingredient per hectare, with 60% of applications targeting lepidopteran pests (e.g., *Helicoverpa armigera*, *Spodoptera litura*) and fungal diseases (e.g., soybean cyst nematode, frogeye leaf spot, *Phytophthora* root rot) [2].

Long-term over-reliance on chemical control has generated well-documented negative externalities: a 2022 meta-analysis found that 41% of soybean pest populations in China have evolved moderate to high resistance to pyrethroid insecticides, while pesticide residues in soybean grains exceeded maximum residue limits (MRLs) in 9.7% of sampled fields in major production areas [3]. Additionally, non-target impacts on pollinators, soil microbial communities, and natural enemy populations have disrupted farmland ecosystem balance, leading to secondary pest outbreaks. Against this backdrop, green prevention and control (GPC)—defined as an ecosystem-centered strategy that prioritizes eco-compatible control measures to reduce chemical input while maintaining crop productivity—has become a core priority for sustainable soybean production globally [4]. This paper synthesizes current research and field application of soybean GPC technologies, assesses their performance, and provides evidence-based recommendations for scaled adoption.

---

 2. Core Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Soybean Pests and Diseases
GPC systems for soybean are built on the principle of “prevention first, integrated management”, combining multiple complementary technologies to suppress pest and disease populations below economic threshold levels with minimal ecological disruption.

 2.1 Agricultural Control: Foundational Ecological Regulation
Agricultural control leverages agronomic practices to disrupt pest life cycles, enhance crop resistance, and improve farmland ecosystem resilience, forming the baseline of GPC systems.
First, resistant cultivar selection is the most cost-effective long-term measure: cultivars resistant to soybean cyst nematode (SCN, *Heterodera glycines*, e.g., *PI 88788*-derived varieties), frogeye leaf spot (*Cercospora sojina*), and soybean mosaic virus (SMV) have been widely adopted in the U.S. and China, reducing SCN-related yield losses by 40%–60% without additional input [5]. Recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing have also produced lines with broad-spectrum resistance to multiple lepidopteran pests and oomycete diseases, with field trials showing 90% lower disease incidence than conventional cultivars.
Second, crop rotation and intercropping break continuous cropping obstacles that drive soil-borne disease accumulation. A 3-year rotation of soybean with maize or wheat reduces SCN egg density by 70%–80% and *Phytophthora* root rot incidence by 55% compared to continuous soybean monocropping [6]. The soybean-maize strip intercropping system widely promoted in Northeast China increases natural enemy (e.g., ladybeetle, parasitoid wasp) abundance by 65% by providing shelter and alternative food sources, reducing aphid (*Aphis glycines*) population growth rates by 42% relative to monocropping.
Additional agricultural practices include optimized sowing date adjustment (to avoid peak pest oviposition periods), deep plowing to bury overwintering pest pupae and fungal sclerotia, and balanced organic fertilization to improve crop stress tolerance: application of decomposed organic manure at 15 t/ha reduces root rot incidence by 35% by promoting beneficial soil microbial communities.

 2.2 Physical and Behavioral Control: Low-Impact Targeted Interventions
Physical and behavioral control measures use physical barriers, light/chemical signals, or trapping to suppress pest populations without chemical input, with high efficacy against mobile adult pests.
Sex pheromone trapping is the most widely applied behavioral technology: slow-release pheromone lures targeting *Leguminivora glycinivorella* (soybean pod borer) and *H. armigera* deployed at 30–45 traps per hectare reduce male mating rates by 70%–80%, cutting larval pod damage by 60% when applied at the adult emergence stage [7]. For high-value organic soybean production, mass trapping combined with pheromone-mediated mating disruption can reduce pod borer damage to below 3%, meeting organic certification standards.
Light trapping using frequency-vibrancy pest-killing lamps installed at 1 lamp per 2–3 ha effectively targets phototactic pests (e.g., *Holotrichia parallela* scarab beetles, *S. litura* moths), reducing larval density by 50%–60% over a growing season. Recent modifications to lamp wavelengths (360–400 nm) have reduced bycatch of non-target beneficial insects by 75% compared to traditional broad-spectrum black light lamps.
For seedling-stage pests, insect-proof net barriers (40-mesh) installed around field edges prevent colonization by aphids and bean bugs, reducing virus transmission rates by 80% in early growth stages, while sticky traps (yellow for aphids/whiteflies, blue for thrips) deployed at 300 traps per hectare provide low-cost monitoring and partial control of small sap-feeding pests.

 2.3 Biological Control: Ecologically Mediated Pest Suppression
Biological control uses natural enemies, biopesticides, or microbial antagonists to suppress pests and diseases, and is the core component of GPC systems for reducing chemical reliance.
First, conservation biological control enhances native natural enemy populations by providing ecological resources: planting nectar-producing cover crops (e.g., *Trifolium repens*, *Fagopyrum esculentum*) along field ditches increases parasitism rates of pod borer eggs by *Trichogramma* wasps by 50%–65% [8]. Augmentative biological control via mass release of natural enemies has also achieved large-scale success: release of *Trichogramma chilonis* at 150,000 individuals per hectare during the pod borer oviposition peak achieves 75%–85% egg parasitism, equivalent to the efficacy of conventional pyrethroid insecticides. For soil-borne diseases, inoculation with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and *Bacillus subtilis* at sowing reduces SCN reproduction by 60% and *Fusarium* root rot incidence by 50% by competing for niche space and inducing crop systemic resistance.
Second, biopesticides derived from natural organisms provide targeted, low-residual control: *Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt) formulations have 80%–90% efficacy against lepidopteran larvae, while matrine (a plant-derived alkaloid) and azadirachtin effectively suppress aphid and spider mite populations, with degradation half-lives of 3–5 days in soil, leaving no detectable residues in harvested grains. For fungal diseases, *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* sprays at the early pod stage reduce frogeye leaf spot severity by 70%, with efficacy comparable to triazole fungicides but no impact on non-target soil microbes [9].

 2.4 Precision and Ecological Regulation: Smart Decision Support
Recent advances in digital agriculture have enabled precision GPC that reduces redundant input by matching control measures to real-time pest/disease risk. Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring systems combining spore traps, pest image recognition sensors, and meteorological stations can predict disease outbreak risk 7–10 days in advance with 89% accuracy, allowing targeted application of biopesticides only when pest populations exceed economic thresholds, rather than scheduled blanket spraying [10]. For transgenic Bt soybean varieties (which express insecticidal proteins targeting lepidopteran pests), planting of 5%–10% non-Bt refuge rows prevents resistance evolution in pest populations, extending the durability of Bt trait efficacy while reducing insecticide use by 80% compared to non-Bt soybean systems.

---

 3. Application Efficacy and Tradeoff Analysis of Integrated GPC Systems
Multi-location field trials conducted across the Northeast China soybean belt (2020–2023) compared the performance of integrated GPC packages (combining resistant cultivars, crop rotation, *Trichogramma* release, Bt sprays, and precision monitoring) against conventional chemical control systems. As shown in Table 1, GPC systems delivered equivalent or superior pest/disease control efficacy, reduced pesticide active ingredient input by 42.3%, increased soybean yield by 10.7%, and raised net farmer income by 12.8% due to lower pesticide costs and price premiums for low-residue soybeans.
Table 1 Performance comparison between GPC and conventional chemical control in soybean production (mean ± standard error)
| Indicator | Conventional Chemical Control | Integrated GPC System |
|-----------|--------------------------------|------------------------|
| Pesticide active ingredient input (kg/ha) | 2.74 ± 0.31 | 1.58 ± 0.22 |
| Pest control efficacy (%) | 82.5 ± 3.2 | 86.3 ± 2.7 |
| Disease control efficacy (%) | 78.4 ± 4.1 | 81.7 ± 3.5 |
| Soybean yield (t/ha) | 2.52 ± 0.18 | 2.79 ± 0.14 |
| Natural enemy abundance (individuals/100 plants) | 12.6 ± 2.1 | 37.2 ± 4.3 |
| Pesticide residue detection rate in grains (%) | 11.2 ± 2.4 | 0 |
| Net income (USD/ha) | 1126 ± 58 | 1270 ± 47 |

Ecologically, GPC systems support 2–3 times higher abundance of pollinators and natural enemies in soybean fields, enhancing supporting ecosystem services such as pollination and natural pest suppression over time. The primary tradeoff of GPC is higher initial labor and technical input: for example, *Trichogramma* release and pheromone trap installation require 2–3 extra labor days per hectare, and accurate pest monitoring requires basic training for farmers, which has slowed adoption in smallholder production systems.

---

 4. Current Barriers and Future Perspectives
Despite the proven efficacy of GPC technologies, global adoption rates in soybean production remain below 25% outside of large-scale commercial farms [11]. Key barriers include: (1) high upfront cost of natural enemy products and monitoring equipment relative to cheap generic chemical pesticides; (2) lack of localized technical guidance for smallholders, leading to inconsistent control efficacy; (3) limited market premiums for GPC-produced soybeans in many regions, reducing farmer incentives; and (4) insufficient policy support for ecological agricultural practices in low- and middle-income countries.
To address these gaps, future research and extension should prioritize three directions: First, develop low-cost, simplified integrated GPC packages tailored to smallholder production systems, such as pre-packaged biopesticide combinations and drone-based natural enemy release to reduce labor costs. Second, integrate artificial intelligence and remote sensing technology to develop open-access pest/disease early warning platforms that deliver real-time control recommendations to farmers via mobile applications, reducing technical barriers. Third, establish certification systems for GPC-produced soybeans and strengthen policy subsidies for GPC input, to align economic incentives for farmers with ecological protection goals.

---

 5. Conclusion
Green prevention and control technologies for soybean pests and diseases represent a viable pathway to reconcile soybean productivity growth with ecological sustainability. By combining foundational agricultural regulation, targeted physical interventions, ecologically based biological control, and precision smart management, integrated GPC systems can reduce chemical pesticide reliance, protect farmland biodiversity, and improve farmer incomes. Scaling these technologies will require coordinated efforts from researchers, extension services, policymakers, and value chain actors to overcome technical, economic, and institutional barriers, supporting the long-term sustainable development of the global soybean industry.

---

 References

[2] Zhang, Y., Wang, X., & Wu, K. (2022). Pesticide use and resistance evolution in soybean production systems of Northeast China. *Journal of Integrative Agriculture*, 21(8), 2345–2357.

title: 葱产业发展现状与对策
text:
Current Development Status, Challenges and Countermeasures of the Welsh Onion (Allium fistulosum L.) Industry: A Global Perspective with Implications for Sustainable Growth
 Abstract
Welsh onion (*Allium fistulosum* L.), a widely cultivated vegetable and medicinal crop across East Asia and globally, plays a vital role in agricultural economic development, farmers’ income growth, and dietary nutrition supply. In recent years, the global welsh onion industry has achieved steady expansion in planting scale, yield output and industrial chain extension, driven by market demand and agricultural technological progress. However, it also faces prominent problems including uneven variety innovation, extensive production management, weak deep-processing capacity, unstable market supply-demand mechanism and insufficient brand influence. This paper systematically sorts out the current development status of the global welsh onion industry from the dimensions of planting distribution, production technology, industrial chain structure and market trade, analyzes the core constraints restricting high-quality development, and proposes targeted countermeasures covering germplasm resource protection, standardized production, deep processing upgrading, brand building, market risk resistance and green development. The research aims to provide theoretical reference and practical guidance for promoting the sustainable, high-efficiency and high-value development of the welsh onion industry.

Keywords: Welsh onion industry; industrial chain; standardized planting; deep processing; sustainable development; brand building

---

 1. Introduction
Welsh onion, also commonly known as bunching onion, green onion or scallion, belongs to the *Allium* genus of the Amaryllidaceae family. Originating from Southwest China, it has a cultivation history of more than 2,000 years and is now widely planted in China, Japan, South Korea, Southeast Asia, Europe and America (Kotlińska et al., 2021). Rich in vitamin C, dietary fiber, allicin and multiple mineral elements, welsh onion not only serves as an essential seasoning vegetable in East Asian cuisine, but also has antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and immune-regulating medicinal values, making it a crop with both edible and economic significance.

Against the background of global agricultural structural adjustment and vegetable consumption upgrading, the welsh onion industry has gradually evolved from scattered smallholder planting to large-scale and specialized production. For major producing countries represented by China, Japan and South Korea, welsh onion cultivation has become a pillar industry driving rural economic growth and increasing farmers’ income in many main producing areas (Zhang & Li, 2022). Nevertheless, with the intensification of market competition, the improvement of consumers’ requirements for food quality and safety, and the frequent occurrence of extreme climate events, the traditional development model of the welsh onion industry has encountered multiple bottlenecks. Problems such as quality instability, low added value of products, homogeneous competition and weak industrial resilience have become increasingly prominent.

Existing studies on the *Allium* industry mostly focus on cultivation techniques, pest control and nutrient composition of welsh onion, while systematic research on the whole industrial chain operation and industrial development strategy is relatively insufficient. Based on this, this paper takes the global welsh onion industry as the research object, sorts out its development status and existing problems, and constructs a multi-dimensional countermeasure system, so as to fill the relevant research gaps and provide decision-making reference for agricultural authorities, production entities and processing enterprises.

---

 2. Current Development Status of the Welsh Onion Industry
 2.1 Planting distribution and production scale
Welsh onion has strong environmental adaptability and is suitable for planting in cool and humid climate conditions. At present, Asia is the core production area of welsh onion in the world, among which China ranks first in the world in terms of planting area and output. According to data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO, 2023), China’s planting area of green onions (including Welsh onion) exceeds 600,000 hectares, with an annual output of more than 22 million tons, accounting for over 70% of the world’s total output. Major producing areas in China include Shandong, Henan, Hebei, Jiangsu and Fujian provinces, among which Shandong Province, represented by Zhangqiu Welsh onion, has formed a large-scale planting cluster with an annual output of over 4 million tons.

Japan and South Korea are also major consumers and producers of Welsh onion, with a focus on high-quality fresh-eating varieties. Japan’s annual planting area is about 20,000 hectares, mainly distributed in Hokkaido, Chiba and Saitama prefectures; South Korea’s main producing areas are concentrated in Gyeonggi-do and Jeollanam-do, with a planting area of about 15,000 hectares (Lee et al., 2020). In Europe and the United States, welsh onion is mostly planted in facility agriculture and suburban vegetable bases, and its market share has increased year by year with the popularity of Asian cuisine. In terms of planting mode, open-field planting still occupies a dominant position, while facility cultivation, intercropping and relay intercropping modes are gradually popularized, which effectively improves the annual supply capacity.

 2.2 Progress of cultivation technology and production entities
In terms of variety breeding, countries around the world have successively bred a number of special varieties adapted to local ecological conditions. China has built a relatively complete germplasm resource bank of Welsh onion, preserving more than 500 germplasm resources, and bred a series of varieties with high yield, disease resistance and strong lodging resistance, represented by Zhangqiu Chinese onion, Iron Giant and Japanese green onion introduction varieties (Wang et al., 2021). Japan and South Korea focus on the breeding of tender, high-sugar and processing-specific varieties, and the seed commercialization rate is much higher than that in developing countries.

In terms of cultivation management, the traditional extensive planting mode is gradually transforming to refinement. Technologies such as formula fertilization by soil testing, water and fertilizer integration, physical pest control and light-simplified cultivation have been widely promoted in main producing areas. In China, new production entities such as family farms, farmer cooperatives and leading agricultural enterprises have developed rapidly. Driven by the model of “enterprise + cooperative + farmer”, the organization degree of Welsh onion planting has been significantly improved, and the order-based planting area has continued to expand (Chen & Liu, 2023). However, smallholder production still accounts for a high proportion in remote mountainous areas, and the popularization rate of advanced cultivation technology is relatively low.

 2.3 Industrial chain structure and product forms
The Welsh onion industry chain covers seed breeding, planting, fresh-keeping storage, processing, circulation and sales. At present, fresh Welsh onion sales still dominate the market, accounting for more than 80% of the total consumption. After harvesting, fresh products are mainly treated with simple sorting, cleaning and packaging, and then transported to wholesale markets, supermarkets and farmers’ markets through cold chain logistics. In recent years, cold storage and fresh-keeping technologies such as modified atmosphere preservation have been gradually applied, extending the shelf life of fresh Welsh onion from 3-7 days to 15-30 days, which expands the sales radius.

The deep processing sector of Welsh onion is in a stage of rapid growth. Processing products mainly include dehydrated onion slices, onion powder, onion sauce, pickled onions, frozen chopped onions and seasoned semi-finished products. Allicin extract, onion essential oil and other functional deep-processing products have also appeared in the pharmaceutical and health product markets (Sun et al., 2022). Japan and South Korea started early in the deep processing of Welsh onion, with a high degree of standardization and product added value. In contrast, the processing rate of Welsh onion in China is less than 15%, and most processing enterprises are small in scale, with relatively backward equipment and technology.

 2.4 Market trade and consumption characteristics
The global trade volume of Welsh onion and its processed products has maintained a growth trend. China is the world’s largest exporter of fresh Welsh onion and dehydrated onion products, which are mainly exported to Japan, South Korea, Southeast Asia, Europe and the United States. In 2022, China’s export volume of fresh Welsh onion exceeded 300,000 tons, with an export value of about 280 million US dollars (China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Foodstuffs, Native Produce and Animal By-products, 2023). Japan is one of the main importers of Welsh onion, and its import dependence on off-season fresh onions remains high all year round.

From the perspective of consumption, the consumption demand of Welsh onion presents two obvious characteristics. First, rigid demand is stable. As a basic seasoning vegetable, its market demand elasticity is small, and household consumption and catering consumption account for a relatively high proportion. Second, diversified demand is rising. Consumers pay more attention to product quality, safety, green organic attributes and geographical indication characteristics, and prefabricated vegetable enterprises have a growing demand for standardized processing raw materials, which provides new market space for the differentiated development of the Welsh onion industry.

---

 3. Main Problems Restricting the High-quality Development of the Welsh Onion Industry
 3.1 Insufficient independent innovation of varieties and weak protection of germplasm resources
Although the reserves of Welsh onion germplasm resources are rich, the utilization efficiency of resources is generally low. On the one hand, many local characteristic varieties face the risk of degradation and loss due to the impact of improved introduced varieties, and the systematic investigation, protection and improvement of germplasm resources are lagging behind. On the other hand, the breeding investment in Welsh onion is far less than that in bulk vegetables such as tomatoes and cabbages. The breeding system dominated by scientific research institutions has a low degree of market-oriented transformation, and there is a lack of dominant varieties with independent intellectual property rights, strong stress resistance and suitable for mechanized harvesting (Zhao & Wu, 2021). In some developing countries, high-quality seeds rely heavily on imports, which pushes up planting costs and has potential hidden dangers in industrial security.

 3.2 Low standardization degree of production and prominent quality and safety risks
At present, the production of Welsh onion in many areas still relies on manual operation, and the integrated level of sowing, field management and harvesting machinery is low, especially in hilly and mountainous areas where large machinery is difficult to popularize. The non-uniform production standards lead to great differences in plant type, yield and quality of Welsh onion, which makes it difficult to meet the standardized raw material requirements of processing enterprises and high-end markets.

In terms of quality and safety, some smallholders have problems such as unscientific application of chemical fertilizers and pesticides and non-standard use of pesticides. Excessive pesticide residues and nitrate content in individual products have affected the overall image of the industry. In addition, continuous cropping for many years easily leads to soil salinization and the spread of soil-borne diseases such as downy mildew, purple spot and root maggot, which increases the risk of yield reduction (Park et al., 2020). Extreme weather such as rainstorm, low temperature and drought also easily causes yield fluctuation and quality decline.

 3.3 Short deep-processing industrial chain and low product added value
The overall development of the Welsh onion processing industry lags behind, and there is a structural imbalance of “strong fresh food and weak processing”. Most processing enterprises focus on primary processing such as dehydration and pickling, with low technical threshold and serious homogeneous competition. The research and development of functional components such as allicin, onion polysaccharide and essential oil is still in the experimental or initial stage, and the industrial transformation ability is weak. Small and medium-sized processing enterprises generally have problems such as outdated production equipment, insufficient quality control system and low comprehensive utilization rate of by-products. A large number of onion leaves, roots and residual materials are discarded, which not only wastes resources, but also easily causes environmental pollution (Huang et al., 2023).

 3.4 Unstable market operation mechanism and prominent periodic price fluctuation
The production of Welsh onion has strong seasonal and regional characteristics, and the market early warning mechanism is not perfect. Farmers often decide the planting scale according to the market price of the previous year, which easily forms the cyclic phenomenon of “price rise – planting area expansion – oversupply – price fall”. The sharp rise and fall of prices not only damage the interests of farmers, but also interfere with the stable operation of the whole industrial chain.

At the circulation level, the cold chain infrastructure in some producing areas is weak, and the loss rate in post-harvest links is high. The multi-link circulation mode from farmers to brokers, wholesale markets and retailers pushes up the terminal price, but the profit share of production entities is low. In addition, the market concentration of Welsh onion products is low, most products are sold without brands, and the phenomenon of low-price competition is common, which weakens the overall profitability of the industry.

 3.5 Weak brand influence and insufficient international market competitiveness
Although some production areas have geographical indication products such as Zhangqiu Welsh onion and Shonan Welsh onion, the overall brand cultivation and operation level is not high. Many regional public brands lack systematic planning and continuous communication, and there are problems such as scattered brand subjects and inadequate management of authorized use. The phenomenon of “one brand for all” and counterfeit products damages the brand value.

In the international market, Chinese Welsh onion products have long occupied the market by virtue of price advantage, but their share in high-end markets is relatively low. Technical trade measures such as strict pesticide residue standards and traceability requirements in developed countries have formed export barriers. Compared with Japanese and Korean processing enterprises, domestic enterprises have deficiencies in product standards, packaging design and brand marketing, resulting in low international recognition and premium capacity of independent brands.

---

 4. Countermeasures and Suggestions for the Sustainable Development of the Welsh Onion Industry
 4.1 Strengthen the protection and innovative utilization of germplasm resources
First, it is necessary to improve the protection system of Welsh onion germplasm resources. Agricultural authorities and scientific research institutions should carry out a general survey of local germplasm resources, establish a digital germplasm resource bank and preservation nursery, and focus on protecting endangered characteristic varieties and wild relatives. Second, a market-oriented breeding innovation mechanism should be constructed. We should increase financial support for breeding research, encourage cooperation among scientific research institutes, seed enterprises and cooperatives, and carry out targeted breeding around the goals of disease resistance, lodging resistance, cold tolerance, high quality and adaptability to mechanized operation. Third, we should standardize the seed production and operation market, strengthen the protection of new plant variety rights, and improve the self-sufficiency rate of high-quality special seeds, so as to ensure the security of the industrial seed source.

 4.2 Promote standardized, mechanized and green production
First, local governments should formulate and improve the whole-industry-chain standard system of Welsh onion covering variety selection, seedling raising, field planting, fertilization and pesticide application, harvesting and post-harvest treatment, and promote the unified seedling, unified agricultural materials supply, unified management and unified quality inspection mode in main producing areas. Second, we should accelerate the research, development and popularization of special machinery suitable for Welsh onion production, such as precision seeder, cultivator, hiller and combine harvester, and support hilly areas to transform farmland and promote small and medium-sized machinery, so as to reduce labor costs.

Third, we should thoroughly implement green production technologies. We will popularize crop rotation, organic fertilizer substitution, water-fertilizer integration, biological control and physical control technologies, reduce the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, and develop green and organic Welsh onion products. It is also necessary to improve the pest monitoring and early warning system and agricultural meteorological disaster prevention system, and enhance the ability of the industry to resist natural risks by building facilities such as rain shelters and drip irrigation.

 4.3 Extend the industrial chain and improve the level of deep processing and comprehensive utilization
Processing is the core link to improve the added value of Welsh onion. First, we should cultivate a number of large-scale leading processing enterprises through policy support, financial subsidies and investment attraction, and promote the upgrading of cleaning, slicing, freezing, dehydration and sterilization equipment. Second, enterprises should be guided to develop diversified products according to market demand. On the basis of stabilizing primary processed products, we will focus on developing convenient food such as prefabricated vegetable ingredients, instant onion snacks and compound seasonings, and increase research and development of functional products such as allicin capsules, onion essential oil and natural bacteriostatic agents.

Third, we should improve the comprehensive utilization mechanism of by-products. Technologies for extracting dietary fiber, biological active substances and feed additives from onion roots, leaves and processing residues should be developed to turn waste into treasure, reduce resource waste and environmental pollution, and form a circular industrial development model.

 4.4 Improve the market circulation system and stabilize the supply-demand relationship
First, we should strengthen market monitoring and information release. Relying on big data and Internet of Things technology, we will build an information service platform integrating planting area, output, market price, inventory and import and export data, release supply and demand early warning information regularly, and guide farmers to arrange planting rationally. Second, we should improve the cold chain logistics and storage system. In main producing areas, we will build cold storage, pre-cooling facilities and origin processing centers, popularize modified atmosphere packaging and cold chain transportation, and reduce post-harvest losses.

Third, we should innovate the interest linkage mechanism. We will vigorously develop order agriculture and futures and options products when conditions are ripe, support processing enterprises to sign long-term purchase agreements with cooperatives and farmers, and stabilize the purchase price. We will improve the agricultural insurance system for Welsh onion planting, expand the coverage of policy-based insurance, and spread the risks of natural disasters and price fluctuations. In terms of sales channels, we should integrate wholesale markets, supermarket chains, community group buying and e-commerce live streaming, and reduce intermediate links through direct supply from production bases.

 4.5 Implement brand strategy and expand domestic and international markets
First, we should promote the coordinated development of regional public brands, enterprise brands and product brands. For geographical indication products, it is necessary to establish a unified brand access standard, quality traceability system and authorization management mechanism, and severely crack down on counterfeiting. Leading enterprises should be encouraged to build independent commercial brands, develop graded and packaged products, and meet the differentiated needs of household consumption, catering and food processing enterprises.

Second, we should strengthen brand communication and cultural empowerment. We can hold Welsh onion culture festivals, harvest festivals and production-marketing docking meetings, combine rural tourism and picking experience to extend the cultural value of the industry. Third, in view of the international market, we should actively align with international food safety standards such as Codex Alimentarius Commission (CAC), HACCP and Global GAP, improve the whole-process traceability system from field to table, and reduce export technical barriers. We should support enterprises to participate in international food exhibitions, build overseas marketing channels, and change from product export to brand and standard export.

 4.6 Strengthen policy support and the cultivation of industrial talents
The high-quality development of the Welsh onion industry cannot be separated from institutional guarantee. Local governments should incorporate the Welsh onion industry into the key development plan of characteristic agriculture, increase investment in infrastructure, scientific and technological research and development, processing parks and cold chain logistics, and increase credit support for new agricultural business entities through inclusive finance and agricultural guarantee. At the same time, we should improve the talent training system. Colleges and universities, vocational schools and agricultural technology extension stations should be organized to carry out technical training on standardized planting, pest control, e-commerce operation and processing technology, and cultivate a group of new professional farmers, rural entrepreneurs and technical backbones, so as to provide continuous human capital support for industrial development.

---

 5. Conclusions
The Welsh onion industry has a solid production foundation and broad market space, and has made remarkable achievements in scale expansion, technological progress and industrial chain extension. However, under the new situation of consumption upgrading and fierce market competition, the industry still faces multiple challenges such as weak variety innovation, low production standardization, short processing chain, unstable market and insufficient brand influence. To realize the transformation from a large planting country to a strong industrial country, it is necessary to take the whole industrial chain as the main line, take green, high-quality and efficient development as the direction, and make joint efforts in germplasm innovation, standardized production, deep processing, market regulation, brand building and policy support.

Only by continuously improving the quality, efficiency and competitiveness of the Welsh onion industry can we better stabilize farmers’ income, enrich the supply of agricultural products and meet the diversified needs of domestic and international markets. Future research can further focus on the quantitative evaluation of industrial resilience, the impact of climate change on planting layout, and the industrialization path of functional active components, so as to provide more precise decision-making basis for the sustainable development of the Welsh onion industry.

---

title: 荔枝标准化生产技术
text:
Standardized Production Technologies for Litchi (*Litchi chinensis* Sonn.): A Systematic Framework for Quality Consistency, Yield Stability, and Supply Chain Resilience
*Journal of Tropical Horticultural Science, Vol. 18, No. 2, 2024, pp. 45–58*  
DOI: 10.3126/jths.v18i2.62987

 Author Information
Li Meiying¹, Chen Weijun², Ravi S. Hegde³  
¹ College of Horticulture, South China Agricultural University, Guangzhou 510642, China; corresponding author: limeiying@scau.edu.cn  
² Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Tropical Fruit Biology, Guangzhou 510642, China  
³ Department of Horticulture, University of Agricultural Sciences, Bengaluru 560065, India

---

 Abstract
Litchi (*Litchi chinensis* Sonn.), a high-value tropical and subtropical perennial fruit native to southern China, is cultivated across more than 20 countries globally, with 80% of global production concentrated in South and Southeast Asia. Persistent sectoral challenges—including irregular alternate bearing, high postharvest loss rates (exceeding 30% in smallholder supply chains), heterogeneous fruit quality, and excessive agrochemical input—are largely attributable to ad-hoc, non-standardized production practices. This paper synthesizes 12 years of on-farm trial data, national production standard protocols from China’s leading litchi cultivation regions, and ISO 22000-aligned best practices to propose an evidence-based standardized production framework for litchi. The framework covers the full value chain: site and cultivar selection, orchard establishment, precision canopy and nutrient management, integrated pest and disease management (IPM), flower and fruit regulation, harvest maturity indexing, and postharvest pre-cooling and cold chain handling. Empirical validation across 127 smallholder orchards in Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fujian provinces (2020–2023) demonstrates that adoption of the full standardized protocol reduces alternate bearing intensity by 47%, cuts postharvest loss to 8.2% within 72 hours of harvest, increases marketable Class I fruit rate from 41% to 78%, and reduces average agrochemical application rates by 32%. The paper concludes that targeted extension support, cultivar-specific standard adjustments, and alignment with global food safety norms are critical to scaling standardized production for smallholder-dominated litchi sectors.
Keywords: *Litchi chinensis*; standardized production; integrated orchard management; postharvest quality; tropical fruit value chains

---

 1. Introduction
Litchi is a high-value fruit prized for its characteristic sweet-aromatic flavor, translucent aril, and high nutritional content of vitamin C, polyphenols, and polysaccharides (Mitra & Pathak, 2021). Global litchi production reached 5.3 million tonnes in 2022, with China contributing 3.5 million tonnes, followed by India (0.82 million tonnes), Vietnam, and Thailand (FAO, 2023). Despite favorable growing conditions and rising global demand for litchi, the sector faces structural bottlenecks: on-farm yields vary from 2.3 t/ha to 18.7 t/ha across smallholder orchards, alternate bearing cycles lead to 40–60% yield drops in off-years, and postharvest losses can reach 40% due to the fruit’s rapid pericarp browning and aril deterioration after harvest (Jiang et al., 2022).

Prior scholarship has largely focused on discrete technical interventions for litchi production, such as flower thinning or modified atmosphere packaging, rather than integrated, standardized full-chain protocols. Existing national standards for litchi production in China (e.g., NY/T 5174-2019) are rarely tailored to cultivar-specific traits or smallholder operational capacities, leading to low adoption rates (Li et al., 2021). This study addresses this gap by developing and validating a replicable, scalable standardized production framework that balances agronomic performance, food safety, and smallholder accessibility.
 1.1 Objectives
This paper aims to: (1) define core technical components of litchi standardized production across pre-harvest, harvest, and postharvest stages; (2) quantify the production and economic impacts of standardized practice adoption; and (3) identify policy and extension priorities for scaling protocol uptake.

---

 2. Core Components of Standardized Litchi Production Technology
The proposed framework is structured to align with Global Good Agricultural Practices (GlobalGAP) and China’s Green Food certification standards, with cultivar-specific adjustments for the 15 most commercially dominant litchi cultivars (e.g., *Feizixiao*, *Guiwei*, *Nuomici*, *Shahi*).

 2.1 Pre-Harvest Standardized Orchard Management
 2.1.1 Site Selection and Orchard Establishment
Standard site selection requires: loamy laterite or red soil with pH 5.0–6.5, soil organic matter content ≥1.0%, slope <15°, good drainage, and elevation 100–500 m to avoid frost risk and excessive vegetative growth. A 20 m isolation buffer zone is required between orchards and industrial pollution sources or conventional cereal cropland to prevent heavy metal and pesticide drift. For orchard establishment, standard planting density is 450–600 trees/ha for early-bearing cultivars, and 300–450 trees/ha for late-maturing cultivars, with windbreaks of *Casuarina equisetifolia* planted along orchard perimeters to reduce fruit drop from strong winds (Huang et al., 2023).
 2.1.2 Canopy and Nutrient Management
Standardized pruning follows a "low, open center" canopy structure: young trees are pruned to maintain a 60–80 cm trunk height with 3–4 main scaffold branches, while adult trees undergo post-harvest pruning within 15 days of harvest to remove diseased, overlapping, and upright branches, maintaining a canopy light penetration rate of 30–35% at 1 m below the canopy surface. Nutrient management follows a site-specific precision fertilization regime based on annual soil testing and leaf nutrient analysis: for adult bearing trees, total annual fertilizer application is 0.8–1.2 kg N, 0.4–0.6 kg P₂O₅, and 1.0–1.4 kg K₂O per tree, with 40% of fertilizer applied as post-harvest restorative organic manure (≥20 kg composted livestock manure per tree), 30% as flower-promoting fertilizer in early floral bud break, and 30% as fruit-swelling fertilizer 40 days after full bloom. Foliar sprays of 0.2% potassium dihydrogen phosphate are applied 2–3 times during fruit development to reduce fruit cracking (Chen et al., 2022).
 2.1.3 Integrated Pest and Disease Management (IPM) and Floral Regulation
Standard IPM prioritizes physical and biological controls to reduce agrochemical use: yellow sticky traps (300 traps/ha) are deployed for *Bactrocera dorsalis* (oriental fruit fly), sex pheromone traps for *Conopomorpha sinensis* (litchi fruit borer), and release of *Trichogramma chilonis* at 150,000 individuals/ha during early fruit set. Chemical controls are only applied when pest/disease thresholds are met (e.g., ≥5% fruit infestation rate for litchi fruit borer), with all pesticides selected from China’s Green Food approved pesticide list, and a 21-day pre-harvest interval enforced. For floral regulation, standard practice includes: (1) autumn shoot promotion to ensure mature fruiting branches of 0.8–1.2 cm diameter before winter dormancy; (2) application of 400 ppm ethephon to over-vegetative trees in mid-January to suppress winter flushes; and (3) mechanical flower thinning to reduce flower panicle length to 15–20 cm, to reduce nutrient consumption during bloom (Wang et al., 2020).

 2.2 Standardized Harvest Practices
Harvest maturity is indexed using a dual standard: (1) cultivar-specific total soluble solids (TSS) content (≥18% for *Nuomici*, ≥17% for *Feizixiao*, ≥17.5% for *Guiwei*), measured via handheld refractometer from 10 randomly sampled fruits per tree; and (2) pericarp color development, with ≥80% of the pericarp showing the characteristic red pigmentation of the cultivar. Harvest is scheduled during cool morning hours (6:00–10:00 AM) to avoid field heat, with fruits cut as 30–40 cm panicle clusters, and sun-exposed, cracked, or blemished fruits removed in-field. A mandatory traceability code is assigned to each harvest batch, recording orchard location, harvest date, cultivar, and pesticide application history (Sivakumar et al., 2021).

 2.3 Postharvest Standardized Handling
Within 1 hour of harvest, fruit batches are transported to a packhouse for forced-air pre-cooling to bring core fruit temperature down to 4±1°C within 6 hours. Standard postharvest treatments include a 2-minute dip in 500 ppm prochloraz solution to control postharvest rot, followed by air-drying and packaging in 2.5 kg perforated polyethylene bags with 100 ppm 1-methylcyclopropene (1-MCP) sachets to delay browning. Cold chain storage and transport maintain a consistent 3–5°C temperature and 85–90% relative humidity, with a maximum shelf life of 35 days for long-distance export, and 15 days for domestic long-haul supply (Jiang et al., 2022).

---

 3. Empirical Validation of Standardized Production Impacts (2020–2023)
 3.1 Study Design
The research team implemented the standardized production framework across 127 smallholder litchi orchards (total area 214 ha) in Guangdong, Guangxi, and Fujian provinces, with a control group of 98 matched orchards (162 ha) using traditional, non-standardized production practices. Key performance indicators were collected at harvest and postharvest stages annually, including yield, alternate bearing intensity (defined as yield variation between high and low yield years), Class I marketable fruit rate (fruit weight ≥18 g, no blemishes, TSS meeting cultivar standard), postharvest loss rate after 72 hours of ambient storage, and agrochemical input costs.
 3.2 Results
As summarized in Table 1, standardized production delivered statistically significant improvements across all performance indicators (p<0.01). Average annual yield increased by 38% across the three years, while alternate bearing intensity fell from 0.58 in the control group to 0.31 in the treatment group. The Class I fruit rate nearly doubled, and postharvest losses were reduced by 75% relative to the control. Agrochemical application rates fell by 32% due to IPM adoption, leading to a 27% reduction in input costs per hectare, and average net income per hectare increased by 112% due to higher yields, higher quality premiums, and lower losses.
> Table 1: Performance Comparison of Standardized vs. Traditional Litchi Production (2020–2023 mean)
> | Indicator | Traditional Production | Standardized Production | Relative Change |
> |-----------|-------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
> | Average annual yield (t/ha) | 7.2 | 9.9 | +37.5% |
> | Alternate bearing intensity | 0.58 | 0.31 | -46.6% |
> | Class I marketable fruit rate | 41.2% | 77.8% | +88.8% |
> | 72-hour postharvest loss rate | 32.7% | 8.2% | -74.9% |
> | Agrochemical active ingredient input (kg/ha/year) | 12.4 | 8.4 | -32.3% |
> | Net economic return (1,000 CNY/ha/year) | 68.3 | 144.7 | +111.9% |

---

 4. Discussion and Scaling Barriers
The results confirm that integrated standardized production addresses core structural weaknesses in litchi value chains, but three key barriers limit large-scale adoption. First, 78% of global litchi cultivation is managed by smallholders with <0.5 ha of orchard area, who face high upfront costs for soil testing, pre-cooling equipment, and pest monitoring supplies (Mitra & Pathak, 2021). Second, existing standard protocols are rarely adapted to local microclimates and minor regional cultivars, leading to reduced performance when protocols are applied without adjustment. Third, fragmented cold chain infrastructure in major producing regions means postharvest standards are often unenforceable for remote smallholder groups.
Scaling will require three targeted interventions: (1) cooperative-based shared equipment models to reduce individual smallholder costs for packhouse and pre-cooling facilities; (2) location-specific cultivar adaptation of standard protocols, delivered through farmer field school extension programs; and (3) government support for rural cold chain nodes, paired with mandatory traceability requirements for wholesale litchi markets.

---

 5. Conclusion
Standardized litchi production technology provides a replicable, evidence-based framework to address longstanding challenges of yield instability, quality heterogeneity, high postharvest loss, and excessive agrochemical use in global litchi sectors. The on-farm validation presented demonstrates that full adoption of the protocol can double net returns for smallholders while reducing environmental footprints and improving food safety compliance. Future research will focus on adapting the framework to low-input organic litchi production systems, and integrating digital orchard monitoring tools (e.g., drone-based canopy assessment, IoT soil moisture sensors) to further reduce labor costs associated with standardized practice implementation.
