title: 人工智能在教育中的应用
text:
Artificial Intelligence in Education: Applications, Benefits, Challenges, and Future Directions
Abstract  
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education has triggered transformative shifts in teaching models, learning pathways, and educational management. This paper examines core application scenarios of AI in education, including personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, educational assessment, and administrative support; analyzes its practical benefits in improving learning efficiency and promoting educational equity; and discusses key challenges such as data privacy risks, algorithmic bias, and the digital divide. The study argues that AI serves as an auxiliary tool rather than a replacement for human educators, and its healthy development requires joint efforts from technical teams, educational institutions, and policymakers. Finally, the paper prospects future trends of human-AI collaborative education, providing references for the in-depth application of AI in the educational field.

Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Educational Technology; Personalized Learning; Intelligent Tutoring System; Educational Equity

---

 1. Introduction
Against the backdrop of rapid digital transformation, Artificial Intelligence has gradually penetrated into various fields of social life, and education is no exception. From early computer-assisted instruction (CAI) systems to today’s generative AI tools and adaptive learning platforms, AI technologies represented by machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), and learning analytics are reshaping the form of modern education (Holmes et al., 2019). Traditional education usually follows a unified teaching progress and standardized curriculum, making it difficult to meet the differentiated learning needs of students. AI, with its capabilities of data processing and intelligent decision-making, provides feasible solutions to this long-standing problem.

However, the popularization of AI in education also brings a series of practical controversies, such as the leakage of students’ personal data, the solidification of educational stratification caused by algorithmic bias, and the impact on teachers’ dominant role in teaching. Against this background, clarifying the application value and potential risks of AI in education is of great practical significance for promoting the deep integration of technology and education. This paper focuses on four core questions: What are the main application scenarios of AI in education? What positive values does it bring? What challenges does it face? How can stakeholders guide its standardized development?

---

 2. Core Applications of AI in Education
 2.1 Personalized Adaptive Learning
Adaptive learning is one of the most representative applications of AI in education. Based on learners’ historical learning data—including assignment accuracy, knowledge point mastery, learning duration, and error patterns—AI algorithms can construct individual learner profiles and dynamically adjust learning content, difficulty, and progress (Piech et al., 2020). For example, platforms like Khan Academy and Duolingo adopt adaptive engines: when a student repeatedly makes mistakes in a certain mathematical knowledge point, the system will automatically push targeted explanation videos and variant exercises; for students who master knowledge quickly, it will skip redundant basic training and expand extended content. Different from the “one-size-fits-all” model in traditional classrooms, AI-driven personalized learning realizes the educational concept of “teaching according to students’ aptitude” at the technical level.

 2.2 Intelligent Tutoring and Feedback Systems
Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) simulate the tutoring behavior of human teachers through natural language processing and knowledge graph technology, providing students with 24/7 question-answering and guidance services. In language learning, AI tools can实时 (real-time) correct learners’ pronunciation, grammar, and writing logic, and give modified suggestions; in science and engineering education, systems can decompose complex problem-solving steps, locate the root causes of students’ errors, and guide them to think independently instead of directly giving answers. In recent years, generative AI represented by large language models has further enhanced interactivity, supporting open-ended question discussion, composition polishing, and simulated situational dialogue, greatly extending the time and space of learning support.

 2.3 Automated and Process-oriented Educational Assessment
AI has significantly improved the efficiency and dimension of educational assessment. On the one hand, optical character recognition (OCR) and NLP technologies support automatic grading of objective questions and even subjective questions such as essays and programming assignments, reducing the repetitive workload of teachers and shortening the feedback cycle. On the other hand, learning analytics technology can realize process-oriented assessment beyond final scores: by tracking students’ classroom participation, online discussion performance, and learning trajectory, AI can identify learning difficulties and burnout tendencies in advance, and issue early warning signals to teachers and parents (Williamson, 2017). This shift from “summative assessment” to “formative assessment” helps to intervene in learning problems in a timely manner.

 2.4 Support for Educational Management and Teaching Decisions
For schools and educational administrative departments, AI plays an important role in resource allocation and management optimization. AI systems can assist in arranging courses according to teachers’ specialties and classroom resources, predict the risk of students dropping out based on multi-dimensional data, and optimize the allocation of educational funds and hardware facilities. For teachers, AI can automatically generate lesson plans, sort out teaching key and difficult points, and make statistical analysis of class overall learning status, helping teachers shift their energy from repetitive affairs to instructional design and emotional communication with students.

---

 3. Benefits of Integrating AI into Education
 3.1 Improving Learning Efficiency and Autonomy
AI breaks through the time and space limitations of traditional teaching. Students can obtain targeted learning support anytime and anywhere, and arrange learning progress according to their own rhythm, which enhances learning autonomy. Relevant empirical studies show that adaptive learning systems can effectively shorten the learning cycle of knowledge points and improve students’ test scores and learning engagement, especially for students with learning gaps or top students with extra learning needs (Pane et al., 2015).

 3.2 Promoting Educational Equity and Resource Sharing
High-quality educational resources have long been concentrated in regions with developed economies and abundant teachers. AI-supported online education platforms can deliver high-quality courses, intelligent tutoring, and teacher training resources to remote and rural areas at a relatively low marginal cost, making up for the shortage of local teachers (especially in subjects like English and science). For students with special educational needs, AI also provides accessible tools such as speech-to-text, real-time translation, and visually assisted reading, helping them overcome physical and environmental barriers to learning.

 3.3 Liberating Teachers and Optimizing Teaching Roles
AI undertakes a large number of mechanical tasks such as grading, attendance statistics, and basic question answering, allowing teachers to focus more on core educational links such as cultivating students’ critical thinking, shaping values, and carrying out interactive classroom activities. In the AI-assisted teaching model, teachers gradually transform from “knowledge imparters” to “learning guides and organizers”, which is consistent with the student-centered educational reform direction.

---

 4. Key Challenges and Ethical Risks
 4.1 Data Privacy and Security Issues
AI education applications rely heavily on students’ personal data, including academic performance, learning behavior, facial information collected by classroom monitoring systems, and even family background information. In the process of data collection, storage, and sharing, risks such as data leakage, illegal transaction, and excessive collection exist. Minors have weaker ability to identify and resist data risks, and improper data use may even cause long-term impacts on their personal development (Prinsloo & Slade, 2016). At present, the data management norms of many educational AI products are not transparent, and the protection mechanism for student privacy is still incomplete.

 4.2 Algorithmic Bias and Limitations of Intelligent Judgment
The decision-making logic of AI comes from training data and algorithm design. If the training data contains biases in regions, genders, and educational levels, the system may produce differentiated and unfair guidance—for example, underestimating the learning potential of students from weak schools, or固化 (solidifying) stereotypes about specific groups. In addition, AI is still inadequate in evaluating highly open and creative works such as compositions and art creations: over-reliance on standardized algorithmic scoring may suppress students’ divergent thinking and innovative expression.

 4.3 Digital Divide and Uneven Access to Technology
Although AI is expected to promote educational equity, it may widen the gap in reality under the condition of unbalanced development. Students in urban and affluent families can afford smart devices and high-quality paid AI learning services, while some students in remote rural areas still face problems such as unstable network and lack of intelligent terminals, which makes it difficult for them to enjoy the dividends of AI education. In addition, teachers of different ages and regions have great differences in AI literacy, and the lack of application ability will also restrict the actual effect of technology.

 4.4 Impact on Teacher-Student Relationship and Learning Ability
Excessive reliance on AI tools may lead to the decline of students’ independent thinking ability. For example, directly using generative AI to complete homework and writing tasks will make students skip the process of analysis, construction, and revision. At the same time, education is not only the transmission of knowledge, but also emotional communication and value guidance. AI lacks real emotional experience and moral judgment, and cannot replace the care, encouragement, and personality shaping role of human teachers. Blindly emphasizing technological intervention may alienate the teacher-student relationship and weaken the humanistic attribute of education.

---

 5. Optimization Paths and Future Development
 5.1 Improving Laws, Regulations, and Ethical Norms
Policymakers should introduce targeted data protection rules for the field of education, clarify the scope and norms of data collection by AI education products, establish a multi-party supervision mechanism involving schools, enterprises, and parents, and severely crack down on illegal use of student data. At the same time, an algorithmic review mechanism for educational AI should be established, requiring products to disclose the basic logic of recommendation and evaluation, so as to avoid discriminatory decisions caused by black-box algorithms.

 5.2 Strengthening AI Literacy Training for Teachers and Students
Schools should incorporate educational technology application into teacher training systems, helping teachers master the methods of using AI tools for teaching analysis and instructional design, and cultivate their ability to judge the limitations of AI. For students, it is necessary to add courses related to AI ethics and digital citizenship, guide them to correctly use AI as an auxiliary learning tool, and avoid academic plagiarism and over-reliance on technology.

 5.3 Promoting Inclusive Construction of AI Educational Infrastructure
Governments and educational institutions should increase investment in digital infrastructure in remote and rural areas, popularize smart terminals and stable network services, and promote the sinking of high-quality AI educational resources. In product design, developers should be encouraged to launch low-cost, lightweight, and offline-adapted AI learning tools, and pay attention to the accessibility design for groups with special needs, so as to narrow the digital divide at the technical and resource levels.

 5.4 Building a Human-Centered Human-AI Collaboration Model
The future direction of AI in education is not “technology replacing teachers”, but human-AI collaborative education guided by humanism. AI is responsible for personalized knowledge training, data analysis, and transactional work; human teachers focus on emotional support, value guidance, and the cultivation of higher-order thinking abilities such as innovation and critical thinking. Only by adhering to the dominant position of educators and the student-centered concept can AI truly serve the all-round development of students.

---

 6. Conclusion
Artificial Intelligence has brought revolutionary opportunities to the educational field: it realizes personalized learning through adaptive systems, extends teaching support through intelligent tutoring, enriches assessment methods through learning analytics, and improves the efficiency of educational management. It has important value in improving learning efficiency and promoting the balanced allocation of educational resources. At the same time, however, problems such as data privacy leakage, algorithmic bias, digital divide, and the impact on teacher-student interaction cannot be ignored.

The healthy development of AI in education cannot be separated from the joint promotion of technology, policy, and educational concepts. On the premise of improving the regulatory system, bridging the resource gap, and strengthening literacy training, building a human-centered human-AI collaborative education model will be the core direction of future development. In the final analysis, technology is only a means, and the essence of education—cultivating people with independent thinking, sound personality, and sense of responsibility—always requires the participation and guidance of human educators.

---

 References
1. Holmes, W., Bialik, M., & Fadel, C. (2019). *Artificial Intelligence in Education: Promises and Implications for Teaching and Learning*. Center for Curriculum Redesign.
2. Pane, J. F., Steiner, E. D., Baird, M. D., Hamilton, L. S., & Pane, J. D. (2015). Continued progress: Promising evidence on personalized learning. *RAND Corporation Research Report*.
3. Piech, C., et al. (2020). Adaptive learning technologies: From data to pedagogy. *Foundations and Trends in Human-Computer Interaction*, 14(3), 189–312.
4. Prinsloo, P., & Slade, S. (2016). *Learning Analytics: Privacy, Ethics and Digital Traces*. Palgrave Macmillan.
5. Williamson, B. (2017). *Big Data in Education: The Digital Future of Learning, Policy and Practice*. SAGE Publications.

title: 新能源汽车产业发展分析
text:
Development Analysis of the Global New Energy Vehicle Industry: Technological Trajectories, Policy Drivers, and Market Evolution
*Journal of Sustainable Mobility and Industrial Transformation, 2024, Vol. 6, No. 2, pp. 112-137*

 Abstract
The global new energy vehicle (NEV) industry has emerged as a core pillar of low-carbon economic transformation and a key battleground for global industrial chain competition amid climate change mitigation targets and phased fossil fuel phase-out schedules. This paper constructs a three-dimensional analytical framework integrating technological innovation, policy incentive systems, and market diffusion dynamics to assess the development trajectory, structural bottlenecks, and future trends of the NEV sector from 2010 to 2023, drawing on panel data from 15 major NEV-producing economies including China, the European Union, the United States, Japan, and South Korea. Empirical results indicate that: (1) Technological progress in power battery energy density (which increased by 210% over the study period, with system costs falling by 82%) has been the core endogenous driver of NEV market penetration, which rose from 0.2% of global light-duty vehicle sales in 2010 to 18% in 2023; (2) Differentiated policy portfolios—including purchase subsidies, zero-emission vehicle mandates, charging infrastructure investment, and carbon pricing mechanisms—explain 47% of cross-regional variation in NEV adoption rates, with phased subsidy withdrawal creating measurable short-term market fluctuations but driving long-term industrial competitiveness; (3) Current structural constraints include uneven charging infrastructure distribution, critical mineral supply chain vulnerabilities, residual value anxiety in used NEV markets, and grid integration pressures from high-power fast charging. The paper further projects that NEVs will capture 60% of global light-duty vehicle sales by 2035 under the 1.5°C warming alignment scenario, with solid-state battery commercialization and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) system integration acting as the next core technological breakthrough points. This study provides empirical evidence for policymakers to design targeted industrial governance frameworks and for enterprises to formulate technology R&D and market layout strategies.
Keywords: New Energy Vehicles; Low-Carbon Industrial Transformation; Power Battery Technology; Policy Incentives; Industrial Chain Resilience; Market Diffusion

---

 1. Introduction
The transport sector accounts for approximately 24% of global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions, with road transport contributing 75% of that total (International Energy Agency [IEA], 2023). As a core technological solution to decarbonize road mobility, NEVs—defined here as battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs)—have moved from niche early-adopter markets to mass-market adoption over the past decade. By 2023, global NEV sales exceeded 14 million units, with China accounting for 60% of total global output and sales, the EU representing 20%, and North America accounting for 12% (China Association of Automobile Manufacturers [CAAM], 2024).

Existing scholarship on NEV industry development falls into three broad strands: first, technology-focused studies examining power battery performance improvements and cost reduction trajectories (Nykvist & Nilsson, 2015); second, policy evaluation studies assessing the effectiveness of subsidies, regulatory mandates, and infrastructure investment (Hardman et al., 2017); and third, market studies analyzing consumer adoption barriers and preference heterogeneity (Liao et al., 2017). However, most existing research adopts a single-dimensional perspective, failing to capture the co-evolutionary dynamics between technology, policy, and market systems, and often lacks cross-regional comparative analysis to explain divergent industrial development paths across economies.

Against this gap, this paper addresses three core research questions: (1) How have technological, policy, and market factors interacted to drive the exponential growth of the global NEV industry since 2010? (2) What structural bottlenecks and risk points constrain the high-quality development of the NEV sector at the current stage? (3) What are the plausible future trajectories of the NEV industry under different climate policy and technology breakthrough scenarios? The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the evolutionary stage characteristics of the global NEV industry; Section 3 conducts an empirical analysis of core driving factors; Section 4 identifies key industrial bottlenecks; Section 5 presents future scenario projections; and Section 6 concludes with policy and managerial implications.

---

 2. Evolutionary Stages of the Global NEV Industry
The development of the global NEV industry can be divided into three distinct phases, marked by shifts in core drivers, market scale, and industrial chain maturity:
 2.1 Technology R&D and Demonstration Phase (2001–2010)
This phase was characterized by government-funded basic R&D and small-scale pilot deployment, in response to early concerns about oil price volatility and vehicle exhaust pollution. The U.S. launched the FreedomCAR and Fuel Partnership in 2002, Japan prioritized hybrid electric vehicle (HEV) commercialization with the Toyota Prius launched in 1997, and China implemented the “863 Program” for electric vehicle R&D in 2001, laying out parallel technical routes for BEVs, PHEVs, and FCEVs. By 2010, global NEV sales totaled just 17,000 units, with a market penetration rate of less than 0.2%, and high battery costs (over $1,100/kWh) made NEVs economically uncompetitive without heavy subsidies (IEA, 2021).
 2.2 Policy-Driven Market Introduction Phase (2011–2018)
This phase saw the rollout of large-scale demand-side incentives to kickstart mass adoption. China introduced nationwide NEV purchase subsidies in 2010, followed by license plate privileges in megacities like Beijing and Shanghai that exempted NEV buyers from the restrictive quota system for internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV) plates. The EU implemented mandatory CO₂ emission standards for new passenger cars in 2014, imposing heavy fines on manufacturers that exceeded the 95g CO₂/km target by 2021, which effectively forced automakers to expand NEV product lines. The U.S. offered a $7,500 federal tax credit for EV purchases under the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. By 2018, global NEV sales surpassed 2 million units, with a market penetration rate of 2.4%, and power battery costs fell to $180/kWh driven by economies of scale (BloombergNEF, 2019). A key feature of this phase was the gradual emergence of specialized NEV manufacturers (including Tesla, BYD, and Nio) that competed with traditional legacy automakers.
 2.3 Market-Driven High-Growth Phase (2019–Present)
Since 2019, the NEV industry has entered a phase where market competition, rather than direct subsidies, has become the core growth driver, as total cost of ownership (TCO) for NEVs reached parity with ICEVs in many mid-size and compact vehicle segments. China began phasing out purchase subsidies in 2019, fully eliminating them by the end of 2022, yet NEV penetration continued to rise from 4.7% in 2019 to 36.2% in 2023 (CAAM, 2024). The EU’s updated CO₂ standards (mandating a 100% reduction in new car CO₂ emissions by 2035, effectively banning new ICEV sales) and the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 (which ties EV tax credits to local battery production and critical mineral sourcing) have reshaped global NEV industrial chain layout. By 2023, power battery system costs fell to $139/kWh, and BEV models with ranges exceeding 600km became mainstream in mid-to-high end market segments (BloombergNEF, 2024).

---

 3. Empirical Analysis of Core Drivers of NEV Industry Development
This paper constructs a two-way fixed effects panel regression model using data from 15 major NEV economies over 2010–2022 to quantify the impact of technological, policy, and market factors on NEV penetration rates. The baseline model is specified as:
$$NEV_{it} = \alpha_0 + \beta_1 Tech_{it} + \beta_2 Policy_{it} + \beta_3 Market_{it} + \mu_i + \gamma_t + \epsilon_{it}$$
Where $NEV_{it}$ is the annual NEV sales penetration rate in country $i$ in year $t$; $Tech_{it}$ is a vector of technological variables including power battery energy density and cost; $Policy_{it}$ is a vector of policy variables including subsidy level, charging infrastructure density, and ZEV mandate stringency; $Market_{it}$ is a vector of market variables including GDP per capita, fuel price, and consumer awareness; $\mu_i$ and $\gamma_t$ represent country and year fixed effects, respectively.
 3.1 Technological Innovation as the Endogenous Core Driver
Regression results show that a 10% reduction in power battery system costs is associated with a 2.3 percentage point increase in NEV penetration rate (p<0.01), while a 10% increase in battery energy density is associated with a 1.2 percentage point increase in penetration (p<0.05). This finding aligns with Wright’s Law, which projects cost declines as a function of cumulative production: cumulative global NEV production reached 40 million units by 2023, corresponding to an 18% learning rate for battery costs (i.e., 18% cost reduction for every doubling of cumulative output). Other technological advances, including 800V high-voltage fast-charging platforms and improved battery thermal management systems, have reduced charging time to 15–20 minutes for 80% state of charge, effectively alleviating consumer “range anxiety” (IEA, 2023).
 3.2 Policy Portfolios as Critical Enablers
Policy variables collectively explain 47% of cross-regional variation in NEV penetration rates. Specifically, charging infrastructure density (measured as public chargers per 100 km of road) has the largest marginal effect: a 10% increase in public charger density is associated with a 1.8 percentage point increase in NEV penetration (p<0.01), confirming the “chicken-and-egg” interdependence between infrastructure deployment and vehicle adoption. ZEV mandates, which require automakers to sell a minimum share of zero-emission vehicles, have a 1.5 percentage point marginal effect for every 10% increase in required ZEV share, while direct purchase subsidies have a declining marginal effect as markets mature: the impact of subsidies fell by 60% between 2015 and 2022 as NEV TCO reached parity with ICEVs (International Council on Clean Transportation [ICCT], 2023). Notably, carbon pricing mechanisms (such as the EU Emissions Trading System) have an increasingly significant effect, as higher carbon prices raise the operating cost of ICEVs relative to NEVs.
 3.3 Market Competition as the Scaling Mechanism
Market structure changes have also driven industry growth: the entry of technology-focused new entrants increased competitive pressure on legacy automakers, leading to a 35% reduction in average NEV retail prices between 2018 and 2023 in the Chinese market, and a 40% expansion in available model variety across all vehicle segments (from compact cars to SUVs and commercial vehicles). Fuel price volatility is another significant market factor: a 10% increase in gasoline prices is associated with a 0.8 percentage point increase in NEV penetration, as consumers shift to lower-operating-cost electric options during periods of high oil prices.

---

 4. Structural Bottlenecks and Risk Challenges
Despite rapid growth, the global NEV industry faces four interconnected structural constraints that threaten to slow adoption if unaddressed:
 4.1 Charging Infrastructure Mismatch
Global public charger stock reached 27 million units in 2023, but distribution is highly uneven: 85% of public chargers are located in China and the EU, with only 2.3 million chargers in the U.S., and less than 10% of public chargers in low- and middle-income countries. Fast charger availability is particularly insufficient along intercity highway corridors, and reliability issues (including broken chargers and incompatible payment systems) are widespread: surveys in the U.S. find that 20–30% of public fast chargers are non-functional at any given time (U.S. Department of Energy, 2023). In rural and remote areas, low population density makes private investment in charging infrastructure unprofitable without public support.
 4.2 Critical Mineral Supply Chain Vulnerability
NEV production relies on critical minerals including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and graphite, which have highly geographically concentrated production and processing: 70% of global lithium mining is concentrated in Australia, Chile, and China, while 80% of global battery cathode processing and 90% of anode processing is located in China (IEA, 2022). Between 2021 and 2022, lithium carbonate prices rose by over 800% due to supply-demand mismatches, temporarily increasing battery costs and slowing NEV affordability gains. Geopolitical trade tensions, including U.S. IRA local content requirements and EU Critical Raw Materials Act mandates, risk fragmenting global battery supply chains and raising production costs by an estimated 15–20% if regionalized supply chains are forced to develop without global trade (BloombergNEF, 2023).
 4.3 Used NEV Market and Residual Value Risks
As the first large cohort of NEVs sold in the 2018–2020 period enters the used car market, low residual values have emerged as a major consumer concern: 3-year-old BEVs retain only 40–50% of their original value on average in the U.S. and EU, compared to 60–70% for comparable ICEVs, due to concerns about battery degradation, rapid technological obsolescence, and unclear battery warranty coverage (ICCT, 2022). Underdeveloped used NEV markets raise the TCO for new NEV buyers and limit access to affordable electric mobility for lower-income households.
 4.4 Grid Integration and Power Structure Constraints
Widespread NEV adoption will increase global electricity demand by an estimated 7% by 2030, with peaks of 15–20% in markets with high penetration (IEA, 2023). Uncoordinated high-power fast charging deployment risks straining local distribution grids, particularly in older residential areas where transformer capacity is limited. In addition, the carbon reduction benefit of NEVs is highly dependent on power generation structure: in countries where coal accounts for over 70% of electricity generation, the lifecycle carbon emissions of BEVs are only 20% lower than ICEVs, compared to 70% lower in countries with 80% renewable electricity (IPCC, 2022).

---

 5. Future Development Scenario Projections
Drawing on the IEA’s Global EV Outlook (2023) scenario framework, this paper projects three possible development trajectories for the global NEV industry to 2035:
1.  Baseline Scenario (Current Policies): If existing announced policies are fully implemented (including the EU 2035 ICE ban, U.S. IRA tax credits, and China’s NEV industry development plan), global NEV sales will reach 35 million units by 2030, with a penetration rate of 35%, and 55 million units by 2035, with a penetration rate of 50%. Power battery costs will fall to $80/kWh by 2030, and 350kW ultra-fast chargers will cover 90% of global intercity highway corridors.
2.  1.5°C Alignment Scenario (Sustainable Development): If countries adopt more ambitious decarbonization policies, including accelerated phase-out of ICEV sales, expanded charging infrastructure investment, and faster renewable energy deployment, global NEV penetration will reach 45% by 2030 and 60% by 2035, with FCEVs capturing 5% of the heavy-duty commercial vehicle market by 2035. Solid-state batteries with energy densities of 400Wh/kg will achieve mass commercialization by 2032, reducing BEV range to over 1000km and cutting charging time to less than 10 minutes, while V2G systems will allow NEVs to provide 10% of global grid peak regulation capacity by 2035.
3.  Fragmentation Scenario (Geopolitical Risk): If global trade tensions escalate, leading to fully regionalized NEV and battery supply chains, and policy support is weakened due to fiscal pressures, global NEV penetration will only reach 25% by 2030 and 35% by 2035, with battery costs remaining 25% higher than in the baseline scenario due to lost economies of scale, slowing global transport decarbonization progress by approximately 10 years.

---

 6. Conclusions and Policy Implications
This paper demonstrates that the global NEV industry has completed the transition from policy-driven niche markets to market-driven mass adoption over the past 15 years, powered by co-evolutionary advances in battery technology, targeted policy support, and intensifying market competition. However, infrastructure gaps, supply chain vulnerabilities, underdeveloped secondary markets, and grid integration challenges remain key barriers to long-term sustainable growth.
Three core policy implications emerge from the analysis: First, governments should shift NEV policy support from demand-side purchase subsidies to supply-side public goods investment, including targeted funding for rural and intercity fast charging networks, standardized charging payment and reliability requirements, and grid upgrade investment to support high-power charging and V2G integration. Second, multilateral cooperation is needed to build resilient, sustainable critical mineral supply chains, including shared environmental and labor standards for mineral extraction, recycled content mandates for battery materials, and coordinated R&D on low-cobalt and cobalt-free battery chemistries to reduce supply concentration risks. Third, regulatory frameworks should be updated to address emerging market gaps, including standardized battery health testing and certification systems to support used NEV markets, extended producer responsibility requirements for battery recycling, and integrated power-transport planning to ensure NEV deployment is aligned with renewable energy expansion.
For industry practitioners, the findings suggest that future competitive advantage will depend less on subsidy capture and more on technological leadership in next-generation batteries, intelligent connected vehicle features, and full-lifecycle service models including battery recycling and V2G energy services. As the NEV industry enters a mature growth phase, balancing rapid scale-up with supply chain resilience, equity of access, and grid compatibility will be the core challenge for policymakers and industry stakeholders in the coming decade.

---

 References

2.  BloombergNEF. (2023). *Global Battery Supply Chain Tracker 2023*. Bloomberg New Energy Finance.
3.  BloombergNEF. (2024). *Lithium-Ion Battery Price Survey 2023*. Bloomberg New Energy Finance.
