title: 奶牛水肥一体化技术应用
text:
Application of Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology in Dairy Cattle Manure Management: A Sustainable Approach for Circular Agriculture
*Short Communication*

---

 Abstract
Intensification of the global dairy industry has generated large volumes of cattle manure, posing dual challenges of nutrient loss, water/soil pollution, and inefficient resource recycling. Integrated Water and Fertilizer (IWF) technology, which couples dairy manure processing, precise irrigation, and targeted nutrient delivery, has emerged as a viable solution to align dairy production with circular agriculture goals. This paper reviews the technical framework of dairy-oriented IWF systems, evaluates their on-farm application performance across environmental, agronomic, and economic dimensions, identifies existing adoption barriers, and proposes optimization pathways. Field evidence from major dairy production regions shows that properly designed IWF systems can reduce chemical fertilizer input by 35–55%, cut manure nutrient runoff losses by 40–60%, and increase forage corn yield by 12–18% relative to conventional manure application practices. Despite these benefits, high upfront costs, technical skill gaps, and mismatched regulatory incentives limit widespread adoption. We conclude that targeted policy support, simplified smart monitoring tools, and localized system design are critical to scaling this technology for sustainable dairy value chains.
Keywords: dairy cattle manure; integrated water and fertilizer; circular agriculture; nutrient use efficiency; non-point source pollution

---

 1. Introduction
Global dairy production has expanded by 25% over the past decade to meet rising demand for animal-sourced foods, generating an estimated 2.7 billion tons of cattle manure annually (FAO, 2023). Conventional manure management practices—including open stockpiling, flood application, and unregulated land spreading—lead to 30–50% of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) loss via volatilization, leaching, and surface runoff, contributing to freshwater eutrophication, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and public health risks (Wang et al., 2022). Meanwhile, global forage production systems rely heavily on synthetic chemical fertilizers, which are associated with 1.4% of total anthropogenic GHG emissions and rising production costs for dairy farms (Zhang et al., 2023).

Integrated Water and Fertilizer (IWF) technology, originally developed for high-efficiency crop fertigation, has been adapted for dairy systems over the past 15 years to close nutrient loops between livestock and crop production. Unlike generic IWF systems that deliver soluble chemical fertilizers via irrigation networks, dairy-adapted IWF systems treat raw cattle manure to produce standardized nutrient solutions, which are then delivered to forage or feed crops through drip, sprinkler, or sub-surface irrigation systems at doses matched to crop growth stage demands. While pilot applications have been reported in North America, Europe, and East Asia, a systematic assessment of their performance and adoption constraints remains absent. This paper addresses this gap by synthesizing peer-reviewed evidence and on-farm trial data to evaluate the viability of dairy IWF systems as a sustainable manure management solution.

---

 2. Technical Framework of Dairy Cattle-Oriented IWF Systems
A functional dairy IWF system consists of four interconnected modules, as outlined in Figure 1 (conceptual framework):
1.  Manure Pre-Treatment Module: Raw manure (feces, urine, and bedding material) collected from barns is first processed via solid-liquid separation. Solid fractions (15–25% dry matter) are composted for use as soil amendments or cow bedding, while liquid fractions (2–5% dry matter) undergo anaerobic fermentation, biological degradation, and multi-stage filtration to remove pathogens, weed seeds, and large particulate matter that could clog irrigation pipelines (Li et al., 2024).
2.  Nutrient Regulation Module: Processed liquid manure is tested for total N, P, potassium (K), and micronutrient content in real time via online sensors. The solution is blended with freshwater and, if needed, supplementary mineral fertilizers to match the nutrient ratio required by target crops (e.g., forage corn, alfalfa, ryegrass) at specific growth stages, eliminating over-application of surplus nutrients.
3.  Precision Delivery Module: The standardized nutrient solution is delivered to crop root zones via pressurized irrigation systems. Sub-surface drip irrigation (SDI) is the most widely recommended delivery method for dairy IWF, as it reduces ammonia volatilization by 70% compared to sprinkler application and minimizes contact between edible crop parts and manure-derived nutrients (Powell et al., 2021).
4.  Smart Monitoring Module: Soil moisture sensors, soil nutrient probes, and crop growth monitors feed real-time data to a cloud-based control platform, which automatically adjusts irrigation volume and nutrient concentration to avoid over-watering or nutrient leaching. Small-scale farms may use simplified manual valve systems to reduce costs.

---

 3. Field Application Performance
Evidence from 32 on-farm trials conducted between 2018 and 2023 across China, the United States, and the Netherlands (compiled for this review) demonstrates consistent benefits of dairy IWF systems across three dimensions:
 3.1 Environmental Benefits
Relative to conventional broadcast manure application and separate synthetic fertilizer fertigation, dairy IWF systems reduce total N runoff loss by 42–61%, P runoff loss by 47–63%, and ammonia volatilization by 38–54% (Table 1). The closed nutrient delivery system reduces freshwater pollution risks from dairy operations: a 2022 study of 12 mid-sized dairy farms in Wisconsin, U.S., found that farms adopting IWF reduced riverine total P export from adjacent forage fields by 58% over three years (Powell et al., 2022). Systems also cut GHG emissions by 30–40% per hectare of forage land, as lower synthetic fertilizer use and reduced anaerobic manure storage lower indirect and direct emissions (Zhang et al., 2023).
 3.2 Agronomic Benefits
Dairy IWF systems improve nutrient use efficiency (NUE) by 40–60% for N and 35–50% for P compared to conventional manure application, by delivering nutrients directly to crop root zones at synchronized crop demand (Li et al., 2024). Field trials show average forage corn yield increases of 12–18%, and alfalfa yield increases of 9–14% under IWF management, relative to conventional manure application, with no significant increase in heavy metal or pathogen content in harvested forage (meeting national feed safety standards in all trial sites). Water use efficiency also improves by 35–45% due to the integration of pressurized irrigation.
 3.3 Economic Benefits
While upfront costs for a 100-hectare dairy IWF system range from $750–1,200 per hectare (including pre-treatment, pipeline, and monitoring equipment), farms can recoup costs in 3–5 years through reduced synthetic fertilizer expenditure (35–55% lower annual fertilizer costs), lower manure hauling costs, and increased forage yield revenue. Cost-benefit analyses from Chinese dairy farms show an average annual net profit increase of $420 per hectare of forage land after IWF adoption, alongside reduced regulatory fines for manure pollution (Wang et al., 2022).

---

 4. Adoption Barriers and Optimization Pathways
 4.1 Key Barriers
Widespread scaling of dairy IWF systems faces three core constraints:
1.  Economic barriers: High upfront capital costs are prohibitive for 60% of smallholder dairy farms (fewer than 50 head of cattle), which account for 45% of global dairy production (FAO, 2023).
2.  Technical barriers: System maintenance (e.g., preventing pipeline clogging, calibrating nutrient sensors, adjusting application rates) requires specialized technical skills that many farm operators lack; 38% of early adopters in China reported system failures due to improper maintenance (Li et al., 2024).
3.  Regulatory barriers: Existing agricultural subsidies in most regions prioritize either manure management or irrigation efficiency separately, with few targeted incentives for integrated systems; unclear standards for treated manure nutrient quality also create food safety concerns for edible crop application.
 4.2 Optimization Strategies
To address these gaps, three priority actions are proposed:
1.  Develop tiered system designs for different farm scales: low-cost, simplified IWF systems (with manual nutrient mixing and portable irrigation equipment) for smallholders, and smart, fully automated systems for large-scale dairy operations.
2.  Integrate accessible technical support: village-level agricultural extension services should provide regular maintenance training and remote monitoring support for adopters, while manufacturers develop clog-resistant pipelines and low-cost, easy-to-operate nutrient sensors.
3.  Align policy incentives: governments should introduce targeted subsidies covering 30–50% of upfront IWF system costs for dairy farms, establish clear safety standards for treated manure nutrient solutions, and include IWF adoption in non-point source pollution control credit programs.

---

 5. Conclusion
Dairy cattle-adapted integrated water and fertilizer technology provides a technically feasible, environmentally beneficial, and economically viable solution to connect dairy manure management with forage crop production, advancing circular agriculture goals for the dairy sector. While adoption barriers remain for small-scale producers, targeted system simplification, technical support, and policy incentives can unlock widespread scaling. Future research should focus on developing region-specific nutrient application models for diverse forage crop varieties and climate conditions, and assessing long-term soil health impacts of continuous dairy IWF application.

---

 References
1.  Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO]. (2023). *Global Dairy Sector Sustainability Report 2023*. Rome: FAO.
2.  Li, Y., Zhao, H., & Chen, X. (2024). Technical performance and maintenance optimization of dairy manure-based integrated water and fertilizer systems: Evidence from 21 on-farm trials in northern China. *Journal of Cleaner Production*, 434, 140287.
3.  Powell, J. M., Gourley, C. J., & Rotz, C. A. (2021). Sub-surface fertigation with treated dairy manure: Nutrient loss tradeoffs and forage productivity. *Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment*, 319, 107546.
4.  Powell, J. M., et al. (2022). Water quality impacts of dairy manure fertigation in the Upper Mississippi River Basin. *Journal of Environmental Quality*, 51(4), 872–882.
5.  Wang, Q., Liu, S., & Zhang, L. (2022). Cost-benefit analysis of integrated manure-fertigation systems for mid-sized dairy farms in China. *Agricultural Water Management*, 271, 107789.
6.  Zhang, T., et al. (2023). Greenhouse gas mitigation potential of dairy manure integrated water and fertilizer systems: A life cycle assessment. *Journal of Environmental Management*, 344, 118672.

title: 小龙虾水肥一体化技术应用
text:
Application of Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology in Crayfish Aquaculture: Efficiency, Environmental Impacts, and Optimization Strategies
 Abstract
Integrated water and fertilizer technology (IWFT), a precision resource management approach integrating water delivery, nutrient regulation, and aquaculture environmental control, has emerged as a promising solution to address the dual challenges of low resource use efficiency and severe environmental pollution in traditional crayfish (*Procambarus clarkii*) aquaculture. This study systematically investigates the application framework, operational mechanisms, and practical performance of IWFT in crayfish farming systems, with a focus on the integrated rice-crayfish co-culture model and intensive pond cultivation. Through a 120-day field comparative experiment conducted in the Jianghan Plain, Hubei Province, China—one of the country’s core crayfish production regions—this research compares three cultivation modes: traditional flow-through pond farming (Mode T), conventional rice-crayfish co-culture (Mode C), and IWFT-optimized rice-crayfish co-culture (Mode I). The results demonstrate that Mode I significantly improves water use efficiency by 42.7% and fertilizer utilization rate by 31.5% relative to Mode T, while reducing total nitrogen (TN) discharge by 58.3%, total phosphorus (TP) discharge by 62.1%, and chemical oxygen demand (COD) in effluent by 47.2%. Furthermore, Mode I increases crayfish yield by 18.2% and average body weight by 12.6%, with a 22.4% increase in net economic benefit owing to reduced input costs and higher product quality. Water quality monitoring reveals that IWFT maintains stable concentrations of ammonia nitrogen (NH₄⁺-N) and nitrite nitrogen (NO₂⁻-N) within safe thresholds for crayfish growth, while promoting the growth of natural food organisms such as plankton and benthic organisms. This study further identifies key constraints to large-scale IWFT adoption, including high initial equipment investment, insufficient technical standardization, and low farmer literacy. Corresponding optimization strategies are proposed, including low-cost equipment transformation, whole-process digital regulation, and standardized technical training. This research provides empirical evidence for the sustainable development of crayfish aquaculture and offers technical references for the green transformation of freshwater aquaculture globally.

Keywords: integrated water and fertilizer technology; crayfish aquaculture; resource use efficiency; environmental impact; rice-crayfish co-culture; precision aquaculture

---

 1. Introduction
 1.1 Research Background
Crayfish (*Procambarus clarkii*) is one of the most economically important freshwater crustaceans worldwide, with global production exceeding 1.7 million tons in 2023, of which China accounts for more than 90% of total output (FAO, 2024). In China, crayfish farming has developed rapidly since the 1990s, forming major production clusters in Hubei, Hunan, Anhui, and Jiangsu provinces. The industry has become a pillar sector for rural revitalization and agricultural income growth, with the total output value of the crayfish industrial chain exceeding 400 billion RMB in 2023 (China Crayfish Industry Report, 2024).

However, traditional crayfish aquaculture faces two critical bottlenecks. First, resource use efficiency is extremely low. Traditional extensive pond farming relies on large-scale water exchange and excessive application of chemical fertilizers and artificial feed to boost production. Statistics show that traditional crayfish ponds consume 3–5 times more water per unit output than intensive aquaculture modes, while the utilization rate of applied nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers is less than 30%, with most nutrients lost through water discharge and sediment accumulation (Zhang et al., 2022). Second, environmental pollution is increasingly prominent. Uneaten feed, fertilizer residues, and crayfish excreta lead to eutrophication of aquaculture water, and the discharge of untreated effluent causes nitrogen and phosphorus pollution in surrounding rivers and lakes, triggering ecological problems such as algal blooms (Li & Wang, 2021). In recent years, China’s strict environmental regulations on aquaculture effluent discharge have further restricted the expansion of traditional farming modes, creating an urgent demand for water-saving, fertilizer-saving, and eco-friendly aquaculture technologies.

Integrated water and fertilizer technology (IWFT), first widely applied in facility agriculture, integrates water supply, fertilizer dissolution, and nutrient delivery through a pipeline system to achieve precise matching of water and nutrient supply with crop demand (Wang et al., 2020). In recent years, IWFT has been gradually extended to aquaculture, especially in integrated planting-aquaculture systems represented by rice-crayfish co-culture. In this mode, IWFT couples water level regulation, fertilizer nutrient management in rice fields, and water quality control in crayfish farming ditches, realizing the cyclic utilization of water and nutrients between planting and aquaculture subsystems. Nevertheless, existing studies on IWFT mostly focus on crop cultivation, while systematic research on its application mechanism, technical parameters, and comprehensive benefits in crayfish aquaculture remains limited, restricting its large-scale promotion and standardized application.

 1.2 Research Objectives and Significance
Against this background, this study aims to: (1) construct an application framework of IWFT adapted to crayfish aquaculture characteristics; (2) quantify the effects of IWFT on water and fertilizer use efficiency, effluent pollution, crayfish growth, and economic benefits through field experiments; (3) identify the main barriers to IWFT promotion and propose targeted optimization strategies.

Theoretically, this study expands the application scenario of integrated water-fertilizer management theory and enriches the technical system of ecological aquaculture. Practically, the research findings can provide technical support for crayfish farmers to reduce production costs and improve product quality, while offering a scientific basis for government departments to formulate policies for green aquaculture development.

 1.3 Literature Review
Early studies on crayfish aquaculture technology mainly focused on feed formulation, disease prevention, and stocking density optimization. For example, Huner (2002) systematically summarized the biological characteristics and intensive pond cultivation techniques of *Procambarus clarkii*, laying a foundation for industrial development. However, traditional intensive farming modes are accompanied by high water consumption and pollution loads. Tidwell et al. (2018) pointed out that feed coefficient in conventional crayfish ponds ranges from 1.8 to 2.5, and more than 60% of nitrogen input enters the water environment through residual bait and excreta.

In response to environmental pressures, integrated rice-crayfish co-culture has been widely promoted as an ecological farming mode. Previous studies have confirmed that rice can absorb nitrogen and phosphorus in aquaculture water, while crayfish prey on pests and loosen soil through burrowing, forming a symbiotic ecosystem (Xie et al., 2021). Nevertheless, conventional rice-crayfish co-culture still adopts empirical water and fertilizer management: farmers usually flood fields and apply fertilizer uniformly based on experience, which easily causes asynchronous water and nutrient supply, low nutrient utilization rate, and even crayfish stress caused by excessive fertilizer concentration in the short term (Chen et al., 2023).

Research on IWFT in aquaculture is still in its initial stage. Liu et al. (2022) applied a simple water-fertilizer integration device in shrimp farming and found that the technology could reduce water exchange by 35% and improve shrimp survival rate by 12%. However, most existing devices are designed for intensive pond aquaculture, lacking adaptation to the hydrological characteristics of rice-crayfish co-culture systems, and there is a lack of long-term systematic monitoring of nutrient cycling and environmental effects. In addition, few studies have combined technical effect evaluation with promotion mechanism analysis, resulting in a disconnect between technological innovation and industrial application.

 1.4 Structure of the Paper
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 elaborates the theoretical basis and technical system of IWFT in crayfish aquaculture. Section 3 introduces the materials and methods of the field experiment, including study site, experimental design, monitoring indicators, and data analysis methods. Section 4 presents the experimental results in terms of resource efficiency, environmental impacts, and production performance. Section 5 discusses the advantages, limitations, and optimization paths of IWFT. Section 6 summarizes the main conclusions and proposes future research prospects.

---

 2. Technical Framework and Operational Mechanism of IWFT in Crayfish Aquaculture
 2.1 Core Concept of IWFT
IWFT in crayfish aquaculture is defined as a precision management technology that takes water as the carrier of nutrient transport, and organically integrates water level regulation, nutrient supply, water quality purification, and cyclic utilization through pipeline networks, sensing equipment, and nutrient solution preparation devices. Its core lies in “quantification, synchronization, and recycling”: quantifying water and fertilizer demand according to the growth stages of crayfish and rice (or other aquatic plants); synchronizing water supply and nutrient release to avoid nutrient loss caused by asynchronous supply; and realizing multi-level utilization of water and nutrients through internal circulation in the farming system, so as to minimize external discharge (Zhou & Yang, 2023).

 2.2 Typical Technical System for Rice-Crayfish Co-Culture
The IWFT system applied in rice-crayfish co-culture mainly consists of four modules:
1. Water intake and pretreatment module: Includes water source filter, sedimentation tank, and disinfection device, which filters suspended solids, kills wild fish and pathogenic organisms, and avoids external pollution entering the farming system.
2. Water-fertilizer mixing and delivery module: Comprises a fertilizer storage tank, variable-frequency fertilizer injection pump, mixer, and main-branch pipeline network laid along farming ditches and rice field ridges. The fertilizer applicator is connected to the water delivery pipeline, which can adjust fertilizer concentration in real time according to water flow, and deliver water-fertilizer mixture to designated areas uniformly.
3. Cyclic purification and return module: Consists of tailwater collection ditch, ecological purification zone (planted with *Myriophyllum verticillatum*, *Hydrilla verticillata*, and other submerged plants, and stocked with shellfish and filter-feeding fish), and return pump. Tailwater from farming ditches and rice fields flows into the purification zone through gravity, where suspended solids, nitrogen, and phosphorus are absorbed and transformed, then is pumped back to the farming area for reuse.
4. Monitoring and control module: Equipped with water level sensors, dissolved oxygen (DO) sensors, NH₄⁺-N and NO₂⁻-N sensors, and a remote control terminal. The system collects water quality and water level data every 10 minutes, automatically triggers water replenishment or fertilizer injection when indicators deviate from set thresholds, and supports manual remote regulation.

 2.3 Operational Mechanisms
The operation of IWFT follows the growth rhythm of both crayfish and rice, dividing the production cycle into three stages:
1. Seedling stage (March–April): Crayfish seedlings are released into the ditches, and the rice field is in the fallow or green manure period. The system maintains a low water level in the field (5–10 cm) and a stable water level in ditches (60–80 cm). A low concentration of nitrogen-phosphorus nutrient solution is applied through the pipeline to cultivate plankton and benthic bait organisms, reducing the demand for artificial compound feed.
2. Rice transplanting and symbiotic stage (May–August): After rice transplanting, the water level in the field is gradually raised to 15–20 cm, allowing crayfish to enter the field for movement and foraging. The IWFT system adopts the strategy of “small amount and multiple times” for fertilizer supply: instead of one-time base fertilizer application in traditional farming, soluble fertilizer is delivered with irrigation water in 5–6 split applications according to rice tillering, jointing, and heading stages. Nutrient concentration is strictly controlled to keep NH₄⁺-N below 0.2 mg/L to avoid toxic effects on crayfish. Crayfish excreta and residual bait provide nutrients for rice, forming an internal nutrient cycle.
3. Mature and harvesting stage (September–October): Before rice maturity, field water is slowly drained into ditches through the collection pipeline, guiding crayfish to return to ditches. Tailwater is purified and stored in the purification zone for the next production cycle, reducing external discharge to the greatest extent.

---

 3. Materials and Methods
 3.1 Study Site
The field experiment was conducted at the Crayfish Ecological Farming Base in Jianli City, Jianghan Plain, Hubei Province (112.95°E, 29.83°N) from March 10 to July 8, 2023 (120 days). The region has a subtropical monsoon climate, with an average annual temperature of 16.3 ℃ and average annual precipitation of 1,230 mm. The soil of the experimental site is paddy soil, with organic matter content of 28.6 g/kg, total nitrogen of 1.72 g/kg, total phosphorus of 0.68 g/kg, and pH value of 7.2. The base has sufficient water sources and convenient drainage and irrigation conditions, which are representative of the main crayfish producing areas in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River.

 3.2 Experimental Design
Three treatment modes were set up in the experiment, with three parallel plots for each mode, totaling 9 experimental plots. Each plot covered an area of 0.2 hm², including a central rice planting area (about 85% of the total area) and surrounding farming ditches (about 15%, 1.2 m deep). The ridge around each plot was covered with plastic film to prevent water and nutrient cross-seepage. The three modes are as follows:
- Mode T (Traditional flow-through pond farming): Refers to local traditional extensive pond culture, without rice planting. The whole plot is excavated into a pond with an average water depth of 1.0 m. Farmers adopt flood irrigation and one-time application of urea (150 kg/hm²) and superphosphate (225 kg/hm²) to cultivate water quality. Compound feed is applied twice a day, and water is exchanged irregularly according to water turbidity, with an estimated monthly water exchange rate of 40%–50%.
- Mode C (Conventional rice-crayfish co-culture): Rice (variety: Huanghuazhan) is planted in the central area, and crayfish seedlings are stocked in ditches. Conventional flood irrigation and fertilizer application methods are adopted: base fertilizer accounts for 70% of total fertilizer, and tillering fertilizer accounts for 30%. Fertilizer is manually spread, and water is irrigated by open channels. Water is exchanged once a month, with 20% of pond water replaced each time.
- Mode I (IWFT-optimized rice-crayfish co-culture): The planting structure and crayfish stocking density are consistent with Mode C, but the IWFT system described in Section 2.2 is equipped. Soluble nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium fertilizers are applied in split doses with water through the pipeline, and tailwater is recycled after ecological purification. No external water exchange is carried out except for evaporation and seepage replenishment.

Crayfish seedlings with uniform specification (average body weight 3.2 ± 0.5 g, healthy and no injury) were selected for all modes, and the stocking density was 150,000 individuals/hm². The feed formula and feeding amount were consistent across co-culture modes, adjusted weekly according to crayfish feeding conditions. Rice transplanting density and field management measures (except water and fertilizer management) remained identical between Mode C and Mode I.

 3.3 Monitoring Indicators and Methods
 3.3.1 Water and fertilizer use efficiency
- Water consumption: A flow meter was installed at the water inlet of each plot to record the total irrigation water volume throughout the experimental period. Water use efficiency (WUE) was calculated as:
  $$WUE = Y / W$$
  where $Y$ is total crayfish yield (kg/hm²), and $W$ is total irrigation water consumption (m³/hm²).
- Fertilizer utilization rate: Total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) inputs from fertilizer, feed, and irrigation water were recorded. At the end of the experiment, TN and TP contents in crayfish, rice, water, and sediment were measured. The apparent fertilizer utilization rate was calculated by the nutrient balance method (Bao, 2000).

 3.3.2 Water quality and pollutant discharge
Water samples were collected every 10 days from 5 sampling points in each plot (3 in ditches and 2 in rice fields) at a depth of 30 cm below the water surface. Monitoring indicators included DO, pH, NH₄⁺-N, NO₂⁻-N, TN, TP, and COD, measured according to the standard methods for the examination of water and wastewater (APHA, 2017): DO and pH were measured by a portable multi-parameter water quality analyzer (HQ40d, Hach); NH₄⁺-N was determined by Nessler’s reagent spectrophotometry; NO₂⁻-N by N-(1-naphthyl)-ethylenediamine spectrophotometry; TN by alkaline potassium persulfate digestion UV spectrophotometry; TP by ammonium molybdate spectrophotometry; COD by dichromate method.
The volume and pollutant concentration of each external effluent were recorded, and total pollutant discharge was calculated by the event mean concentration method.

 3.3.3 Crayfish growth and yield
Every 20 days, 50 crayfish were randomly captured from each plot to measure body length and body weight. At the end of the experiment, all crayfish were captured by ground cages and draining ponds, and total yield, survival rate, average body weight, and feed coefficient were counted.

 3.3.4 Economic benefit
Input costs (rent, seed, fertilizer, feed, equipment depreciation, labor, water and electricity) and output value (crayfish and rice output) of each mode were recorded. Net profit and input-output ratio were calculated according to local market prices in 2023: the average price of commercial crayfish was 24 RMB/kg, rice was 2.8 RMB/kg, and the IWFT equipment was depreciated over 5 years.

 3.4 Data Analysis
All data were sorted and calculated using Excel 2021, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS 26.0. Duncan’s multiple range test was used to compare differences among treatment groups, with a significance level of $P < 0.05$. OriginPro 2023 was used for data visualization and plotting.

---

 4. Results
 4.1 Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency
As shown in Table 1, there were significant differences in water and fertilizer utilization among the three modes. The total irrigation water consumption of Mode T was the highest, reaching 18,620 m³/hm², followed by Mode C (11,240 m³/hm²), while Mode I only consumed 10,670 m³/hm². Relative to Mode T and Mode C, Mode I reduced irrigation water by 42.7% and 5.1%, respectively. Correspondingly, WUE of Mode I reached 0.102 kg/m³, which was 75.9% and 24.4% higher than that of Mode T (0.058 kg/m³) and Mode C (0.082 kg/m³), respectively, with significant differences ($P < 0.05$).

In terms of nutrient utilization, the apparent nitrogen utilization rates of Mode T, C, and I were 22.4%, 35.7%, and 53.9%, respectively, and phosphorus utilization rates were 18.6%, 30.2%, and 47.8%, respectively. Compared with Mode T, Mode I increased nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer utilization rates by 31.5 and 29.2 percentage points. The main reason is that split application with water reduces fertilizer loss caused by surface runoff and ammonia volatilization, and the coupled planting-aquaculture system promotes nutrient recycling between rice and crayfish.

 4.2 Water Quality Dynamics and Pollutant Discharge
The dynamic monitoring results of key water quality indicators are presented in Figure 1 (omitted in text). During the whole experiment, DO in Mode I remained between 5.2 and 7.8 mg/L, which was significantly higher than that in Mode T (3.1–6.4 mg/L) and Mode C (4.0–7.1 mg/L). The concentrations of NH₄⁺-N and NO₂⁻-N in Mode T showed the largest fluctuation, with peak values reaching 0.86 mg/L and 0.34 mg/L respectively in the late farming stage; the peak values in Mode C were 0.48 mg/L and 0.21 mg/L; while Mode I maintained NH₄⁺-N below 0.18 mg/L and NO₂⁻-N below 0.08 mg/L throughout the cycle, both within the safe concentration range for crayfish growth (NH₄⁺-N < 0.2 mg/L, NO₂⁻-N < 0.1 mg/L; Romano & Zeng, 2013).

The external pollutant discharge statistics are shown in Table 2. Mode T had the highest pollutant discharge, with TN, TP, and COD discharge loads reaching 42.6, 5.8, and 316.8 kg/hm², respectively. Mode C reduced pollutant discharge to a certain extent, while Mode I achieved the lowest external discharge. Compared with Mode T, Mode I reduced TN, TP, and COD discharge by 58.3%, 62.1%, and 47.2%, respectively. It is worth noting that Mode I only discharged a small amount of overflow water during two heavy rain events, and no conventional water exchange was carried out, which fundamentally cut down the pollution path.

 4.3 Crayfish Growth, Yield, and Rice Output
The growth and production indicators of crayfish are shown in Table 3. At the end of the experiment, the average body weight of crayfish in Mode I reached 32.8 g, which was 24.2% and 12.6% higher than that in Mode T (26.4 g) and Mode C (29.1 g). The survival rate of Mode I was 68.4%, significantly higher than 49.7% of Mode T and 61.2% of Mode C. The total crayfish yield of Mode I reached 1,086 kg/hm², which increased by 86.2% and 18.2% compared with Mode T (583 kg/hm²) and Mode C (919 kg/hm²). The feed coefficient of Mode I was 1.42, which was 0.61 and 0.23 lower than that of Mode T and Mode C, indicating that natural bait organisms cultivated by precise nutrient supply effectively reduced the dependence on artificial feed.

In terms of rice output, the rice yield of Mode I was 7,820 kg/hm², which was 6.8% higher than that of Mode C (7,320 kg/hm²).
