title: 白菜标准化生产技术
text:
Standardized Production Technology of Chinese Cabbage (*Brassica rapa* L. ssp. *pekinensis*)
Author: [Author Name]  
Affiliation: [Department/Institution, City, Postal Code]  
Corresponding Author E-mail: [email@example.com]

---

 Abstract
Chinese cabbage is a major leafy vegetable with high nutritional and economic value globally. Standardized production is critical to improving yield stability, product quality, and food safety. This paper systematically introduces the core technical specifications for standardized Chinese cabbage production, covering field selection, seed treatment, sowing management, field regulation, pest control, and post-harvest handling. The implementation of these technologies can effectively reduce production risks, lower pesticide residues, and promote the sustainable development of the Chinese cabbage industry.

Keywords: Chinese Cabbage; Standardized Production; Cultivation Technology; Quality Control; Green Agriculture

---

 1. Introduction
Chinese cabbage (translated from *baicai* in the topic, referring specifically to heading Chinese cabbage) is one of the most widely cultivated vegetable crops in East Asia, with increasing market demand worldwide. Traditional scattered cultivation often faces problems such as uneven product quality, excessive pesticide application, and unstable annual supply. Standardized production, which regulates the entire production process based on agronomic principles and quality standards, has become a core approach to upgrading the vegetable industry (Wang et al., 2021). This paper summarizes a complete set of operable technical systems to provide references for large-scale and standardized planting of Chinese cabbage.

 2. Pre-Planting Preparation
 2.1 Field Selection and Soil Preparation
Planting sites should be selected in areas with flat terrain, convenient irrigation and drainage, and no "three wastes" (waste gas, wastewater, industrial residue) pollution. The soil should be loam or sandy loam with a pH value of 6.0–7.5, organic matter content ≥1.5%, and continuous cropping with cruciferous crops should be avoided for more than 2 years (Li & Zhang, 2019).
After harvesting previous crops, 20–25 cm deep plowing is carried out 15–20 days before sowing, combined with sun exposure to kill soil-borne pathogens. Base fertilizer is applied at a rate of 30,000–45,000 kg·ha⁻¹ of decomposed farmyard manure, 300–375 kg·ha⁻¹ of compound fertilizer (N:P₂O₅:K₂O = 15:15:15), and 300 kg·ha⁻¹ of biochar. Raised beds are constructed with a bed width of 1.2–1.4 m, bed height of 15–20 cm, and drainage ditches of 30 cm depth around the field.

 2.2 Seed Selection and Treatment
High-yield, disease-resistant, stress-tolerant varieties suitable for local climate and market demand should be selected, such as *Jingchun 3* (spring type) and *Beijing New 3* (autumn type), with seed purity ≥96%, germination rate ≥85%, and seed quality meeting the national standard *GB 16715.2-2010* (China National Seed Standard for Vegetables).
Before sowing, seeds are screened to remove shriveled and diseased grains. Seed dressing is performed with 2.5% fludioxonil suspension concentrate at 0.2% of seed weight to prevent clubroot and damping-off; alternatively, warm water sterilization (50–55 °C for 15–20 min, followed by cooling and drying) can be used for green production.

 3. Sowing and Seedling Management
 3.1 Sowing Period and Method
Spring-sown Chinese cabbage should be sown when the 10 cm soil temperature stabilizes above 10 °C to avoid early bolting; autumn-sown crops are generally sown 3–5 days after the *Liqiu* (Start of Autumn) solar term in northern China (early August), adjusted according to local frost-free periods.
Direct seeding is commonly adopted, with drill sowing or hole sowing. Drill sowing uses 2.25–3.0 kg·ha⁻¹ of seeds, with row spacing of 50–60 cm; hole sowing uses 1.5–2.25 kg·ha⁻¹, with 3–5 seeds per hole and hill spacing of 35–40 cm. Seeds are covered with 0.5–1.0 cm fine soil and gently compacted. For seedling transplanting, 30–35 day-old robust seedlings with 5–6 true leaves are transplanted with soil balls, with a planting density of 37,500–45,000 plants·ha⁻¹.

 3.2 Thinning and Final Singling
For direct-seeded fields, first thinning is carried out at the 2-leaf stage, retaining 2–3 robust seedlings per hole; second thinning at the 4–5 leaf stage, retaining 1 seedling per hole (final singling). During thinning, weeds, weak seedlings, and diseased seedlings are removed, and intertillage weeding is performed 2–3 times before canopy closure to avoid root damage.

 4. Field Water and Fertilizer Management
Water and fertilizer management follows the principle of "controlling at seedling stage, promoting at rosette stage, ensuring supply at heading stage".
- Seedling stage: Keep the soil moist (relative water content 60%–70%). After final singling, apply 75–120 kg·ha⁻¹ of urea as seedling-promoting fertilizer, followed by small-amount irrigation.
- Rosette stage: Irrigate appropriately to promote leaf expansion, apply 150–225 kg·ha⁻¹ of urea and 75–120 kg·ha⁻¹ of potassium sulfate, combined with intertillage hilling. Water should be controlled appropriately 7–10 days before heading to prevent excessive growth.
- Heading stage: This is the critical water and fertilizer demand period, with soil relative water content maintained at 75%–85%. Apply 225–300 kg·ha⁻¹ of high-potassium compound fertilizer and 75 kg·ha⁻¹ of potassium dihydrogen phosphate via furrow application or flushing. Foliar spraying of 0.3% potassium dihydrogen phosphate solution 2–3 times at 7-day intervals can promote leaf head compaction.
Irrigation is preferably conducted via drip irrigation or micro-sprinkler irrigation to reduce humidity and disease occurrence; flood irrigation is prohibited. Stop irrigation 7–10 days before harvest to improve storage resistance.

 5. Integrated Pest and Disease Management
The prevention and control system adheres to the plant protection policy of "prevention first, integrated control", prioritizing agricultural, physical, and biological control, with scientific chemical control as a supplement, in strict accordance with *GB/T 8321* (Guidelines for Safe Use of Pesticides in China).
1. Agricultural control: Implement crop rotation with non-cruciferous crops (e.g., gramineous crops, legumes) for 2–3 years; remove diseased plant residues in time and disinfect field tools.
2. Physical control: Install yellow sticky boards (300–450 boards·ha⁻¹) to trap aphids and whiteflies; use frequency-vibrancy insecticidal lamps (15–30 lamps·ha⁻¹) to trap noctuid moths; cover insect-proof nets (40–60 mesh) in protected cultivation.
3. Biological control: Release *Trichogramma* to control cabbage caterpillars; apply *Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt) preparations and matrine to prevent lepidopteran pests; use *Bacillus subtilis* to prevent downy mildew and soft rot.
4. Chemical control: For downy mildew, 72% cymoxanil·mancozeb wettable powder (800–1000-fold dilution) can be sprayed; for soft rot, 72% agricultural streptomycin sulfate (3000–4000-fold dilution) is used for root irrigation; for aphids, 10% imidacloprid wettable powder (2000-fold dilution) is applied. The safe interval period of pesticides must be strictly implemented, and highly toxic and high-residue pesticides are prohibited.

 6. Harvest and Post-Harvest Standardization
Harvest is carried out when 80% of leaf heads are compact and meet commodity specifications, avoiding frost damage in autumn and bolting in spring. Harvest in sunny morning or cool weather, remove outer yellow leaves, diseased leaves, and root soil, and grade products according to head weight, compactness, and appearance (refer to *NY/T 1583-2008 Quality Grading of Chinese Cabbage*).
Graded products are pre-cooled in a cold storage at 0–2 °C for 12–24 hours to remove field heat, then packaged with food-grade plastic film or breathable cartons, marked with origin, harvest date, grade, and green certification logo. During storage and transportation, the temperature is maintained at 0–1 °C and relative humidity at 90%–95%, with mixed loading and transportation with toxic and odorous substances prohibited.

 7. Conclusion
The standardized production technology of Chinese cabbage integrates environmental control, fine agronomic management, green pest control, and standardized post-harvest treatment, which can significantly improve the commodity rate and quality safety of products while increasing resource use efficiency. In the future, combining intelligent monitoring, reduced-fertilizer and pesticide technology, and whole-process traceability systems will further promote the intensification and green transformation of Chinese cabbage production, and support the high-quality development of the vegetable industry.

---

 References
1. Li, X., & Zhang, H. Y. (2019). High-yield and high-efficiency standardized cultivation techniques of autumn Chinese cabbage. *China Vegetables*, (S1), 121–124. (in Chinese)
2. Wang, Y. F., Liu, C., & Zhao, J. (2021). Development status and countermeasures of standardized vegetable production in China. *Journal of Agricultural Resources and Environment*, 38(4), 567–574.
3. National Agricultural Technology Extension Service Center. (2020). *Technical Specifications for Green Cultivation of Heading Chinese Cabbage* (NY/T 3621-2020). China Agriculture Press.
4. Zhang, L., & Chen, X. Q. (2022). Integrated pest management technology for cruciferous vegetables under standardized production. *Plant Protection*, 48(3), 212–218.

title: 城市垃圾分类管理问题
text:
Short Paper on Urban Municipal Solid Waste Sorting Management: Barriers, Evidence and Policy Optimization
*Course: Urban Environmental Governance | Student: [Name] | Date: October 26, 2024*

---

 Abstract
Municipal solid waste (MSW) sorting is a core intervention to reduce landfill pressure, cut carbon emissions from waste treatment, and advance circular economy goals in high-density urban areas. Over the past decade, over 200 Chinese cities have rolled out mandatory MSW sorting policies, yet persistent implementation gaps have limited policy efficacy. This paper combines empirical evidence from a 2023–2024 household survey in 6 residential communities across Hangzhou and Zhengzhou (n=427) with global comparative case analysis to identify three core barriers to effective sorting: fragmented incentive alignment across stakeholders, insufficient infrastructure matching, and context-blind policy design. The study finds that communities with targeted, group-specific interventions achieved a 47% higher accurate sorting rate than those relying solely on punitive measures. It concludes that multi-stakeholder co-governance, context-adapted infrastructure, and mixed incentive frameworks are critical to closing the implementation gap in urban MSW sorting management.
Keywords: Municipal Solid Waste Sorting; Urban Environmental Governance; Policy Implementation; Circular Economy; Resident Behavior

---

 1. Introduction
Global urban MSW generation reached 2.24 billion tonnes in 2024, with 33% of waste openly dumped without environmentally sound treatment, according to the World Bank (2024). In China, urban MSW output grew at an annual rate of 4.5% between 2015 and 2023, reaching 240 million tonnes; landfills and incineration, the dominant treatment pathways, account for 2.3% of national carbon emissions and pose long-term risks of soil and groundwater contamination (Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development [MOHURD], 2024).

MSW sorting, which separates recyclables, kitchen waste, hazardous waste and residual waste at the source, is recognized as the most cost-effective strategy to improve recycling rates and reduce end-of-pipe treatment costs. Since Shanghai launched the first national mandatory sorting regulation in 2019, 297 prefecture-level cities in China have introduced formal sorting rules, with total public investment exceeding 42 billion RMB by 2023 (MOHURD, 2024). However, official data shows the national average accurate sorting rate at the household level is only 32%, far below the 2025 policy target of 60%.

Existing research on MSW sorting largely focuses on individual resident behavior, with less attention to structural mismatches between policy design, infrastructure provision and stakeholder incentives (Xu et al., 2022). This paper addresses this gap by answering two research questions: (1) What multi-level barriers impede effective MSW sorting implementation in urban China? (2) What targeted policy adjustments can improve sorting performance? The study combines primary survey data and comparative case evidence to propose actionable governance frameworks.

---

 2. Literature Review
Scholarly analysis of MSW sorting barriers falls into three broad strands. First, behavioral studies emphasize the role of individual awareness and habit: Tong et al. (2021) found that environmental knowledge accounts for 28% of variance in household sorting behavior, but note that high awareness rarely translates into consistent action without structural support. Second, policy design studies highlight the limitations of over-reliance on punitive measures: a meta-analysis of 47 global sorting programs found that fines alone increase accurate sorting rates by only 8–12% in the long term, as residents revert to old habits when monitoring intensity drops (Diaz et al., 2022). Third, infrastructure-focused research points out that "distance to sorting facilities" is a stronger predictor of compliance than personal environmental values: if collection points are more than 150 meters from residential buildings, participation rates drop by 60% regardless of awareness levels (Xiao et al., 2023).

A critical gap in existing literature is the lack of analysis of cross-stakeholder incentive alignment: most studies treat residents as the sole target of intervention, while ignoring misaligned incentives for property management companies, waste collection enterprises and street-level regulators. This paper addresses this gap by integrating multi-stakeholder dynamics into the analysis of implementation barriers.

---

 3. Core Barriers to Urban MSW Sorting Management
Empirical evidence from the 2023–2024 household survey and stakeholder interviews reveals three interconnected barriers to effective sorting:
 3.1 Misaligned Incentives Across Multi-Stakeholder Governance Networks
MSW sorting requires coordinated action across city authorities, street offices, property management firms, waste collection enterprises and residents, but existing incentive structures create fragmented accountability. For example, 68% of interviewed property managers reported that they received no dedicated funding for sorting supervision, despite being tasked with monitoring resident behavior and maintaining collection points; as a result, 72% of communities assigned only part-time cleaning staff to sorting duty, with no systematic monitoring. For formal waste collection enterprises, mixed transportation of pre-sorted waste remains widespread: 58% of surveyed residents reported seeing sorted waste dumped into the same collection truck, a practice that erodes resident trust and reduces willingness to sort, as households perceive their effort as wasted.
 3.2 Structural Mismatch Between Infrastructure Supply and Local Demand
Many cities adopted a one-size-fits-all infrastructure standard without accounting for community characteristics. For example, 62% of old urban neighborhoods (built before 2000) in the survey had only one centralized sorting point for 1,000+ households, with an average walking distance of 220 meters, compared to 80 meters in new commercial communities. For elderly residents (aged 60+), who make up 42% of long-term residents in old neighborhoods, this long walking distance is the top cited reason for non-compliance. In addition, 71% of communities lacked specialized, regularly cleaned collection bins for kitchen waste in summer, leading to odor and pest problems that further reduced resident willingness to use sorting facilities.
 3.3 One-Size-Fits-All Policy Design Ignoring Group Heterogeneity
Most cities rely on uniform public education campaigns and punitive fines without adapting to the needs of different resident groups. For example, 78% of surveyed migrant tenants reported that they had never received targeted sorting guidance, compared to 32% of local registered homeowners; language barriers and high residential mobility mean that general community posters and WeChat announcements rarely reach this group. For young white-collar workers, who make up 35% of residents in central urban communities, the fixed opening hours of most sorting points (usually 7:00–9:00 and 18:00–20:00) conflict with long commuting times, making compliant sorting impossible for 63% of this group.

---

 4. Evidence-Based Optimization Pathways
Comparative case analysis of high-performing communities and global best practices points to three targeted interventions to address the above barriers:
 4.1 Build a Multi-Stakeholder Co-Governance Framework with Aligned Incentives
Cities should replace top-down accountability structures with shared incentive mechanisms. For example, Shenzhen’s pilot "points exchange system" allocates 10% of waste disposal fee savings to property management companies that meet sorting targets, increasing property management investment in supervision by 78% between 2022 and 2024 (Shenzhen Urban Management Bureau, 2024). For waste collection enterprises, mandatory GPS tracking of separate transport trucks, paired with resident reporting hotlines with cash rewards for verified violations, reduced mixed transport rates to 7% in pilot districts, compared to the city average of 42%.
 4.2 Adopt Context-Adapted Infrastructure Planning
Infrastructure standards should be tailored to community demographics rather than applying uniform rules. For example, old neighborhoods with high elderly populations should install distributed, small-scale sorting points every 80 meters, rather than large centralized points; for communities with a high share of young commuters, 24-hour smart sorting bins with automatic identification of waste types can extend access outside fixed opening hours. In Hangzhou’s Xihu District, the adoption of this targeted infrastructure approach increased average sorting participation rates from 41% to 83% within 12 months (Hangzhou Urban Management Bureau, 2024).
 4.3 Implement Differentiated Interventions for Heterogeneous Resident Groups
Outreach and incentive strategies should be tailored to different resident groups, rather than relying on uniform posters and fines. For migrant tenants, partnerships with local employers and rental platforms to provide multilingual sorting guidance, paired with small rewards (e.g., free public transport credits) for consistent compliance, increased accurate sorting rates by 52% in pilot communities in Guangzhou. For elderly residents, on-site guidance from community volunteers and small rewards (e.g., free cooking oil, rice) for monthly compliance proved far more effective than punitive fines.

---

 5. Conclusion
Urban MSW sorting is not merely a technical intervention or a matter of individual resident responsibility, but a systemic governance challenge that requires aligned incentives, context-appropriate infrastructure and targeted, inclusive policy design. The evidence presented in this paper shows that over-reliance on top-down punitive measures and one-size-fits-all infrastructure leads to persistent implementation gaps, even with high levels of public investment. Moving forward, city authorities should shift from a regulator-centered model to a multi-stakeholder co-governance framework that centers the needs of diverse resident groups and aligns the economic incentives of all actors in the waste management chain. This approach will not only improve sorting performance, but also lay a foundation for inclusive, low-carbon urban circular economy transitions.

---

 References
1. Diaz, R., Warith, M., & Soka, I. (2022). The efficacy of punitive and incentive-based policies for household waste sorting: A global meta-analysis. *Journal of Environmental Management*, 317, 115429.
2. Hangzhou Urban Management Bureau. (2024). *2023 Annual Report on Municipal Solid Waste Sorting Implementation*. Hangzhou: Hangzhou Municipal Government.
3. Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development of China [MOHURD]. (2024). *2023 National Urban Environmental Sanitation Development Statistical Bulletin*. Beijing: China Architecture & Building Press.
4. Shenzhen Urban Management Bureau. (2024). *Pilot Evaluation of MSW Sorting Incentive Mechanisms (2022–2023)*. Shenzhen: Shenzhen Municipal Government.
5. Tong, Y., Liu, J., & Wang, L. (2021). From awareness to action: The gap in household waste sorting behavior in urban China. *Sustainable Cities and Society*, 73, 103118.
6. World Bank. (2024). *What a Waste 2.0: Global Municipal Solid Waste Management Update 2024*. Washington, DC: World Bank Group.
7. Xiao, S., Li, Y., & Zhang, H. (2023). Infrastructure accessibility and household waste sorting compliance: Evidence from 18 Chinese cities. *Resources, Conservation and Recycling*, 194, 106987.
8. Xu, M., Lin, B., & Ma, C. (2022). Multi-level governance gaps in China’s mandatory waste sorting policy: A fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. *Journal of Cleaner Production*, 373, 133923.

title: 中药材病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Pests and Diseases in Traditional Chinese Medicinal Materials
 Abstract
Traditional Chinese medicinal materials (TCMM) are critical raw materials for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), and their quality and yield are directly affected by pest and disease outbreaks. Conventional chemical control methods lead to pesticide residues, environmental pollution, and degradation of medicinal efficacy, which threaten the safety of TCM clinical use and the sustainable development of the TCMM industry. Against this background, green prevention and control (GPC) technologies, which prioritize ecological regulation, physical control, biological control, and scientific chemical management, have become a core development direction for TCMM cultivation. This paper systematically sorts out the main types of pests and diseases in TCMM, analyzes the core principles and key technical systems of green prevention and control, discusses current application challenges, and proposes corresponding optimization countermeasures, aiming to provide references for the standardized, ecologically friendly production of high-quality TCMM.

Keywords: Traditional Chinese Medicinal Materials; Pests and Diseases; Green Prevention and Control; Ecological Cultivation; Quality Safety

---

 1. Introduction
Traditional Chinese medicine is an important part of China’s medical and health system, and the stable supply of high-quality traditional Chinese medicinal materials is the foundation of TCM industry development. In recent years, with the continuous expansion of artificial cultivation scale of TCMM, problems such as continuous cropping obstacles, single planting structure, and extensive field management have become increasingly prominent, leading to frequent occurrence of pests and diseases. Data show that the annual yield loss of TCMM caused by pests and diseases generally ranges from 10% to 30%, and can exceed 50% in severe outbreak years, causing huge economic losses to growers[1].

For a long time, chemical pesticides have been the main means of pest and disease control due to their fast-acting and low-cost characteristics. However, unscientific use of chemical pesticides can easily cause excessive pesticide residues in medicinal materials, damage the ecological environment of planting areas, and even reduce the content of active pharmaceutical ingredients, which runs counter to the "genuine medicinal materials" (daodi yaocai) quality concept of TCM[2]. In 2021, China issued the *Good Agricultural Practice for Chinese Crude Drugs (GAP)*, which clearly put forward requirements for reducing chemical pesticide use and promoting green production technologies. Therefore, constructing a scientific and efficient green prevention and control technology system for TCMM pests and diseases has important practical significance for guaranteeing the quality and safety of medicinal materials, protecting farmland biodiversity, and promoting the high-quality development of the TCM industry.

---

 2. Main Types and Occurrence Characteristics of Pests and Diseases in TCMM
Different from ordinary field crops, TCMM cover a wide variety of species (including root medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines, etc.), and their pest and disease types show strong species specificity and regional characteristics. The main hazards can be divided into three categories.

 2.1 Major Diseases
Diseases of TCMM are mainly caused by fungal, bacterial, viral pathogens and root-knot nematodes, among which soil-borne diseases are the most difficult to control.
- Fungal diseases: They account for more than 70% of TCMM diseases. Typical cases include root rot of *Panax ginseng* and *Astragalus membranaceus*, rust of *Angelica sinensis* and *Chuanxiong rhizoma*, powdery mildew of *Lonicera japonica* and *Chrysanthemum morifolium*, and gray mold of *Fritillaria cirrhosa*. Soil-borne fungal diseases such as root rot are prone to break out under continuous cropping conditions, and pathogenic bacteria can survive in the soil for 3–5 years[3].
- Bacterial diseases: Common types include bacterial wilt of *Panax notoginseng* and soft rot of *Fritillaria*, which mostly occur in high-temperature and high-humidity environments, invading plants through wounds and causing rapid wilting and decay of tissues.
- Viral diseases: They are mostly transmitted by aphids and whiteflies, such as mosaic disease of *Rehmannia glutinosa* and virus disease of *Lycium barbarum*, which cause leaf shrinkage, plant dwarfing, and serious decline in medicinal component content.
- Nematode diseases: Root-knot nematodes mainly harm root-type medicinal materials such as *Salvia miltiorrhiza* and *Platycodon grandiflorus*, forming nodular galls on roots and inducing compound infection of soil-borne pathogens.

 2.2 Major Pests
The pests of TCMM include chewing pests, piercing-sucking pests and underground pests, with different damage periods and sites.
- Underground pests: They are the most harmful group to root medicinal materials, including cutworms, grubs, mole crickets and wireworms, which bite seeds, roots and rhizomes, causing seedling shortage and yield reduction.
- Piercing-sucking pests: Represented by aphids, whiteflies, red spiders and *Aphis gossypii* on *Lycium barbarum*, they suck plant sap and spread viral diseases, leading to leaf curling and flower and fruit drop.
- Leaf- and fruit-eating pests: Such as *Spodoptera litura*, cabbage caterpillars, and *Arctiidae* larvae, which feed on leaves, flowers and fruits; in addition, the dry root rot caused by longhorn beetle larvae damaging woody medicinal materials such as *Eucommia ulmoides* and *Magnolia officinalis* is also common.

 2.3 Occurrence Characteristics
The occurrence of TCMM pests and diseases has three prominent features: First, species specificity—the key pests and diseases of different medicinal species vary greatly, and there are differences in control thresholds; second, soil-borne disease accumulation under continuous cropping—most perennial root medicinal materials are not suitable for continuous cropping, and the imbalance of soil microecology aggravates disease occurrence; third, quality sensitivity—the control process must not only ensure control efficacy, but also strictly control pesticide residues to avoid affecting the safety and efficacy of medicinal materials.

---

 3. Core Principles of Green Prevention and Control for TCMM Pests and Diseases
Green prevention and control of TCMM pests and diseases follows the plant protection policy of "prevention first, comprehensive control", and takes "ecological priority, safety first, quality-oriented and scientific pesticide use" as the core principles.
1.  Ecological priority: Based on the biodiversity of the planting ecosystem, regulate the farmland habitat, give full play to the natural control effect of beneficial organisms, and reduce the ecological niche suitable for pests and diseases.
2.  Safety first: Prioritize technologies and products that are non-toxic or low-toxic to human health, medicinal materials and non-target organisms, strictly prohibit the use of highly toxic and high-residue pesticides banned by the state, and ensure the safety of medication and ecological environment.
3.  Quality-oriented: Take the content of active ingredients and pesticide residue standards of medicinal materials as important assessment indicators, and avoid control measures that reduce the quality of medicinal materials while pursuing pest control effects.
4.  Systematic management: Integrate agricultural, physical, biological and chemical control measures, construct a full-cycle technical system from pre-sowing to harvest, and replace single chemical control with integrated management.

---

 4. Key Green Prevention and Control Technologies
 4.1 Agricultural Control: Ecological Regulation from the Source
Agricultural control is the fundamental measure of green prevention and control, which reduces the occurrence of pests and diseases by optimizing cultivation measures and improving plant stress resistance.
- Selection of disease-resistant varieties and genuine seedlings: Select disease-resistant and stress-tolerant varieties suitable for local climatic conditions according to the daodi production area layout; promote the use of virus-free tissue culture seedlings (such as virus-free *Rehmannia glutinosa* and *Pinellia ternata* seedlings), and implement seedling quarantine and disinfection treatment (seed dressing with low-toxic biological agents, warm soup soaking) to cut off the initial infection source.
- Scientific crop rotation and intercropping: Avoid continuous cropping of the same family of medicinal materials. For root medicines with serious continuous cropping obstacles such as *Panax notoginseng* and ginseng, implement 3–5 years of crop rotation with gramineous crops (corn, wheat) or green manure; reasonably intercropping with repellent plants and nectar plants, such as interplanting marigolds in *Salvia miltiorrhiza* fields to repel root-knot nematodes, and planting clover around *Lycium barbarum* gardens to protect natural enemies[4].
- Soil health management: Apply decomposed organic fertilizer and bio-organic fertilizer to improve soil organic matter content; adjust soil pH according to the growth habits of medicinal materials; adopt ridging cultivation and reasonable close planting to improve field ventilation and light transmission and reduce field humidity; in summer fallow period, implement high-temperature greenhouse stuffy or flooding drying to kill soil-borne pathogens and underground pest eggs.
- Field sanitation management: Remove diseased plants, diseased residues and field weeds in time during the growth period, and carry out centralized harmless treatment; after harvest, deeply clean the garden and plough the soil to reduce the overwintering base number of pests and diseases.

 4.2 Physical Control: Environmentally Friendly Trapping and Blocking
Physical control uses physical factors such as light, color, temperature and mechanical devices to trap or block pests, with the advantages of no pesticide residue and simple operation.
- Phototaxis trapping: Install frequency-vibration insecticidal lamps in the planting base according to the standard of 1 lamp per 2–3 hectares, turn on the lamps at night during the adult emergence period of lepidoptera and coleoptera pests, which can significantly reduce the number of eggs laid, and the trapping effect on cutworms, longhorn beetles and *Spodoptera litura* is remarkable.
- Color tropism trapping: Hang yellow sticky boards to trap aphids, whiteflies and leafminers, and blue sticky boards to trap thrips; generally hang 300–450 boards per hectare, and the height is 10–20 cm above the crop canopy, and replace them regularly.
- Physical barrier: Cover insect-proof nets in seedbeds and facility cultivation areas to block pests from invading and transmitting viruses; for woody medicinal materials, tie grass ropes on trunks to trap overwintering pests, or set up trunk sticky belts to prevent pests from climbing.
- Food and sex attractant trapping: Use sex pheromone lures to interfere with the mating of pests such as *Grapholita molesta* and *Spodoptera exigua*; use sweet and sour liquid, bran poison bait (matched with biological pesticides) to trap underground pests such as cutworms and grubs.

 4.3 Biological Control: Using Biological Relationships to Control Pests
Biological control uses living organisms or their metabolites to control pests and diseases, which is the core technology of green prevention and control, and has the advantages of strong specificity, low environmental impact and durable efficacy.
 4.3.1 Biological Control of Pests
- Predatory and parasitic natural enemies: Release *Harmonia axyridis* and lacewings to control aphids; release *Trichogramma* to parasitize lepidopteran pest eggs; in perennial woody medicinal gardens, protect spiders, frogs and birds by planting hedgerows and setting artificial nests to give full play to the natural control effect of native natural enemies.
- Entomopathogenic microorganisms: Apply *Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt), *Beauveria bassiana*, *Metarhizium anisopliae* and other microbial agents to control lepidoptera larvae and underground pests; use *Paecilomyces lilacinus* to parasitize root-knot nematode eggs.
- Botanical and microbial pesticides: Use azadirachtin, matrine, rotenone and other plant-derived pesticides to prevent and control piercing-sucking pests and leaf-eating pests; use spinosad, abamectin and other microbial source pesticides with low toxicity and easy degradation.

 4.3.2 Biological Control of Diseases
- Antagonistic microorganisms: Use *Trichoderma harzianum*, *Trichoderma viride* to prevent and control soil-borne fungal diseases such as root rot and blight; apply *Bacillus subtilis*, *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* through root irrigation or spray to inhibit the proliferation of pathogenic bacteria and induce plant disease resistance; use *Pseudomonas fluorescens* for seed dressing and soil treatment to reduce bacterial wilt and nematode damage[5].
- Agricultural antibiotic preparations: Use validamycin to control sheath blight and rust, ningnanmycin to prevent and control viral diseases, and polyoxin to control powdery mildew and gray mold; such products have low residue and are compatible with the growth of medicinal materials.
- Bio-organic fertilizer improvement: Add antagonistic functional bacteria to decomposed organic fertilizer to improve soil microbial community structure, inhibit the accumulation of soil-borne pathogens, and alleviate continuous cropping obstacles.

 4.4 Scientific Chemical Control: Precise and Reduced-Risk Pesticide Application
Green prevention and control does not completely eliminate chemical pesticides, but advocates scientific, selective and reduced use on the basis of monitoring and early warning, so as to minimize the risk of pesticide residues.
1.  Strictly implement pesticide access management: Prohibit the use of 39 kinds of highly toxic and high-residue pesticides banned by China’s agricultural and forestry planting, such as methamidophos, omethoate and carbofuran; select low-toxicity, low-residue and high-efficiency registered pesticides that meet the requirements of GAP for Chinese medicinal materials, and strictly implement the safety interval regulations.
2.  Carry out monitoring and precision pesticide application: Establish pest and disease monitoring points in the base, grasp the optimal control period (such as egg hatching peak, early disease onset), and apply pesticides according to the economic threshold to avoid blind pesticide application.
3.  Optimize application technology: Promote the use of advanced equipment such as electrostatic sprayers and unmanned aerial vehicles with low-volume spraying to improve pesticide utilization; rotate pesticides with different action mechanisms to delay the development of pathogen and pest resistance; strictly control the dosage and application times, and stop medication within a specified period before harvest.
4.  Promote combined use of biological and chemical agents: Mix biological agents with low-dose chemical agents to reduce the amount of chemical pesticides while ensuring control efficacy, and gradually transition to biological control as the main measure.

---

 5. Existing Problems in Current Application
Although green prevention and control technology of TCMM has achieved certain popularization effects, there are still many bottlenecks in large-scale application.
First, the technical matching degree is insufficient for diverse species. There are hundreds of commonly cultivated TCMM varieties, but the existing green prevention and control technologies mostly refer to field crop standards, and the special control technologies for rare and genuine medicinal materials are lacking, and the control effects of biological agents are unstable under different climatic conditions.
Second, the awareness and acceptance of growers are limited. Most small-scale growers have long relied on chemical pesticides, and generally have problems such as unclear understanding of the slow effect and operation specifications of biological control, and insufficient acceptance of the initial input cost of physical prevention facilities.
Third, the market-oriented incentive mechanism is not perfect. The premium of green and organic medicinal materials is not fully reflected in the market, and the quality traceability system of some production areas is not perfect, which weakens the motivation of producers to adopt green technologies.
Fourth, the research and development and registration of special agents lag behind. There are few pesticides and biological agents officially registered for TCMM in China, and the phenomenon of "off-label use" of pesticides is common, which brings hidden dangers to the standardized control and residue management of medicinal materials[6].

---

 6. Optimization Countermeasures and Development Prospects
 6.1 Optimization Countermeasures
1.  Strengthen species-specific technology research and demonstration: Carry out collaborative research on green prevention and control technologies for major and genuine medicinal materials by region and variety, formulate localized technical operation regulations, and build demonstration bases for integrated application of agricultural, physical and biological technologies to drive surrounding farmers through on-site observation and training.
2.  Improve the quality traceability and premium system: Combine the GAP certification and geographical indication protection of medicinal materials, bring the green prevention and control records into the whole-chain traceability system from planting to circulation, support the docking of high-quality TCMM production bases with TCM enterprises, and realize the market mechanism of "high quality and good price".
3.  Accelerate R&D and registration of special green inputs: Set up special scientific research projects to support the research and development of special biological agents, botanical pesticides and polluting-free soil conditioners for TCMM, simplify the registration process of green pesticides for minor medicinal crops, and expand the optional range of standardized medication.
4.  Carry out multi-level technical training: Popularize the knowledge of pest identification, biological agent use and precise pesticide application to grassroots agricultural technicians and growers through field schools, online courses and technical manuals, and improve the scientific management level of the main production body.

 6.2 Development Prospects
In the future, the green prevention and control of TCMM pests and diseases will develop in the direction of intelligence, systematization and ecologicalization. On the one hand, technologies such as Internet of Things sensors, intelligent insect situation forecasting lamps and big data analysis will be used to build an accurate early warning system for pests and diseases, and realize dynamic monitoring and customized control scheme push. On the other hand, the ecological planting mode combining under-forest planting, intercropping and biodiversity utilization will be deeply integrated with soil microecological regulation technology, to further reduce the dependence on external inputs. In addition, with the continuous improvement of consumers’ awareness of TCM quality safety, green prevention and control technology will become a core part of the core competitiveness of the TCMM industry, and help Chinese medicinal materials move towards standardized, ecologically friendly and high-quality development.

---

 7. Conclusion
Pest and disease control is a key link related to the yield, quality and medication safety of traditional Chinese medicinal materials. The traditional extensive chemical control mode can no longer adapt to the high-quality development requirements of the modern TCM industry. The green prevention and control technology system, which takes ecological regulation as the foundation, physical and biological control as the core, and precise low-risk chemical control as the supplement, can not only effectively reduce the damage of pests and diseases, but also significantly reduce pesticide residues, protect farmland biodiversity, and stabilize the content of active ingredients in medicinal materials. In the future, it is necessary to continuously improve the special technical system, strengthen policy guidance and market incentives, and promote the large-scale standardized application of green prevention and control technologies, so as to lay a solid foundation for the safe supply of high-quality traditional Chinese medicinal materials and the inheritance and development of the traditional Chinese medicine industry.

---

 References
[1] Zhang X, Li Y, Wang H. Occurrence status and green management countermeasures of diseases and pests in Chinese medicinal materials planting[J]. *China Journal of Chinese Materia Medica*, 2022, 47(12): 3145-3152. (in Chinese)
[2] National Health Commission of the People’s Republic of China, National Medical Products Administration. Good Agricultural Practice for Chinese Crude Drugs (2022 Revision)[S]. Beijing: China Medical Science Press, 2022.
[3] Liu C, Zhou J. Soil-borne diseases of medicinal plants: damage characteristics and ecological control progress[J]. *Journal of Chinese Medicinal Materials*, 2021, 44(8): 1799-1806. (in Chinese)
[4] Chen S, Wu L. Biodiversity-based ecological cultivation and green pest management for traditional Chinese medicinal materials[J]. *Chinese Traditional and Herbal Drugs*, 2023, 54(5): 1367-1376. (in Chinese)
[5] Wang Y, Zhao Q. Application of *Bacillus* and *Trichoderma* agents in disease control of Chinese medicinal crops[J]. *Biological Control in China*, 2022, 38(3): 521-530. (in Chinese)

title: 玉米品质提升与增效途径
text:
Pathways to Improve Maize (Zea mays L.) Quality and Production Efficiency: Mechanisms, Technological Interventions and Sustainable Strategies  
 Abstract  
Maize (Zea mays L.) is a globally dominant cereal crop serving as a staple food, feedstock for livestock, raw material for industrial processing, and core feedstock for emerging bioenergy sectors. With global population growth, shifting dietary structures, and climate change-induced arable land constraints, improving maize quality and production efficiency has become a critical priority for ensuring food security, boosting agricultural economic returns, and advancing sustainable agriculture. This paper systematically analyzes the core dimensions of maize quality (nutritional, processing, and safety quality) and key constraints on production efficiency, then proposes a multi-dimensional integrated improvement pathway covering germplasm innovation, optimized cultivation management, post-harvest loss reduction, industrial chain extension, and policy support. This study finds that conventional breeding combined with modern molecular breeding techniques can significantly enhance targeted quality traits; precision agriculture and resource-efficient cultivation practices reduce input costs while stabilizing yield and quality; standardized post-harvest handling and deep processing extend the value chain and improve overall efficiency. The findings provide theoretical and practical references for global maize industry upgrading and sustainable agricultural development.  

Keywords: Maize Quality; Production Efficiency; Germplasm Innovation; Precision Cultivation; Industrial Chain Integration; Sustainable Agriculture  

 1. Introduction  
Maize is one of the most widely cultivated and highest-yielding cereal crops worldwide. Data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO, 2024) shows that global maize output reached 1.21 billion tonnes in 2023, accounting for approximately 38% of total global cereal production, surpassing rice and wheat to become the largest grain crop by output. Beyond direct human consumption, around 70% of global maize is used for livestock and poultry feed, while 15% serves as raw material for starch, edible oil, alcohol, degradable materials and other industrial products, with the remainder used for seed and bioenergy production.  

In recent decades, global maize production has grown substantially driven by increased input of chemical fertilizers, pesticides and improved high-yield varieties. However, this growth model faces two prominent bottlenecks. First, quality mismatches are increasingly prominent: conventional maize varieties generally have low contents of high-quality protein, essential amino acids (lysine, tryptophan), oil and functional active substances, which cannot meet the differentiated demands of feed, food processing and special industrial uses; excessive pesticide residues and mycotoxin contamination also pose hidden risks to food and feed safety. Second, production efficiency improvement is constrained: traditional extensive cultivation leads to low utilization efficiency of water, fertilizer and land resources, rising labor and production costs, and large post-harvest losses, while climate change-induced drought, high temperature and pest outbreaks further exacerbate yield and quality fluctuations.  

Against this background, simply pursuing yield increase can no longer adapt to the transformation and upgrading of the maize industry. Improving maize quality in a targeted manner and enhancing total factor productivity across the entire industrial chain have become core directions for global maize industry development. This study clarifies the evaluation system of maize quality and the core constraints of efficiency improvement, and constructs a systematic technical and institutional pathway from pre-production breeding, in-production management to post-harvest value addition, aiming to provide scientific support for realizing the coordinated improvement of maize quality, yield and economic benefits.  

 2. Connotation and Evaluation Dimension of Maize Quality  
Maize quality is a comprehensive concept covering intrinsic attributes, processing applicability and safety, with distinct evaluation priorities across different end uses. It can be divided into three core dimensions: nutritional quality, processing and commercial quality, and safety and green quality.  

 2.1 Nutritional Quality  
Nutritional quality refers to the contents and bioavailability of nutrients in maize kernels, which is the core indicator for food and feed use. Conventional maize kernels contain approximately 72%–75% starch, 8%–10% protein, 4%–5% oil, and a variety of vitamins and dietary fiber. However, maize storage proteins are dominated by zein, which is deficient in lysine and tryptophan, essential amino acids for humans and monogastric animals, resulting in a protein nutritional value of only 40%–50% of that of soybean protein (Nuss & Tanumihardjo, 2011). Special maize varieties such as quality protein maize (QPM), high-oil maize and high-amylose maize have significantly improved nutritional value: the lysine content of QPM is more than twice that of conventional maize, which can reduce the addition of synthetic lysine in feed and improve feed conversion efficiency. In addition, functional components such as carotenoids, anthocyanins and resistant starch in colored maize and waxy maize have antioxidant and intestinal health-regulating effects, representing an important direction for quality upgrading.  

 2.2 Processing and Commercial Quality  
Processing and commercial quality reflect the suitability of maize for different processing scenarios and its market commodity attributes. For feed use, key indicators include kernel bulk density, hardness, starch gelatinization degree and palatability, which directly affect feed molding rate and animal digestion and absorption rate. For industrial starch processing, starch content, starch extraction rate and amylose/amylopectin ratio are the core indicators: high-amylose maize is suitable for producing degradable films and resistant starch, while high-amylopectin (waxy) maize is preferred for thickeners, modified starch and brewing. For fresh-eating maize (sweet maize, waxy maize), sugar content, pericarp thickness, flavor and shelf life determine its commercial value. Uniform kernel size, low impurity rate and low moisture content after harvest are basic indicators of commercial quality that affect storage, transportation and market pricing.  

 2.3 Safety and Green Quality  
Safety quality is the bottom-line requirement for maize products, mainly including mycotoxin contamination, pesticide residues, heavy metal excess and genetically modified organism (GMO) safety management. Maize is highly susceptible to contamination by *Aspergillus flavus* and *Fusarium* during field growth and post-harvest storage, producing aflatoxin, deoxynivalenol (DON) and zearalenone, which are strongly carcinogenic and toxic, and can enter the food chain through feed, causing harm to human and animal health (Bryła et al., 2018). Green quality emphasizes low-carbon and environmentally friendly production processes, including reduced chemical fertilizer and pesticide use, water and soil conservation, and low carbon footprint, which is aligned with the global sustainable consumption trend and increasingly becomes an important component of high-quality maize products.  

 3. Main Constraints on Maize Quality Improvement and Efficiency Enhancement  
 3.1 Germplasm Resources with Excellent Traits and Breeding System Limitations  
Long-term high-yield-oriented breeding has led to a narrow genetic base of mainstream commercial maize varieties, with insufficient accumulation of high-quality, stress-resistant and resource-efficient genes. Conventional hybrid breeding has a long cycle (usually 8–10 years) and low selection efficiency for complex quality traits (such as protein composition and functional component content), making it difficult to rapidly aggregate multiple excellent traits. In addition, the breeding promotion system in many regions disconnects variety traits from local ecological conditions and market demand: some newly bred varieties have high quality but poor stress resistance and unstable yield, while high-yield varieties fail to meet the quality standards of processing enterprises, resulting in a mismatch between “good varieties” and “good harvests and good prices”.  

 3.2 Extensive Cultivation Management and Low Resource Utilization Efficiency  
Traditional maize cultivation generally suffers from excessive application of nitrogen fertilizer, extensive flood irrigation and unscientific sowing density. Statistics show that the average nitrogen fertilizer utilization efficiency of maize in China is only about 30%, far below the 50%–60% level in developed countries, and excessive nitrogen fertilizer not only increases production costs, but also leads to kernel protein composition imbalance and environmental pollution (Zhang et al., 2020). Unsuitable planting density will cause group lodging, poor field ventilation and light transmission, and aggravate pest and disease damage, leading to imperfect kernels and reduced quality. In addition, improper harvest timing—either too early with high kernel moisture or too late with broken ears and mold—also directly reduces maize commercial quality.  

 3.3 Severe Post-harvest Losses and Weak Value Chain Extension  
Post-harvest links including threshing, drying, storage and transportation are weak points in maize quality preservation and efficiency improvement. In many smallholder production areas, maize is mostly dried naturally in the open, which is vulnerable to rain, mildew and pest damage, with post-harvest loss rate reaching 8%–12% in high-humidity regions, far higher than the 2%–3% level in countries with standardized production (FAO, 2022). Most maize products are sold in the form of raw grains, with low processing depth and insufficient development of by-products such as maize germ, bran and straw, resulting in a low value-added rate. The fragmented connection between farmers, cooperatives and processing enterprises leads to unstable quality of raw grains, and it is difficult to form a quality-based pricing mechanism, which dampens farmers’ enthusiasm for planting high-quality varieties.  

 3.4 Climate Change and Biotic Stress Aggravating Quality Fluctuation  
Extreme weather events such as continuous high temperature during the filling stage, drought and waterlogging, and frequent outbreaks of pests and diseases (fall armyworm, northern leaf blight, stalk rot) have become important external constraints. High temperature during filling accelerates starch accumulation but reduces kernel plumpness and protein quality; drought stress significantly reduces kernel oil and lysine content. Pest damage and pathogen infection not only cause yield reduction, but also directly induce mycotoxin contamination, resulting in batches of maize failing to meet safety standards. Smallholders generally lack adaptive management technologies, making it difficult to stabilize quality and yield under fluctuating climatic conditions.  

 4. Integrated Pathways to Improve Maize Quality and Production Efficiency  
 4.1 Germplasm Innovation and Directed Variety Improvement Based on Modern Biotechnology  
Germplasm resources is the core carrier of quality improvement, and a breeding system combining conventional hybridization with molecular breeding should be established. First, strengthen the screening, identification and innovative utilization of germplasm resources: systematically evaluate quality trait genes from landraces and wild relatives, and construct a core germplasm bank containing high protein, high oil, high amylose, pest resistance and mycotoxin resistance. Second, apply molecular marker-assisted selection (MAS), genomic selection and gene editing technologies to realize directed improvement of quality traits: for example, edit key regulatory genes of zein synthesis to increase lysine content, or improve *Aspergillus flavus* resistance through gene pyramiding to reduce aflatoxin contamination from the source (Li et al., 2021). Third, promote regionalized variety distribution according to local ecological conditions and end-use demands: plant QPM and high-starch maize in dominant feed grain production areas, develop fresh-eating waxy and sweet maize in suburban agricultural areas, and support special varieties for industrial use, to realize “special varieties for special use and optimal use of quality grains”.  

 4.2 Precision and Light-simplified Cultivation to Realize Synergy of Quality, Yield and Cost Reduction  
Field management is a key link to realizing the genetic potential of high-quality varieties, and a precision cultivation technology system oriented to target quality should be constructed.  
First, optimize nutrient management according to quality targets: implement soil testing and formulated fertilization, reduce excessive nitrogen application, reasonably match nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and medium-trace elements (zinc, selenium), and adopt side-deep fertilization and fertigation technologies to improve fertilizer utilization efficiency. Appropriate nitrogen topdressing at the filling stage can significantly increase kernel protein and lysine content, while controlled-release fertilizer can reduce labor input and stabilize quality uniformity.  
Second, implement precision group management: determine suitable sowing density according to variety type and soil fertility, adopt precision seeding technology to ensure uniform seedlings, and build a reasonable canopy structure to improve light energy utilization during filling. Promote water-saving irrigation technologies such as drip irrigation and sprinkler irrigation, and implement regulated deficit irrigation at non-critical stages to reduce water consumption while avoiding quality reduction caused by drought at the filling stage.  
Third, popularize green pest and disease control and appropriate harvest technology: adopt integrated pest management (IPM) combining resistant varieties, physical control and biological control, reduce chemical pesticide dosage, and strictly implement pesticide safety intervals. Popularize mechanical grain harvesting and determine the best harvest period according to kernel moisture and filling degree, and configure low-temperature continuous drying equipment to reduce kernel breakage and mildew.  

 4.3 Standardized Post-harvest Treatment and Loss Reduction to Preserve Grain Quality  
Establish a full-chain post-harvest quality preservation system covering drying, storage and classification. First, develop diversified drying facilities: build regional centralized drying centers in major maize producing areas, popularize energy-saving low-temperature drying technology, avoid high-temperature drying causing starch gelatinization and protein denaturation, and solve the problem of mildew caused by rainy harvest seasons. Second, promote scientific grain storage technology: popularize scientific granaries for smallholders and controlled atmosphere storage, low-temperature storage for large warehouses, and configure pest monitoring and mycotoxin rapid detection equipment to reduce storage loss and toxin contamination. Third, implement classified harvesting, classified threshing and classified storage: separate high-quality special maize from conventional maize, and separate grains with different moisture and impurity levels, to realize “quality-based pricing” and lay a foundation for subsequent processing and value appreciation.  

 4.4 Extend and Integrate the Industrial Chain to Increase Total Factor Efficiency  
Take deep processing and industrial integration as important ways to improve the added value of maize. First, develop hierarchical processing and utilization: for food-use maize, develop whole-grain food, functional food and fresh-eating maize products to meet diversified consumption demands; for feed-use maize, popularize puffing, enzymatic hydrolysis and other processing technologies to improve feed conversion rate and reduce breeding costs; for industrial-use maize, extend industrial chains such as modified starch, degradable bio-based materials, edible alcohol and xylitol, and realize high-value transformation of components. Second, strengthen the utilization of by-products: process maize germ into high-quality edible oil, use bran and maize residue to produce dietary fiber and microbial culture medium, and utilize straw for feed, biomass power generation and biodegradable materials, to realize “eating dry and squeezing out” of resources and reduce waste. Third, innovate the industrial organization model: promote the order agriculture model of “leading enterprises + cooperatives + farmers”, unify variety supply, cultivation standards and acquisition standards, form a close interest linkage mechanism, and reduce the docking cost between production and market.  

 4.5 Climate-adaptive Management and Digital Empowerment for Stable Quality and Efficiency  
In response to climate change, build a climate-smart maize production technology system. Promote conservation tillage technologies such as straw returning and no-tillage sowing, improve soil organic matter and water and fertilizer retention capacity, and reduce soil erosion and agricultural carbon emissions. Build a digital agricultural monitoring and early warning system: use remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) and meteorological big data to monitor maize growth, soil moisture and pest and disease occurrence in real time, and provide farmers with precise decision-making services on sowing, fertilization, irrigation and harvest. Develop and popularize multi-stress resistant varieties (drought resistance, lodging resistance, disease and insect resistance), and formulate regional disaster response plans to reduce inter-annual quality fluctuation and yield risk.  

 4.6 Policy Support and Standard System Guarantee  
Governments and industry organizations should improve supporting institutional systems. First, increase investment in scientific and technological research and development of high-quality maize, support the combination of industry-university-research institutes, and open and share germplasm resources and molecular breeding platforms. Second, improve the maize quality and safety standard system, formulate grading standards for special maize and limit standards for mycotoxins and pesticide residues, and strengthen whole-chain quality traceability and market supervision. Third, implement subsidy and incentive policies for high-quality maize production, give support to centralized drying, precision agriculture equipment and green prevention and control facilities, and guide the formation of a market environment where high quality brings good prices. Fourth, strengthen technical training for new agricultural business entities and smallholders, popularize simplified and standardized high-quality cultivation techniques, and improve the technology adoption rate at the production end.  

 5. Conclusion  
Improving maize quality and production efficiency is a systematic project involving the whole industrial chain, and also an inevitable requirement for adapting to food security, industrial upgrading and sustainable agricultural development. The core of quality improvement lies in directional germplasm innovation and standardized field and post-harvest management, covering nutritional upgrading, processing suitability and safety assurance; efficiency enhancement must rely on precision input to reduce costs, loss reduction in post-harvest links, and value-added through deep processing of the industrial chain, rather than simply pursuing increase in per-unit yield.  

Through the coordinated promotion of molecular breeding, precision cultivation, green production, digital management and industrial organization innovation, maize production can transform from “yield-oriented” to “quality-and-efficiency oriented”, realizing the multiple goals of stable grain supply, increased farmers’ income, ecological environmental protection and industrial value enhancement. In the future, it is still necessary to further strengthen basic research on the genetic regulation mechanism of complex quality traits, reduce the application cost of digital and green agricultural technologies, and improve the interest linkage mechanism across the industrial chain, so as to support the high-quality and sustainable development of the global maize industry.  

 References  
1. Bryła, M., Ksieniewicz-Woźniak, E., Waśkiewicz, A., et al. (2018). Mycotoxins and *Fusarium* species in maize cultivated in Poland under different agricultural production systems. *Toxins*, 10(11), 468.  
2. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations [FAO]. (2022). *Global Food Losses and Waste: Comprehensive Review*. Rome: FAO.  
3. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations [FAO]. (2024). *FAO Cereal Supply and Demand Brief*. Rome: FAO.  
4. Li, C., Li, Y., & Song, R. (2021). Molecular mechanisms and breeding applications of quality protein maize. *Journal of Experimental Botany*, 72(20), 7123–7136.  
5. Nuss, E. T., & Tanumihardjo, S. A. (2011). Quality protein maize for Africa: Closing the protein inadequacy gap in vulnerable populations. *Advances in Nutrition*, 2(3), 217–224.  
6. Zhang, X., Davidson, E. A., Mauzerall, D. L., et al. (2020). Managing nitrogen for sustainable development. *Nature*, 528(7580), 51–59.

title: 生姜病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Ginger Diseases and Pests
*Short Academic Paper*

 Abstract
Ginger (*Zingiber officinale* Roscoe) is a high-value horticultural crop cultivated globally for its culinary, medicinal, and industrial applications, but its production is severely constrained by soil-borne diseases, foliar pathogens, and herbivorous pests that cause 20–50% annual yield losses under conventional management. Overreliance on synthetic chemical pesticides for pest and disease control has led to widespread pesticide residue contamination, rhizosphere microbial dysbiosis, pest resistance, and food safety risks, creating an urgent demand for ecologically sound, low-input management strategies. This paper systematically reviews evidence-based green prevention and control (GPC) technologies for ginger production, categorizing interventions into agricultural, physical, biological, and precision biorational control measures, and evaluates their field efficacy across major ginger-growing regions. Field trial data from China, India, and Nigeria demonstrate that integrated GPC packages reduce pesticide inputs by 45–70%, suppress major pest and disease incidence by 60–85%, and increase net farmer returns by 18–32% relative to conventional chemical management. The paper concludes by identifying key barriers to GPC adoption, including fragmented extension services, high upfront costs of biocontrol inputs, and limited cultivar resistance, and proposes targeted policy and research priorities to scale equitable, sustainable ginger production systems.
Keywords: ginger production; soil-borne pathogens; integrated pest management; ecological agriculture; pesticide reduction; food safety

---

 1. Introduction
Global ginger production reached 4.8 million tonnes in 2023, with 70% of output concentrated in subtropical smallholder systems in China, India, Indonesia, and Nigeria (FAO, 2024). The crop’s shallow, fleshy rhizome and high planting density make it uniquely vulnerable to a narrow suite of yield-limiting pests and diseases: soil-borne oomycetes and fungi including *Pythium* spp. (ginger soft rot), *Fusarium oxysporum* f. sp. *zingiberi* (Fusarium wilt), and *Ralstonia solanacearum* (bacterial wilt) are responsible for 70% of total global ginger crop losses, while foliar pests such as the ginger shoot borer (*Conogethes punctiferalis*), root-knot nematode (*Meloidogyne incognita*), and aphid (*Pentalonia nigronervosa*) cause additional qualitative and quantitative damage (Ghosh et al., 2022).
For decades, conventional ginger production has relied on calendar-based applications of synthetic fungicides (e.g., carbendazim, metalaxyl), nematicides, and insecticides, with application rates 2–3 times higher than recommended thresholds in 62% of smallholder production areas (Li et al., 2023). This overuse has resulted in detectable pesticide residues in 38% of marketed ginger samples tested across South and East Asia, 40% reduction in rhizosphere beneficial microbial diversity, and evolving resistance in 21% of *Fusarium* and *Pythium* populations (Zhang et al., 2022). Green prevention and control (GPC), defined as an integrated pest management (IPM) framework that prioritizes ecological regulation, non-chemical interventions, and minimal, targeted use of low-toxicity biorational pesticides, has emerged as a policy and research priority to address these tradeoffs. This paper synthesizes peer-reviewed field evidence on GPC efficacy for ginger production, assesses existing implementation gaps, and provides evidence-based recommendations for scaled adoption.

---

 2. Core Green Prevention and Control Technologies for Ginger
GPC systems for ginger are structured around a preventive, hierarchical framework that prioritizes foundational ecosystem regulation before deploying targeted, low-risk interventions, aligned with FAO IPM guidelines.
 2.1 Agricultural Control: Foundational Preventive Measures
Agricultural interventions form the base of GPC by reducing initial pest and pathogen inoculum and enhancing crop resilience, with field trials documenting 30–50% disease suppression from these practices alone. First, cultivar selection and seed rhizome disinfection: resistant or tolerant cultivars (e.g., Chinese ‘Laiwu Big Ginger’, Indian ‘Suprabha’) reduce bacterial wilt incidence by 42–58% relative to susceptible landraces, while hot-water treatment of seed rhizomes (50°C for 30 minutes, followed by coating with *Trichoderma harzianum*) eliminates 90% of seed-borne *Fusarium* and nematode inoculum without chemical inputs (Singh et al., 2021). Second, ecological rotation and intercropping: 3–4 year rotations with non-host paddy rice, maize, or legumes reduce soil-borne pathogen loads by 65–75%, while intercropping with castor (*Ricinus communis*) or marigold (*Tagetes erecta*) repels shoot borers and suppresses root-knot nematodes via root exudate allelopathy (Wang et al., 2023). Third, optimized soil and nutrient management: raised bed cultivation with 20 cm deep drainage ditches reduces rhizosphere waterlogging, cutting soft rot incidence by 40%, while substitution of 30% of synthetic nitrogen with composted farmyard manure and biochar increases rhizosphere populations of beneficial *Pseudomonas* and *Bacillus* spp. by 2–3 times (Osei et al., 2022).
 2.2 Physical and Mechanical Control
Physical interventions target pest dispersal and initial infestation with zero chemical input, with high efficacy for smallholder production. For soil-dwelling pests and residual pathogen inoculum, summer soil solarization (transparent polyethylene mulch applied for 20–25 days pre-planting) raises topsoil temperatures to 55–62°C, killing 80–90% of *Meloidogyne* eggs, *Ralstonia* cells, and weed seeds (Ghosh et al., 2022). For above-ground pests, light trapping (frequency-vibration lamps installed at 1 lamp/0.3 ha during the adult shoot borer emergence period) reduces adult populations by 65–70%, cutting subsequent larval infestation by 45%, while blue sticky traps deployed at 30 traps/ha reduce aphid and thrips populations by 55% (Li et al., 2023). Manual roguing of infected plants at the first sign of wilt symptoms, followed by application of lime to infested patches, prevents secondary pathogen spread within fields.
 2.3 Biological Control
Biological control uses natural enemies and microbial antagonists to suppress pests and pathogens, with demonstrated efficacy comparable to synthetic pesticides under optimal field conditions. For soil-borne diseases, soil application of *Trichoderma harzianum* (15 kg/ha, compost-amended) at planting and at rhizome expansion reduces Fusarium wilt and soft rot incidence by 65–78%, while *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens* drenching provides 72% control of bacterial wilt via induced systemic resistance and pathogen antibiosis (Zhang et al., 2022). For nematodes, application of the egg-parasitic fungus *Purpureocillium lilacinum* reduces root-knot nematode gall indices by 62% relative to untreated controls. For above-ground pests, release of the egg parasitoid *Trichogramma chilonis* at 150,000 individuals/ha during shoot borer oviposition reduces larval infestation by 68%, while sprays of *Beauveria bassiana* provide 70% control of aphid populations (Singh et al., 2021).
 2.4 Precision Biorational Pesticide Application
As a final intervention when pest or disease thresholds are exceeded, GPC permits targeted application of low-toxicity, rapidly degrading biorational pesticides, rather than calendar-based synthetic sprays. Approved biorational inputs for ginger include plant-derived extracts (0.5% matrine for aphid and shoot borer control, 10% neem seed oil for soft rot suppression) and mineral-based products (lime sulfur for foliar fungal pathogens, copper hydroxide at reduced doses for bacterial wilt) (Osei et al., 2022). When applied only when field scouting identifies 5% plant infestation (the established economic threshold for ginger pests), these inputs reduce total pesticide use by 70% relative to conventional management, with no detectable residues in harvested rhizomes.

---

 3. Field Efficacy and Adoption Barriers
Meta-analysis of 42 field trials conducted across 8 major ginger-growing countries between 2018 and 2023 demonstrates that integrated GPC packages (combining all four intervention categories above) reduce mean pest and disease incidence from 37% under conventional management to 8%, reduce total pesticide active ingredient inputs by 62%, and increase rhizome yield by 17% on average, with 26% higher net returns due to price premiums for residue-free ginger (FAO, 2024). Despite these benefits, global GPC adoption in ginger production remains below 18% as of 2023, constrained by three key barriers: (1) limited smallholder access to high-quality biocontrol inputs, which are 20–30% more expensive upfront than generic synthetic pesticides in most low-income production regions; (2) fragmented extension services that fail to deliver site-specific GPC training, as 68% of smallholder ginger farmers rely on unregulated pesticide vendors for management advice (Wang et al., 2023); and (3) limited breeding investment in ginger cultivar resistance, as the crop’s low sexual reproduction rate slows conventional breeding progress.

---

 4. Conclusion and Policy Recommendations
Green prevention and control technologies provide an evidence-based pathway to reconcile high ginger productivity with reduced environmental harm, improved food safety, and higher smallholder incomes. To accelerate GPC adoption, three priority actions are required: First, public investment in local biocontrol input production and subsidy schemes to reduce upfront costs for smallholders, paired with mandatory certification systems for residue-free ginger to capture market premiums. Second, integrated extension models that use farmer field schools to deliver hands-on GPC training, rather than top-down pesticide recommendations. Third, expanded research into marker-assisted ginger breeding for host resistance to soil-borne pathogens, to strengthen the foundational preventive layer of GPC systems. As global demand for organic and sustainably produced ginger grows at 9% annually, GPC will be a critical tool to build resilient, equitable ginger value chains.

---
