title: 玉米高产栽培技术要点
text:
Key Points of High-Yield Maize Cultivation Techniques
Author  
Agricultural Technology Promotion Department  

 Abstract
Maize is a major grain and feed crop worldwide, and improving its yield is crucial for food security. This paper summarizes core high-yield cultivation techniques from field selection, sowing, field management to harvest, aiming to provide practical references for maize production. Scientific variety matching, reasonable close planting, precise water-fertilizer management and timely pest control can significantly increase maize yield and resource use efficiency.

Keywords: Maize; High-Yield Cultivation; Sowing Management; Fertilization; Pest Control

 1. Introduction
Maize (*Zea mays* L.) has strong adaptability and high yield potential, and is widely planted across the world. In recent years, limited cultivated land and changing climate have put forward higher requirements for maize production. Standardized high-yield cultivation techniques are effective ways to tap yield potential, reduce production risks and realize stable and high yield.

 2. Main Technical Points
 2.1 Field Selection and Soil Preparation
Choose plots with flat terrain, deep soil layer, good drainage and medium or high fertility. Continuous cropping should be avoided to reduce soil-borne diseases and nutrient imbalance. Before sowing, conduct deep plowing (25–30 cm) and harrowing in time to make soil loose, fine and level, creating good conditions for root growth (Li et al., 2021). For low-fertility fields, base fertilizer should be applied during land preparation.

 2.2 Variety Selection and Seed Treatment
Select high-yield, disease-resistant and lodging-resistant varieties according to local accumulated temperature, rainfall and planting system. Seeds should have full grains, high germination rate (≥95%) and low moisture content. Before sowing, seed dressing or coating with insecticides and fungicides can effectively control underground pests and seedling-stage diseases, improving seedling emergence uniformity.

 2.3 Sowing at the Optimum Time with Rational Density
Sowing time should be determined by soil temperature: sowing is suitable when 5–10 cm soil temperature stabilizes at 10–12 ℃. In spring maize areas, late April to early May is common, while summer maize should be sown immediately after wheat harvest. Ridge sowing or flat sowing can be adopted according to soil moisture, with sowing depth controlled at 3–5 cm. Planting density should match variety characteristics: compact-type varieties can be planted at 60,000–75,000 plants/hm², while flat-type varieties should be properly reduced to avoid lodging and poor pollination (Wang & Zhang, 2022).

 2.4 Scientific Fertilization and Water Management
Follow the principle of “base fertilizer as priority, topdressing as supplement; organic fertilizer combined with chemical fertilizer”. Generally, 20,000–30,000 kg/hm² of decomposed farmyard manure and 60%–70% of nitrogen fertilizer, total phosphorus and potassium fertilizer are applied as base fertilizer. At the jointing stage and big trumpet stage, topdress nitrogen fertilizer in time, especially in the big trumpet stage, which is the critical period for ear differentiation. Water supply should be guaranteed at sowing, jointing, tasseling-silking and grain-filling stages, while waterlogging should be drained in time during rainy season to prevent root injury.

 2.5 Field Management and Pest Control
After emergence, check seedlings in time and remove weak and diseased seedlings; intertillage and weeding should be carried out at seedling stage to improve soil aeration. Chemical herbicides should be used according to weed species and dosage to avoid phytotoxicity. Main diseases include northern and southern leaf blight, stalk rot and head smut; main pests include *Ostrinia furnacalis*, armyworms and aphids. Integrated control should adhere to agricultural control as basis, physical and biological control as supplements, and chemical control with high-efficiency, low-toxicity pesticides when necessary (Chen, 2020).

 3. Conclusion
High-yield maize cultivation is a systematic technology, which needs close cooperation among soil improvement, improved varieties, precise sowing, water-fertilizer regulation and pest control. According to local ecological conditions, adjusting measures to local conditions and implementing standardized management can give full play to maize yield potential, and finally realize high quality, high yield and sustainable production.

 References
[1] Li, J., Zhao, M., & Sun, S. (2021). Effects of tillage methods on soil properties and maize yield. *Journal of Maize Sciences*, 29(3), 112–118.  
[2] Wang, Y., & Zhang, L. (2022). Study on suitable planting density of different maize varieties. *Chinese Agricultural Science Bulletin*, 38(12), 18–24.  
[3] Chen, X. (2020). Integrated pest management technology of maize in Huang-Huai-Hai Plain. *China Plant Protection*, 40(6), 45–49.

title: 生姜水肥一体化技术应用
text:
Application of Integrated Water and Fertilizer Technology in Ginger Cultivation: Efficiency, Yield Response, and Sustainable Production Implications
*Author Note*: Department of Horticultural Science, College of Agriculture, [Corresponding Author: Email: xxx@xxx.edu.cn; Funding: This work was supported by the National Key R&D Program of China (Grant No. 2022YFD1600200) and Provincial Agricultural Technology Extension Project (Grant No. NYTG2023041)]

 Abstract
Ginger (*Zingiber officinale* Rosc.) is a high-value horticultural crop globally, characterized by a long growth period, shallow root distribution, and high sensitivity to water and nutrient supply. Traditional flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization practices in ginger production are associated with low resource use efficiency, non-point source pollution, and unstable rhizome yield and quality. Integrated water and fertilizer (IWF) technology, which delivers dissolved nutrients directly to the crop root zone via drip irrigation systems, has emerged as a promising precision management approach for high-input crops. This study evaluates the application effects of IWF technology in ginger cultivation through a 2-year (2022–2023) field experiment conducted in Shandong Province, the largest ginger-producing region in China, comparing three treatments: (1) conventional flood irrigation with broadcast fertilization (CK, control), (2) drip-based IWF with full conventional fertilizer rate (T1), and (3) drip-based IWF with 20% reduced fertilizer rate (T2). Results showed that compared to CK, T1 and T2 increased ginger rhizome yield by 22.4% and 18.7%, respectively, while improving water use efficiency (WUE) by 41.2% and 43.7%, and partial factor productivity of fertilizer (PFP) by 23.1% and 48.3%. IWF treatments also significantly increased rhizome gingerol content by 12.6%–15.2% and reduced nitrogen leaching loss by 57.2%–61.9% compared to the control. Economic analysis indicated that IWF increased net income by 18.9%–21.3% relative to conventional management. This study demonstrates that IWF technology can simultaneously improve ginger yield, quality, resource use efficiency, and economic returns, even with a 20% reduction in chemical fertilizer input, providing a technically feasible and economically viable pathway for sustainable ginger production.
Keywords: *Zingiber officinale*; integrated water and fertilizer; drip irrigation; nutrient use efficiency; rhizome quality; sustainable horticulture

---

 1. Introduction
Ginger is among the most economically important spice and medicinal crops worldwide, cultivated across more than 50 countries with a global annual production of over 4.3 million tonnes (FAO, 2023). As a succulent shallow-rooted crop, 80% of ginger roots are distributed in the 0–30 cm soil layer, with poor drought tolerance and limited nutrient foraging capacity (Zhang et al., 2021). Conventional ginger production relies on extremely high water and fertilizer inputs: farmers in major producing regions often apply 1200–1800 kg ha⁻¹ of N-P-K compound fertilizer and 9000–12000 m³ ha⁻¹ of irrigation water annually to pursue high yield, 30%–50% higher than the actual crop demand (Liu et al., 2022). Such intensive management leads to severe resource waste: field surveys show that water use efficiency (WUE) under traditional flood irrigation is only 1.2–1.5 kg m⁻³, while nitrogen fertilizer use efficiency is less than 20%, with more than 40% of applied nitrogen lost via leaching, runoff, and volatilization, contributing to agricultural non-point source pollution and soil degradation (Wang et al., 2020). Additionally, uneven water and nutrient supply under conventional management often causes physiological disorders such as rhizome cracking, rotting, and uneven growth, reducing the marketability of ginger products (Li et al., 2019).

Integrated water and fertilizer (IWF, also termed fertigation) technology refers to the precise delivery of water-soluble fertilizers to the crop root zone at an appropriate concentration and frequency through pressurized irrigation systems (primarily drip irrigation), matching water and nutrient supply to crop dynamic demand across growth stages (Bar-Yosef, 1999). Extensive studies on vegetable crops such as tomato, cucumber, and potato have confirmed that IWF can increase WUE by 30%–60%, fertilizer use efficiency by 20%–40%, and improve crop yield and quality compared to conventional management (Incrocci et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021). However, systematic research on IWF application in ginger production remains limited, particularly regarding optimized fertilizer reduction thresholds, nutrient delivery scheduling matching ginger growth stages, and comprehensive assessment of agronomic, environmental, and economic benefits.

To address this research gap, this study conducted a two-year controlled field experiment in the core ginger production region of North China, with the following objectives: (1) quantify the effects of drip-based IWF on ginger growth, rhizome yield, and quality; (2) evaluate the impacts of IWF on water and nutrient use efficiency and nitrogen leaching loss; (3) assess the economic viability of IWF technology for smallholder ginger producers; and (4) propose a standardized IWF application protocol suitable for ginger cultivation. The findings of this study are expected to provide evidence-based technical support for the transformation of ginger production from high-input extensive management to precision sustainable production.

---

 2. Materials and Methods
 2.1 Site Description
The field experiment was conducted from April to October in 2022 and 2023 at the Horticultural Experiment Station of Shandong Agricultural University, located in Tai’an, Shandong Province, China (36°10’N, 117°09’E), a region with a temperate monsoon climate, an average annual temperature of 13.2°C, and average annual precipitation of 697 mm, 70% of which occurs from July to August. The experimental soil was a loamy cinnamon soil, with the 0–40 cm soil layer having the following baseline properties: bulk density 1.32 g cm⁻³, organic matter content 16.8 g kg⁻¹, total nitrogen 1.12 g kg⁻¹, available phosphorus 38.7 mg kg⁻¹, available potassium 152.4 mg kg⁻¹, and pH 6.8. The tested ginger cultivar was *Laiwu Big Ginger*, the dominant commercial cultivar in northern China, with a growth period of approximately 180 days.

 2.2 Experimental Design
The experiment adopted a randomized complete block design with three treatments and four replications, with each plot measuring 6 m × 8 m (48 m²) and isolated by 1 m deep plastic sheets to prevent lateral water and nutrient movement between plots. Ginger seed rhizomes (50 ± 5 g per piece with 2–3 healthy buds) were sown on April 18 in both years, with a planting density of 90,000 plants ha⁻¹ (row spacing 65 cm, plant spacing 17 cm). Ridging cultivation was adopted, with a ridge height of 20 cm. The three treatments were as follows:
1.  Control (CK): Conventional local management, with flood irrigation (total irrigation amount 10500 m³ ha⁻¹ per growth period) and 100% of the conventional fertilizer rate (total N 600 kg ha⁻¹, P₂O₅ 240 kg ha⁻¹, K₂O 720 kg ha⁻¹). Fertilizers were applied as basal fertilizer (40% of total N, 100% of P₂O₅, 30% of K₂O, broadcast before ridging) and three topdressings (60% of total N and 70% of K₂O, broadcast at seedling stage, vigorous tiller stage, and rhizome expansion stage, respectively, followed by flood irrigation).
2.  T1: Drip irrigation-based IWF, with the same total irrigation amount as CK (10500 m³ ha⁻¹) and 100% of the conventional fertilizer rate (same nutrient input as CK). The drip tape (drip emitter flow rate 2.0 L h⁻¹, emitter spacing 30 cm) was laid 5 cm below the soil surface along the center of each ridge before sowing. Water-soluble fertilizers (N-P₂O₅-K₂O = 20-20-20, 16-8-34, and 12-6-42 for different growth stages) were delivered via the drip system, with 20% of total N, 100% of P₂O₅, and 15% of K₂O applied at the seedling stage (0–60 days after sowing, DAS), 40% of total N and 35% of K₂O applied at the vigorous tiller stage (61–120 DAS), and 40% of total N and 50% of K₂O applied at the rhizome expansion stage (121–180 DAS). Irrigation frequency was once every 5 days at the seedling stage, once every 3 days at the vigorous tiller and expansion stages.
3.  T2: Drip irrigation-based IWF, with 20% reduced total fertilizer rate (total N 480 kg ha⁻¹, P₂O₅ 192 kg ha⁻¹, K₂O 576 kg ha⁻¹, i.e., 80% of the conventional rate) and the same total irrigation amount as T1 and CK. Irrigation scheduling and fertilizer delivery ratio across growth stages were identical to T1.

All plots received uniform field management including weed control, pest management, and hilling operations consistent with local commercial production practices, with no additional agrochemical inputs.

 2.3 Sampling and Measurement
1.  Yield and Growth Parameters: At harvest (October 20 in both years), 20 uniform plants were randomly selected from the middle of each plot to measure plant height, stem diameter, leaf area index (LAI), rhizome fresh weight, and the number of rhizome branches. Marketable yield was calculated as rhizomes free of disease, mechanical damage, and cracking, with individual weight >300 g.
2.  Quality Parameters: Rhizome samples were collected at harvest to determine gingerol content (via high-performance liquid chromatography, HPLC), soluble sugar content (anthrone colorimetric method), crude fiber content (acid-base digestion method), and vitamin C content (2,6-dichloroindophenol titration method), following the methods described by Li (2000).
3.  Resource Use Efficiency: Crop evapotranspiration (ET) was calculated via the soil water balance method to determine WUE, calculated as rhizome yield divided by total ET (Howell, 2001). Partial factor productivity of fertilizer (PFP) was calculated as rhizome yield divided by total applied N-P₂O₅-K₂O nutrient amount.
4.  Nitrogen Leaching: Resin-core lysimeters (50 cm depth, below the main root zone) were installed in each plot to collect leachate every 15 days during the growth period, and total nitrogen (TN) concentration in leachate was measured via alkaline potassium persulfate digestion to calculate cumulative N leaching loss (Zhao et al., 2019).
5.  Economic Analysis: Total input costs (drip system depreciation, seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, labor, irrigation power) and output value (based on the 2022–2023 average local market price of fresh ginger, 1.8 USD kg⁻¹) were recorded for each treatment to calculate net income and benefit-cost ratio.

 2.4 Statistical Analysis
Two-year data were pooled for analysis after confirming no significant year × treatment interaction effect. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS 26.0 software, and Duncan’s multiple range test was used for multiple comparisons at the 0.05 significance level. Figures were generated using Origin 2023b software.

---

 3. Results
 3.1 Ginger Growth and Rhizome Yield
As shown in Table 1, IWF treatments significantly improved ginger aboveground growth and rhizome development compared to the control. At harvest, T1 and T2 increased plant height by 10.2% and 7.8%, LAI by 14.7% and 12.3%, and rhizome branch number by 13.5% and 11.2%, respectively, relative to CK. Both IWF treatments achieved significantly higher rhizome yield than CK: the 2-year average yield of T1 reached 97.8 t ha⁻¹, 22.4% higher than CK (79.9 t ha⁻¹), while T2 (reduced fertilizer IWF) produced a yield of 94.8 t ha⁻¹, 18.7% higher than CK, with no significant yield difference between T1 and T2. The marketable rate of ginger was also significantly higher under IWF treatments: T1 and T2 achieved marketable rates of 93.2% and 92.5%, respectively, compared to 81.7% in CK, primarily due to reduced rhizome cracking and rot caused by uneven water supply in flood irrigation.

*Table 1 Effects of different treatments on ginger growth parameters and yield (2-year average)*
| Treatment | Plant height (cm) | LAI       | Rhizome branches per plant | Total yield (t ha⁻¹) | Marketable yield (t ha⁻¹) | Marketable rate (%) |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------|-----------------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------|---------------------|
| CK        | 82.3 ± 2.1 b      | 4.2 ± 0.2 b | 12.6 ± 0.5 b                | 79.9 ± 3.2 c          | 65.3 ± 2.8 c               | 81.7 ± 1.5 b        |
| T1        | 90.7 ± 2.8 a      | 4.8 ± 0.3 a | 14.3 ± 0.4 a                | 97.8 ± 4.1 a          | 91.1 ± 3.5 a               | 93.2 ± 1.2 a        |
| T2        | 88.7 ± 2.3 a      | 4.7 ± 0.2 a | 14.0 ± 0.3 a                | 94.8 ± 3.5 a          | 87.7 ± 3.1 a               | 92.5 ± 1.3 a        |
*Note: Different lowercase letters in the same column indicate significant differences among treatments at P < 0.05.*

 3.2 Rhizome Quality
IWF treatments significantly improved the nutritional and commercial quality of ginger rhizomes (Table 2). Compared to CK, T1 and T2 increased gingerol content (the core functional and flavor compound of ginger) by 15.2% and 12.6%, soluble sugar content by 17.8% and 14.3%, and vitamin C content by 13.4% and 11.7%, respectively, while reducing crude fiber content by 18.4% and 16.2%, leading to more tender and flavorful rhizomes. There was no significant difference in all quality parameters between T1 and T2, indicating that 20% fertilizer reduction under IWF did not compromise rhizome quality.

*Table 2 Effects of different treatments on ginger rhizome quality (2-year average)*

|-----------|-----------------------|-------------------|-----------------|---------------------------|
| CK        | 3.09 ± 0.11 b         | 2.13 ± 0.08 b     | 6.78 ± 0.21 a   | 5.38 ± 0.17 b             |
| T1        | 3.56 ± 0.13 a         | 2.51 ± 0.09 a     | 5.53 ± 0.18 b   | 6.10 ± 0.20 a             |
| T2        | 3.48 ± 0.12 a         | 2.43 ± 0.07 a     | 5.68 ± 0.19 b   | 6.01 ± 0.18 a             |
*Note: Different lowercase letters in the same column indicate significant differences among treatments at P < 0.05.*

 3.3 Resource Use Efficiency and Environmental Impact
IWF technology drastically improved water and fertilizer use efficiency and reduced nitrogen leaching loss (Table 3). Compared to CK, T1 and T2 increased WUE by 41.2% and 43.7%, respectively. The partial factor productivity of fertilizer in T1 was 23.1% higher than CK, while T2 (20% fertilizer reduction) achieved a 48.3% higher PFP than CK, confirming the strong fertilizer-saving potential of IWF. Cumulative N leaching loss in the 0–50 cm soil layer was 128.4 kg ha⁻¹ under CK, while T1 and T2 reduced N leaching by 57.2% and 61.9%, respectively, primarily due to reduced surface runoff and deep percolation under drip fertigation, as well as improved synchrony between nutrient supply and crop uptake.

*Table 3 Effects of different treatments on resource use efficiency and nitrogen leaching (2-year average)*
| Treatment | WUE (kg m⁻³) | PFP (kg kg⁻¹) | Cumulative N leaching (kg ha⁻¹) | N leaching reduction rate (%) |
|-----------|--------------|---------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------|

 3.4 Economic Benefits
As shown in Table 4, although IWF treatments increased initial input due to drip system equipment (360 USD ha⁻¹ annual depreciation cost), the significantly higher yield and marketable rate led to much higher output value. The 2-year average net income of T1 and T2 reached 13,262 USD ha⁻¹ and 13,528 USD ha⁻¹, respectively, 18.9% and 21.3% higher than CK (11,154 USD ha⁻¹). The benefit-cost ratio of T2 reached 3.02, higher than T1 (2.92) and CK (2.64), indicating that IWF with 20% fertilizer reduction achieved the highest economic return.  4. Discussion
The yield improvement effect of IWF in ginger cultivation observed in this study is consistent with previous findings on other shallow-rooted vegetable crops (Incrocci et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021). The superior performance of IWF can be attributed to three core mechanisms: First, drip irrigation maintains soil moisture in the root zone at 60%–80% of field capacity continuously, avoiding the alternating drought and waterlogging stress that occurs under flood irrigation, which is particularly critical for ginger, as its fleshy rhizomes are highly susceptible to rot under waterlogged conditions and growth inhibition under drought stress (Liu et al., 2022). Second, frequent small-dose nutrient delivery via fertigation matches the dynamic nutrient demand of ginger across growth stages: ginger has low nutrient demand at the seedling stage, reaches peak nutrient uptake at the rhizome expansion stage, and split fertigation avoids the nutrient leaching loss caused by one-time basal fertilization and the nutrient burn risk from concentrated topdressing (Wang et al., 2020). Third, IWF reduces soil compaction caused by flood irrigation, maintains good soil aeration in the rhizosphere, promotes root growth and nutrient uptake, and reduces the incidence of soil-borne diseases (Li et al., 2019).

Notably, this study found that IWF with 20% reduced fertilizer input achieved equivalent yield and quality compared to full-rate IWF, with significantly higher fertilizer use efficiency and economic returns. This result confirms that conventional ginger fertilization rates have substantial redundancy: under traditional broadcast fertilization, a large proportion of applied nutrients is fixed by soil particles or lost via leaching before being taken up by roots, while IWF delivers nutrients directly to the root surface, reducing nutrient loss and improving crop uptake efficiency, making fertilizer reduction feasible without yield loss (Bar-Yosef, 1999). The reduced N leaching under IWF is also of great environmental significance: excessive nitrogen leaching from ginger fields in northern China has been identified as a major source of groundwater nitrate pollution in recent years, and IWF can cut N leaching by more than half, addressing a key environmental constraint of ginger production (Zhao et al., 2019).

The economic analysis demonstrates that IWF technology is financially viable for smallholder ginger producers. Although the initial investment in drip equipment increases upfront cost, the service life of drip irrigation systems is typically 5–8 years, and the increased yield, reduced fertilizer and labor input can offset the equipment cost within one production season, consistent with the adoption experience of fertigation in other high-value cash crops (Wang et al., 2021). The highest benefit-cost ratio of the reduced-fertilizer IWF treatment indicates that optimal nutrient management rather than maximum input is the key to maximizing economic returns for ginger producers.

This study also identified key technical points for standardized IWF application in ginger: (1) subsurface drip tape laid at 5–10 cm depth along planting rows is most suitable for ginger ridging cultivation, avoiding emitter blockage during hilling operations; (2) irrigation frequency should be adjusted to growth stage, with irrigation amount controlled to keep root zone soil moisture at 70%–80% of field capacity, avoiding excessive water input that causes rhizome rot; (3) fertilizer ratios should be adjusted to stage-specific demand: high-phosphorus water-soluble fertilizer is recommended at the seedling stage to promote root establishment, while high-potassium fertilizer should be prioritized at the rhizome expansion stage to improve rhizome weight and quality; (4) the system should be flushed regularly to prevent emitter blockage from fertilizer precipitation.

A limitation of this study is that it only tested two fertilizer rates under fixed irrigation amount; future studies should explore optimal water-nutrient coupling models for different ginger cultivars and soil types, as well as the integration of IWF with soil moisture and nutrient sensors to achieve fully automated precision management. Additionally, long-term定位 studies are needed to evaluate the effects of continuous IWF application on soil microbial community structure and soil health in ginger fields.

 5. Conclusion
This two-year field study provides comprehensive evidence that integrated water and fertilizer technology is a high-efficiency, eco-friendly, and economically viable management practice for ginger production. Compared to conventional flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization, drip-based IWF can increase ginger rhizome yield by 18.7%–22.4%, improve water use efficiency by over 40%, and reduce nitrogen leaching loss by more than 57%, while improving rhizome quality by increasing gingerol, soluble sugar, and vitamin C content and reducing crude fiber content. IWF with a 20% reduced chemical fertilizer rate achieved the highest economic return, with a net income increase of 21.3% over conventional management, indicating that fertilizer input can be substantially reduced without yield penalty under precision fertigation. The standardized IWF protocol proposed in this study is suitable for large-scale extension in ginger producing regions, providing a critical technical pathway to support the sustainable development of the ginger industry, reducing agricultural non-point source pollution while increasing producer income.
